# The Programme-Objective Approach: Set a Quantified Goal First, and the Work Needed to Reach It Is the Strategy

**What it is** — "The basis of programming is the programme-objective approach, in accordance with which the contents, volume and organisation of training loads are determined by the *objectives* of the preparation (see Fig 6.8). The objectives consist of three main components: the desired improvement in performance; the appropriate changes in technical-tactical, psychological and competition preparedness; the necessary modification of special physical preparedness" (italics in the original; PDF p. 379 / printed p. 368, checked against the page image). "In practice, the selection of a programming strategy is performed by means of a logical 'if-then' approach... if one sets a specific and quantitatively defined goal, then the precise work and methods necessary to accomplish this goal constitute the appropriate strategy."

Two framing points on the same page:
- **Construction aims at economy.** Construction "involves regulating its contents to provide the effective use of loading of different primary emphasis, i.e. the organisation of the contents over time, so that the required training effect occurs with a minimal expenditure of energy" (6.12.1). Two categories of construction follow: "one based on structural organisation and the other on time management" (how loads of different emphasis are combined, and how loading is regulated within cycles and stages).
- **Level is harder than timing.** Closing section 6.11, just above the 6.12 heading: "The art of controlling the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state consists, firstly, of achieving the necessary level of conditioning and, secondly, achieving it at the required time, as dictated by the competition calendar. Research shows that achievement of the second requirement is not especially complex. However, the probability of successfully achieving the first requirement is much smaller" (PDF p. 379).

**Why it works** — The authors present it as logic rather than evidence: a quantified target makes the required work derivable. Fig 6.8, which they cite, is outside this batch. No study is cited for the claim that reaching the level is harder than timing it.

**When to apply** — Starting any plan by writing the performance target and the changes in technical and physical preparedness it requires, with numbers, before choosing exercises or a periodisation model. The eight-step sequence of 6.15 is the operational version ([[framework--eight-step-sequence-for-programming-annual-training]]). Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 32, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)). Inference: the if-then rule is the planning counterpart of Eric's testing rule, since each training element has to trace back to a stated objective.

**When NOT to apply** — The approach assumes the goal can be "quantitatively defined" and the work to reach it is known; in team sports the outcome (winning) is not a single measurable performance, and the authors do not address that. The "level is harder than timing" sentence is the authors' summary of unnamed research ("Research shows"); no study is named, so treat it as their view.

**Example** — The authors give no worked example on this page. Inference: a coach sets "standing triple jump from 9.2 m to 9.6 m by the June championship" and then derives the jump, strength and technique work and its timing from that target, rather than starting from a favourite weekly template.

# Complex (Concurrent) Training Suits Beginners and Average Athletes; for Highly Qualified Athletes the Authors Favour Single-Emphasis Workouts, Microcycles and Stages

**What it is** — The authors define the two ways of organising training: "Complex loading involves prescription of multi-faceted training regimes to achieve several different fitness objectives over the same period, whereas the concentrated loading method concentrates for a given period on producing a single major specific fitness quality via the use of a unidirectional regime of training" (PDF p. 379 / printed p. 368). "For instance, a complex workout might comprise resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting; a complex microcycle (typically a week) might employ those same training means on different days or during different sessions on the same day." Using complex means requires knowing how the means interact through "the acute and delayed after-effects of each" (PDF p. 379).

Their case against complex training for top athletes (PDF pp. 380-381 / printed pp. 369-370, all pages checked against the images):
- **The supporting research is old and used weak athletes.** The early studies (Krestovnikov, 1951; Letunov et al., 1954; Zimkin, 1956; Korobkov et al, 1960; Matveyev, 1970) found complex loading gave balanced fitness and better strength, speed and endurance than unidirectional work. The authors call these concepts "indisputable in principle," but "the research supporting these ideas was done many years ago and utilised athletes of low qualification... under modern conditions this loading would be applicable only to beginners or athletes of average qualification" (PDF p. 380).
- **Verkhoshansky's verdict.** "According to Verkhoshansky (1977), there generally appears to be little advantage for high-level athletes to utilise the complex system of training, although one should not dismiss their possible value at different stages of training with certain individuals in specific cases" (PDF p. 380).
- **Three deficiencies for highly qualified athletes.** (1) Their very high special preparedness needs "strong and relatively prolonged training influences of appropriate emphasis. Complex training does not achieve this." (2) "Complex training, with its multifaceted influence on the body, cannot create the conditions necessary for producing highly specific physical preparedness." (3) "Extensive complex loading to simultaneously perfect sport technique and special physical preparedness inevitably leads to general fatigue and deterioration of this control" (PDF p. 380). These deficiencies "are not as noticeable in athletes of average qualification."
- **Evidence for single-emphasis units.** Single-emphasis workouts make adaptation "more marked" (Handelsman & Stetsenko, 1980); sessions devoted solely to technique are "very effective in improving technical skill" (Struchkov, 1980; Mironenko, 1981; Petrovsky, 1977); single-ability sessions "exert a more profound effect on special preparedness" than multi-objective sessions (five studies cited); single-emphasis microcycles "powerfully stimulate the trainability of swimmers (Kudelin, 1980)" and strength-emphasis microcycles "significantly raise the special physical preparedness of track-and-field jumpers (Mironenko, 1981)" (PDF p. 381).
- **The resolution: complexity over time.** "*The conjugate sequence system does not reject the complex (concurrent) method as the most general principle of training, but only extends it so that it meets the requirements of conditioning highly qualified athletes.* Complexity should be understood in terms of its evolution over time, not its contents and structure at a given instant" (italics in the original; PDF p. 384 / printed p. 373). Complex preparation "is limited as a general principle for training all athletes at all stages of development."

**Why it works** — The authors' reasons are the three deficiencies above: too weak a stimulus in any one direction, too little specificity, and fatigue that degrades technical control. Their stated mechanism for the alternative is "the summation of positive, accumulated after-effects of preceding loading of different primary emphasis" (PDF p. 384). No effect sizes are given for any cited study.

**When to apply** — Deciding whether a well-trained athlete's week should mix every quality in each session or give whole sessions and whole weeks to one emphasis. Eric's baseline: "Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 182, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the baseline and the authors agree that not everything is trained hard at once; the baseline still trains other qualities "at a retention dose," closer to Issurin's multi-targeted blocks than to a single emphasis.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin.** Issurin's multi-targeted block model trains a minimal number of targets per block, not one ([[block-periodization--issurin/principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), and the library's brief of Issurin 2016 records the multi-targeted model's 28-study support against insufficient evidence for the concentrated-unidirectional model in team, combat and swimming preparation ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]], pp. 6-7, 11). Inside the book there is a caveat a few pages later: a swimming week built from single-emphasis workouts of different kinds still "typifies the complex (multi-faceted) form of training organisation" and "fails to produce a definite increase in speed, aerobic or anaerobic productivity" (PDF pp. 387-388 / printed pp. 376-377; see [[case-study--unidirectional-weekly-microcycles-swimming-and-speed-strength]]). So single-emphasis workouts alone are not enough; the authors want the emphasis held across a microcycle or stage. Unidirectional loading "is effective only if it forms part of a complex of several means of a single primary emphasis involving a variety of methods" (PDF p. 381). The argument is for highly qualified athletes; for beginners the authors keep complex training.

**Example** — The authors' own example of a complex unit: a workout of "resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting," or a week using those means on different days (PDF p. 379). Their single-emphasis examples are the swimmer and jumper microcycles of Kudelin (1980) and Mironenko (1981) (PDF p. 381).

**Related** — [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[framework--sequential-and-concurrent-variants-of-systematic-means]], [[claim--concentrated-strength-loading-limited-period-qualified-athletes-and-volume-saving]], [[case-study--unidirectional-weekly-microcycles-swimming-and-speed-strength]], [[claim--strength-and-speed-training-response-shifts-with-training-age]], [[block-periodization--issurin/principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]], [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]

# Concentrated Strength Loading: a Substitutable Block of Up to 2 Months, Claimed Best for Highly Qualified Athletes and to Cut Annual Strength Volume by 13-15%

**What it is** — Chapter 6 restates the concentrated method and adds claims not in the Chapter 5 entry on its conditions (PDF pp. 381-382 / printed pp. 370-371, both checked against the page images):
1. **Duration.** "The main novelty of this method consists of exerting a concentrated training influence on the body with a high volume of unidirectional loading for a limited period (of up to 2 months)" (PDF p. 381, citing Verkhoshansky, 1977). Earlier on the same page: "the primary use of unidirectional training for prolonged stages (4-12 weeks) of training can be very effective." The two figures sit a paragraph apart; 12 weeks is longer than 2 months, and the book does not reconcile them (the 4-12 weeks refers to "unidirectional training," the 2 months to "concentrated" loading).
2. **The strength block as a planning unit.** "Concentrated strength loading constitutes a relatively independent part or block of training to create a functional foundation for the subsequent enhancement of technical skill or those motor abilities which chiefly determine success in a given sport." The block's means must fit "the training specifics of that type of sport," and "The strength block should have a specific place in the annual cycle." "To achieve the principal aims of organising loading in the annual cycle, the coach must select a certain strength block or substitute one block for another, depending on the situation and the individual. Obviously, in order to do this, he needs to prepare a detailed selection of appropriate strength blocks in advance" (PDF p. 381). Concentrated strength loading matters "not only for raising the athlete's physical fitness, but also for regulating the entire complex of loading over the annual cycle in all sports."
3. **Evidence claimed.** "The effectiveness of concentrated strength loading has been confirmed by many coaches and special research in a number of speed-strength, cyclic and team sports (Varakin, 1979; Zhdanovich, 1980; Rudokene, 1981; Naraliev, 1981; Ptushkin, 1981; Verkhoshanskaya, 1982; Kabachkova et al, 1982). In particular, it has been established that this system is most appropriate for highly qualified athletes. Moreover, the use of concentrated strength loading enables the general annual volume of strength loading to be reduced (by 13-15%), when compared with the conventional approach (Mironenko, 1981; Antonova, 1982)" (PDF p. 382).
4. **Advanced stages.** "In more advanced stages, the concentrated unidirectional method of loading is the most effective way of further increasing the high level of physical fitness which athletes achieve with multi-year training," provided one finds "regimes of concentrated loading which definitely do not produce negative training effects (Verkhoshansky, 1977)" (PDF p. 382).

**Two volume-saving figures.** Chapter 5 says "the training volume over a macrocycle can be reduced by as much as 20%" with the conjugate sequence system for advanced athletes (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294; see [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]]). Chapter 6 says the "general annual volume of strength loading" falls by 13-15%. These measure different things (all training volume over a macrocycle versus annual strength volume), so they are recorded side by side, not as a contradiction.

**Why it works** — The authors give a mechanism at PDF p. 381: the concentrated influence "produces a brief, fairly stable state of incomplete restoration which is associated with the persistent and relatively prolonged disturbance of homeostasis. This triggers extensive functional changes which are prerequisites for subsequent supercompensation and the raising of the body to a higher level of special preparedness." The cited studies are named without design, sample size or effect size.

**When to apply** — Building an annual plan for qualified athletes around one or two strength blocks, each designed for the sport and kept ready to swap in or out. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract: lay out the competition calendar, key non-training dates (holidays, exam weeks), and phase-by-phase volume/intensity waves, then adapt the route as circumstances change while still reaching the same destination" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the authors' "detailed selection of appropriate strength blocks in advance" is a concrete way to make that roadmap adaptable.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin** for team sports. The book says concentrated strength loading was confirmed in "team sports" (PDF p. 382); the library's brief of Issurin 2016 records that concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports "improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance," and that Issurin judged the evidence "insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation" (brief, p. 6). See [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]. The method is stated as most appropriate for highly qualified athletes, not novices. It has costs, set out on the same page: a "brief but consistent decrease in speed-strength" ([[case-study--antonova-and-levchenko-high-strength-volume-lowers-explosive-qualities]]).

**Example** — The authors' sports examples are general (speed-strength, cyclic and team sports, PDF p. 382). Inference: a strength coach keeps three prepared strength blocks for a jumper (a general-strength block, a speed-strength block, a reactive block) and chooses which to run in the second preparation phase according to how the first block went.

# Antonova (Women Long Jumpers) and Levchenko (Sprinters): Months of Peak Strength Volume Lowered Explosive Qualities, Which Rose Again When Loading Fell

**What it is** — Under "Problems with Concentrated Loading" the authors report two Soviet studies (PDF p. 382 / printed p. 371, checked against the page image). They open with the general cost: concentrated strength loading "leads to a brief but consistent decrease in speed-strength, which diminishes the athlete's special work-capacity and complicates the task of improving technical skills and speed of movement."
1. **Antonova (1982), women long jumpers.** The study analysed "the connection between the organisation and the volume of training loads, the changes in the force-time characteristics of the take-off in jumping, the sport results and the explosive strength." "It was found that in the months with the largest training volumes, there was a noticeable decrease in the special-strength preparedness and sporting results. However, these same qualities rose during the subsequent months of reduced loading."
2. **Levchenko (1980), sprinters.** It examined "the interdependence between the dynamics of the volume of special strength-training means, the elasticity of the muscles and the control results of the standing triple-jump of highly qualified sprinters during the spring-summer stage (15 weeks) of training." "An increase in the volume of special strength-training means results in increased muscle stiffness and decreased explosive force. Unfavourable conditions were thus created for improving technique and running speed and the likelihood of injury increased significantly."

The authors add that "voluminous strength loading is detrimental to the technique of the weightlifting movements (Khlystov, 1976; Vorobyev et al, 1978), javelin throwing (Ruvinsky, 1980) and punching speed in boxing (Filimonov, 1979)," and conclude: "Rather than negating the value of concentrated loading, these findings stress the importance of knowing when this method may be appropriate to use."

**Why it works** — The book reports correlations between volume and outcomes; it gives no sample sizes, effect sizes or statistics for either study. The only mechanism offered is Levchenko's observed rise in "muscle stiffness" with strength volume. The book does not define how stiffness or elasticity was measured.

**When to apply** — As the evidence behind expecting a temporary drop in jump and sprint qualities during high-volume strength phases, and a rebound when volume falls. The authors' remedy follows on the same page: "if concentrated loading is used, then *cybernetic periodisation* or programming based on Perceived Ratings of Effort and Ratings of Technique, as well as formal testing, can assist greatly in preventing overtraining (see 6.2.2)." Section 6.2.2 defines cybernetic periodisation as a scheme in which "the original preplanned periodisation scheme is regularly modified by subjective and objective feedback" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329, text layer). Eric's baseline: "Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74, Explicit). Inference: a daily jump measure is the kind of "formal testing" that would catch the drop Antonova and Levchenko describe.

**When NOT to apply** — Both groups were qualified track athletes ("highly qualified sprinters" for Levchenko; the long jumpers' level is not stated). The injury statement ("the likelihood of injury increased significantly") gives no injury counts. The book does not say whether loads were heavy or moderate, only that volume rose. This duplicates in part the Chapter 5 warning in [[claim--excess-heavy-strength-volume-impairs-speed-strength-and-technique]], which cites Kotz, Filinov and Deniskin; the Chapter 6 page adds the Antonova and Levchenko studies and spells the boxing author "Filimonov, 1979."

**Example** — The authors' own example is the Antonova finding: results fell in the highest-volume months and rose in the reduced-loading months that followed (PDF p. 382).

# Keep Technique Work in a Concentrated Strength Block: Learn Components at Low Intensity During the Block, Perfect the Whole Skill at High Intensity as the Delayed Effect Appears

**What it is** — The authors reject reading block loading as strength only: "*Although there is a primary emphasis on a specific motor quality at different stages of training, this does not mean that technique work is totally omitted during the stage of concentrated strength loading*" (italics in the original; PDF p. 382 / printed p. 371). Their rules (PDF pp. 382-383 / printed pp. 371-372, both checked against the page images):
1. **Daily technique, with freshness for the hard parts.** "One must work on improving technique daily, especially in speed-strength and complex-technical types of sports, with 'freshness' of the body being an important prerequisite for development of technique (Dyachkov, 1966; Ozolin, 1970; Ratov, 1979). Separate tasks of technical training which do not require maximum intensity of effort can be performed with the body in a lowered functional state, but the execution of other tasks under such conditions is unacceptable."
2. **Two stages of technical work in the preparatory period.** "During the first stage, one perfects those *components of technique* which need improvement and during the second, the emphasis is on executing *the sport exercise as a whole* with high intensity of effort" (italics in the original; PDF p. 383). High-intensity whole-skill work "should begin in the preparatory period, since it would be too late were it to commence in the competitive period" (PDF p. 382).
3. **During the block: motor learning at low intensity.** One should "primarily emphasize motor learning, i.e. mastering the more precise variants of technique, oriented to that specific level of speed-strength preparedness which will be provided by the concentrated loading... this task is carried out at low intensity," by "special supplementary exercises, by imitation of the rhythmic pattern (but not the tempo) and its related individual elements, and by execution of the whole sports exercise, not at full strength, but under less demanding conditions" (PDF p. 383).
4. **After the block: perfecting at high intensity.** "During the LDTE stage of strength loading, the athlete begins perfecting technique and adapting it to his increasing speed-strength preparedness. This is where one models competition conditions in training to stabilise the perfected technique of the competition exercise at the necessary high intensity of effort" (PDF p. 383).

Fig 6.32(a) (PDF p. 383, checked against the page image) draws this for speed-strength and complex-technical sports: a shaded concentrated strength block on the left, labelled "Learning" below the axis, a dotted line, then "Perfecting." The "STATE" curve (overall fitness state) drops below the zero line during the block and rises after it to the highest level at the right; the Technique and GPP curves continue through both stages. The figure has no numeric scale.

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the lowered functional state during concentrated loading ("Noting that one's functional state will be lowered during this stage, this task is carried out at low intensity," PDF p. 383) and the later rise in speed-strength, which the technique is "oriented to." They add that each cycle of technical improvement consists of "the preliminary development of the motor qualities which the athlete needs to reproduce in the near future, accompanied by the immediate accommodation of technique to that level," and that with this system "the athlete will not be unduly concerned about technique and his achievements will not stagnate" (PDF p. 383). No study is cited for the two-stage scheme itself.

**When to apply** — Any off-season strength block for a speed-strength athlete: keep a daily technique slot, load it with drills, rhythm work and sub-maximal whole movements while the block is heavy, and move full-speed, competition-like technique to the weeks after the block. The 6.14.1 model states the same rule (technique "is included at reduced intensity using the separate elements and their links," PDF p. 394 / printed p. 383). Eric's baseline: "The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 101, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: the authors' scheme does not wait for strength to be built before skill work starts; it runs low-intensity skill learning alongside the strength block, which is a different reading of "foundation" than a strict stepwise hierarchy.

**When NOT to apply** — Speed sports with a cyclic structure separate the two more sharply: "Speed work is excluded totally from the concentrated strength loading stage," though intermuscular coordination work is allowed (PDF p. 384 / printed p. 373; see [[framework--speed-sport-block-organisation-and-two-glycolytic-peaks]]). The rule concerns the authors' concentrated-block method for qualified athletes; it says nothing about technique learning in novices outside a block. The authors do not give a dose or a proportion of time for the technique slot. Section 6.10 already places technical training in the delayed-effect window ([[heuristic--time-technique-and-competition-strength-work-to-the-ldte-window]]); the 6.12.2 pages add the learning-then-perfec

15	# The Programme-Objective Approach: Set a Quantified Goal First, and the Work Needed to Reach It Is the Strategy
16	
17	**What it is** — "The basis of programming is the programme-objective approach, in accordance with which the contents, volume and organisation of training loads are determined by the *objectives* of the preparation (see Fig 6.8). The objectives consist of three main components: the desired improvement in performance; the appropriate changes in technical-tactical, psychological and competition preparedness; the necessary modification of special physical preparedness" (italics in the original; PDF p. 379 / printed p. 368, checked against the page image). "In practice, the selection of a programming strategy is performed by means of a logical 'if-then' approach... if one sets a specific and quantitatively defined goal, then the precise work and methods necessary to accomplish this goal constitute the appropriate strategy."
18	
19	Two framing points on the same page:
20	- **Construction aims at economy.** Construction "involves regulating its contents to provide the effective use of loading of different primary emphasis, i.e. the organisation of the contents over time, so that the required training effect occurs with a minimal expenditure of energy" (6.12.1). Two categories of construction follow: "one based on structural organisation and the other on time management" (how loads of different emphasis are combined, and how loading is regulated within cycles and stages).
21	- **Level is harder than timing.** Closing section 6.11, just above the 6.12 heading: "The art of controlling the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state consists, firstly, of achieving the necessary level of conditioning and, secondly, achieving it at the required time, as dictated by the competition calendar. Research shows that achievement of the second requirement is not especially complex. However, the probability of successfully achieving the first requirement is much smaller" (PDF p. 379).
22	
23	**Why it works** — The authors present it as logic rather than evidence: a quantified target makes the required work derivable. Fig 6.8, which they cite, is outside this batch. No study is cited for the claim that reaching the level is harder than timing it.
24	
25	**When to apply** — Starting any plan by writing the performance target and the changes in technical and physical preparedness it requires, with numbers, before choosing exercises or a periodisation model. The eight-step sequence of 6.15 is the operational version ([[framework--eight-step-sequence-for-programming-annual-training]]). Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 32, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)). Inference: the if-then rule is the planning counterpart of Eric's testing rule, since each training element has to trace back to a stated objective.
26	
27	**When NOT to apply** — The approach assumes the goal can be "quantitatively defined" and the work to reach it is known; in team sports the outcome (winning) is not a single measurable performance, and the authors do not address that. The "level is harder than timing" sentence is the authors' summary of unnamed research ("Research shows"); no study is named, so treat it as their view.
28	
29	**Example** — The authors give no worked example on this page. Inference: a coach sets "standing triple jump from 9.2 m to 9.6 m by the June championship" and then derives the jump, strength and technique work and its timing from that target, rather than starting from a favourite weekly template.

46	# Complex (Concurrent) Training Suits Beginners and Average Athletes; for Highly Qualified Athletes the Authors Favour Single-Emphasis Workouts, Microcycles and Stages
47	
48	**What it is** — The authors define the two ways of organising training: "Complex loading involves prescription of multi-faceted training regimes to achieve several different fitness objectives over the same period, whereas the concentrated loading method concentrates for a given period on producing a single major specific fitness quality via the use of a unidirectional regime of training" (PDF p. 379 / printed p. 368). "For instance, a complex workout might comprise resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting; a complex microcycle (typically a week) might employ those same training means on different days or during different sessions on the same day." Using complex means requires knowing how the means interact through "the acute and delayed after-effects of each" (PDF p. 379).
49	
50	Their case against complex training for top athletes (PDF pp. 380-381 / printed pp. 369-370, all pages checked against the images):
51	- **The supporting research is old and used weak athletes.** The early studies (Krestovnikov, 1951; Letunov et al., 1954; Zimkin, 1956; Korobkov et al, 1960; Matveyev, 1970) found complex loading gave balanced fitness and better strength, speed and endurance than unidirectional work. The authors call these concepts "indisputable in principle," but "the research supporting these ideas was done many years ago and utilised athletes of low qualification... under modern conditions this loading would be applicable only to beginners or athletes of average qualification" (PDF p. 380).
52	- **Verkhoshansky's verdict.** "According to Verkhoshansky (1977), there generally appears to be little advantage for high-level athletes to utilise the complex system of training, although one should not dismiss their possible value at different stages of training with certain individuals in specific cases" (PDF p. 380).
53	- **Three deficiencies for highly qualified athletes.** (1) Their very high special preparedness needs "strong and relatively prolonged training influences of appropriate emphasis. Complex training does not achieve this." (2) "Complex training, with its multifaceted influence on the body, cannot create the conditions necessary for producing highly specific physical preparedness." (3) "Extensive complex loading to simultaneously perfect sport technique and special physical preparedness inevitably leads to general fatigue and deterioration of this control" (PDF p. 380). These deficiencies "are not as noticeable in athletes of average qualification."
54	- **Evidence for single-emphasis units.** Single-emphasis workouts make adaptation "more marked" (Handelsman & Stetsenko, 1980); sessions devoted solely to technique are "very effective in improving technical skill" (Struchkov, 1980; Mironenko, 1981; Petrovsky, 1977); single-ability sessions "exert a more profound effect on special preparedness" than multi-objective sessions (five studies cited); single-emphasis microcycles "powerfully stimulate the trainability of swimmers (Kudelin, 1980)" and strength-emphasis microcycles "significantly raise the special physical preparedness of track-and-field jumpers (Mironenko, 1981)" (PDF p. 381).
55	- **The resolution: complexity over time.** "*The conjugate sequence system does not reject the complex (concurrent) method as the most general principle of training, but only extends it so that it meets the requirements of conditioning highly qualified athletes.* Complexity should be understood in terms of its evolution over time, not its contents and structure at a given instant" (italics in the original; PDF p. 384 / printed p. 373). Complex preparation "is limited as a general principle for training all athletes at all stages of development."
56	
57	**Why it works** — The authors' reasons are the three deficiencies above: too weak a stimulus in any one direction, too little specificity, and fatigue that degrades technical control. Their stated mechanism for the alternative is "the summation of positive, accumulated after-effects of preceding loading of different primary emphasis" (PDF p. 384). No effect sizes are given for any cited study.
58	
59	**When to apply** — Deciding whether a well-trained athlete's week should mix every quality in each session or give whole sessions and whole weeks to one emphasis. Eric's baseline: "Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 182, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the baseline and the authors agree that not everything is trained hard at once; the baseline still trains other qualities "at a retention dose," closer to Issurin's multi-targeted blocks than to a single emphasis.
60	
61	**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin.** Issurin's multi-targeted block model trains a minimal number of targets per block, not one ([[block-periodization--issurin/principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), and the library's brief of Issurin 2016 records the multi-targeted model's 28-study support against insufficient evidence for the concentrated-unidirectional model in team, combat and swimming preparation ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]], pp. 6-7, 11). Inside the book there is a caveat a few pages later: a swimming week built from single-emphasis workouts of different kinds still "typifies the complex (multi-faceted) form of training organisation" and "fails to produce a definite increase in speed, aerobic or anaerobic productivity" (PDF pp. 387-388 / printed pp. 376-377; see [[case-study--unidirectional-weekly-microcycles-swimming-and-speed-strength]]). So single-emphasis workouts alone are not enough; the authors want the emphasis held across a microcycle or stage. Unidirectional loading "is effective only if it forms part of a complex of several means of a single primary emphasis involving a variety of methods" (PDF p. 381). The argument is for highly qualified athletes; for beginners the authors keep complex training.
62	
63	**Example** — The authors' own example of a complex unit: a workout of "resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting," or a week using those means on different days (PDF p. 379). Their single-emphasis examples are the swimmer and jumper microcycles of Kudelin (1980) and Mironenko (1981) (PDF p. 381).
64

82	**What it is** — Chapter 6 restates the concentrated method and adds claims not in the Chapter 5 entry on its conditions (PDF pp. 381-382 / printed pp. 370-371, both checked against the page images):

84	2. **The strength block as a planning unit.** "Concentrated strength loading constitutes a relatively independent part or block of training to create a functional foundation for the subsequent enhancement of technical skill or those motor abilities which chiefly determine success in a given sport." The block's means must fit "the training specifics of that type of sport," and "The strength block should have a specific place in the annual cycle." "To achieve the principal aims of organising loading in the annual cycle, the coach must select a certain strength block or substitute one block for another, depending on the situation and the individual. Obviously, in order to do this, he needs to prepare a detailed selection of appropriate strength blocks in advance" (PDF p. 381). Concentrated strength loading matters "not only for raising the athlete's physical fitness, but also for regulating the entire complex of loading over the annual cycle in all sports."
85	3. **Evidence claimed.** "The effectiveness of concentrated strength loading has been confirmed by many coaches and special research in a number of speed-strength, cyclic and team sports (Varakin, 1979; Zhdanovich, 1980; Rudokene, 1981; Naraliev, 1981; Ptushkin, 1981; Verkhoshanskaya, 1982; Kabachkova et al, 1982). In particular, it has been established that this system is most appropriate for highly qualified athletes. Moreover, the use of concentrated strength loading enables the general annual volume of strength loading to be reduced (by 13-15%), when compared with the conventional approach (Mironenko, 1981; Antonova, 1982)" (PDF p. 382).
86	4. **Advanced stages.** "In more advanced stages, the concentrated unidirectional method of loading is the most effective way of further increasing the high level of physical fitness which athletes achieve with multi-year training," provided one finds "regimes of concentrated loading which definitely do not produce negative training effects (Verkhoshansky, 1977)" (PDF p. 382).

88	**Two volume-saving figures.** Chapter 5 says "the training volume over a macrocycle can be reduced by as much as 20%" with the conjugate sequence system for advanced athletes (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294; see [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]]). Chapter 6 says the "general annual volume of strength loading" falls by 13-15%. These measure different things (all training volume over a macrocycle versus annual strength volume), so they are recorded side by side, not as a contradiction.
89	
90	**Why it works** — The authors give a mechanism at PDF p. 381: the concentrated influence "produces a brief, fairly stable state of incomplete restoration which is associated with the persistent and relatively prolonged disturbance of homeostasis. This triggers extensive functional changes which are prerequisites for subsequent supercompensation and the raising of the body to a higher level of special preparedness." The cited studies are named without design, sample size or effect size.
91	
92	**When to apply** — Building an annual plan for qualified athletes around one or two strength blocks, each designed for the sport and kept ready to swap in or out. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract: lay out the competition calendar, key non-training dates (holidays, exam weeks), and phase-by-phase volume/intensity waves, then adapt the route as circumstances change while still reaching the same destination" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred (transcript)). The book says concentrated strength loading was confirmed in "team sports" (PDF p. 382); the library's brief of Issurin 2016 records that concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports "improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance," and that Issurin judged the evidence "insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation" (brief, p. 6). 148	2. **Two stages of technical work in the preparatory period.** "During the first stage, one perfects those *components of technique* which need improvement and during the second, the emphasis is on executing *the sport exercise as a whole* with high intensity of effort" (italics in the original; PDF p. 383). High-intensity whole-skill work "should begin in the preparatory period, since it would be too late were it to commence in the competitive period" (PDF p. 382).
149	3. **During the block: motor learning at low intensity.** One should "primarily emphasize motor learning, i.e. mastering the more precise variants of technique, oriented to that specific level of speed-strength preparedness which will be provided by the concentrated loading... this task is carried out at low intensity," by "special supplementary exercises, by imitation of the rhythmic pattern (but not the tempo) and its related individual elements, and by execution of the whole sports exercise, not at full strength, but under less demanding conditions" (PDF p. 383).
150	4. **After the block: perfecting at high intensity.** "During the LDTE stage of strength loading, the athlete begins perfecting technique and adapting it to his increasing speed-strength preparedness. This is where one models competition conditions in training to stabilise the perfected technique of the competition exercise at the necessary high intensity of effort" (PDF p. 383).
151	
152	Fig 6.32(a) (PDF p. 383, checked against the page image) draws this for speed-strength and complex-technical sports: a shaded concentrated strength block on the left, labelled "Learning" below the axis, a dotted line, then "Perfecting." The "STATE" curve (overall fitness state) drops below the zero line during the block and rises after it to the highest level at the right; the Technique and GPP curves continue through both stages. The figure has no numeric scale.
153	
154	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the lowered functional state during concentrated loading ("Noting that one's functional state will be lowered during this stage, this task is carried out at low intensity," PDF p. 383) and the later rise in speed-strength, which the technique is "oriented to." They add that each cycle of technical improvement consists of "the preliminary development of the motor qualities which the athlete needs to reproduce in the near future, accompanied by the immediate accommodation of technique to that level," and that with this system "the athlete will not be unduly concerned about technique and his achievements will not stagnate" (PDF p. 383). No study is cited for the two-stage scheme itself.
155	
156	**When to apply** — Any off-season strength block for a speed-strength athlete: keep a daily technique slot, load it with drills, rhythm work and sub-maximal whole movements while the block is heavy, and move full-speed, competition-like technique to the weeks after the block. The 6.14.1 model states the same rule (technique "is included at reduced intensity using the separate elements and their links," PDF p. 394 / printed p. 383). Eric's baseline: "The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 101, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: the authors' scheme does not wait for strength to be built before skill work starts; it runs low-intensity skill learning alongside the strength block, which is a different reading of "foundation" than a strict stepwise hierarchy.
157	
158	**When NOT to apply** — Speed sports with a cyclic structure separate the two more sharply: "Speed work is excluded totally from the concentrated strength loading stage," though intermuscular coordination work is allowed (PDF p. 384 / printed p. 373; see [[framework--speed-sport-block-organisation-and-two-glycolytic-peaks]]). The rule concerns the authors' concentrated-block method for qualified athletes; it says nothing about technique learning in novices outside a block. The authors do not give a dose or a proportion of time for the technique slot. Section 6.10 already places technical training in the delayed-effect window ([[heuristic--time-technique-and-competition-strength-work-to-the-ldte-window]]); the 6.12.2 pages add the learning-then-perfecting split, the daily freshness rule and the low-intensity means to use inside the block. Inference: in team sports the sport coach, not the strength staff, usually owns technical practice, so the strength staff can control only the timing of their own heavy work relative to it.
159	
160	**Example** — The authors give Fig 6.32(a) as their illustration, not a named athlete. Inference: a long jumper in a six-week strength block does approach-rhythm runs and short-approach jumps at moderate effort three or four days a week, then after the block moves to full-approach jumps at competition speed as speed-strength rises.
161	
162	**Related** — [[heuristic--time-technique-and-competition-strength-work-to-the-ldte-window]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[principle--technical-mastery-needs-competition-intensity-practice]], [[claim--excess-heavy-strength-volume-impairs-speed-strength-and-technique]], [[case-study--antonova-and-levchenko-high-strength-volume-lowers-explosive-qualities]], [[heuristic--follow-a-concentrated-block-with-moderate-volume-explosive-work]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]]

177	# After Large Volumes, the Delayed Training Effect Needs a Prolonged Reduction in Loading, Far Longer Than the Usual 1-2 Week Unload
178	
179	**What it is** — The authors (PDF p. 383 / printed p. 372, checked against the page image): "A relatively prolonged stage of reduction in the volume of training is necessary to promote the LDTE. However, in practice, coaches usually aim to achieve large volumes of accumulated loading and do not always emphasize the role of restoration. Although they provide recuperation pauses within the microcycle and the so-called overload microcycles to provide some rest, they still do not effectively utilise prolonged reduction of loading after large volumes." Such methods are needed "not only for restoration, but also for the development and optimal use of those physiological processes which underlie adaptation. These processes occur relatively slowly and an extended period is necessary for their completion, which is far longer than the 1-2 weeks usually allocated for reduction of loading." They add a warning about extra work: "By overestimating the loading required for developing special preparedness, athletes frequently not only undertake an excessive volume of work, but also execute this volume when it is clearly contraindicated, namely when restoration is vital. Therefore, additional volumes of loading not only do not offer increased training benefits, but also become a major barrier to stimulating the restoration which is sorely needed by the body."
180	
181	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is that the adaptive processes behind the LDTE "occur relatively slowly." They do not name the processes on this page or give a measured duration here. Inference: this matches the book's Chapter 6 figure of 4-12 weeks for the long-term delayed effect, cited in [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]] (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364), but this page itself gives only "far longer than the 1-2 weeks."
182	
183	**When to apply** — After a concentrated, high-volume block: plan a stage of reduced volume measured in weeks, not a single deload week, and do not fill it with more volume. Speed and technique work rise during this stage in the authors' models ([[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]]).
184	
185	**When NOT to apply** — The rule is about the period after large accumulated volumes, not routine week-to-week loading. Section 6.10 sets out the delayed effect and its timed volume cut ([[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]); this 6.12.2 page adds the critique that the usual 1-2 week reduction is too short and that extra volume blocks restoration. Tension with another library source: Bompa's step-loading paradigm uses one unloading week after three loading weeks (3:1) as the standard wave ([[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]]). The two address different situations (a routine wave versus the aftermath of a concentrated block), so this is not recorded as a contradiction, but a 3:1 deload should not be taken as enough reduction for the LDTE in the authors' sense. The authors themselves report 3- and 4-week stages with a final restoration week as the most common practice and say "all of them, depending on circumstances, can produce good results" (PDF p. 385 / printed p. 374). Reduced volume is not reduced intensity: speed work begins at the LDTE stage "together with the necessary gradual rise in the training intensity" (PDF p. 384 / printed p. 373).
186	
187	**Example** — The authors give no worked case on this page. Inference: after a six-week concentrated strength block, a jumper keeps strength volume low for the following four to six weeks while jump and sprint intensity rises, instead of returning to full volume after one easy week.
188

203	
204	# Speed Sports: No Speed Work During the Strength Block, Speed Starts as the Delayed Effect Rises, and Glycolytic Loading Has Two Peaks
205	
206	**What it is** — For "speed sports with a cyclical movement structure" (Fig 6.32b caption, PDF p. 383 / printed p. 372) the authors separate strength and speed more sharply than in speed-strength sports (PDF p. 384 / printed p. 373; both pages checked against the images):
207	1. **Speed out of the block.** "Speed work is excluded totally from the concentrated strength loading stage. However, it is possible during this stage to perfect the athlete's motor skill, which directly determines high speed of movement." That skill is intermuscular coordination with "no tension in the muscle groups which do not directly take part in executing the motor tasks," and "This type of work is quite compatible with the athlete's decreased functional state, provided it is executed in the optimal range of intensity of effort and frequency of movement."
208	2. **Speed starts with the LDTE.** "Speed work begins only at the beginning of the LDTE of strength loading (when the 'State' curve rises above the time axis), together with the necessary gradual rise in the training intensity."
209	3. **Two anaerobic-glycolytic peaks.** High competition speed "is determined largely by specific speed-endurance." The glycolytic loading "exhibits two peaks": the first "is timed to end near the conclusion of the stage of concentrated strength loading. Specialised strength means are employed and the objective is to develop special strength-endurance which is primarily of a local nature"; the second "follows the period during which volume of speed work reaches a peak. Distance methods (in cyclic sports) or specialised means and methods (in one-on-one events and team sports) are employed... this type of work should be done in segments of small volume and combined with speed work."
210	4. **Protect explosive strength.** "Along with the rise in strength-endurance, explosive strength tends to decrease when the second peak of the anaerobic-glycolytic loading occurs. Therefore, in those sports where explosive strength is of great importance, it is necessary to include a sufficiently intensive, small volume of maintenance loading."
211	
212	Fig 6.32(b), read from the image (PDF p. 383, no numeric scale): a shaded concentrated strength wave on the left; most curves (Vmax, S-E, Speed, STATE, An-Gly) dip or stay low during it and rise after it ends, with Vmax ending highest at the right. Individual curves are hard to follow where they cross.
213	
214	**Why it works** — The authors give the reason for allowing coordination work during the block (it is compatible with a lowered functional state) and for the maintenance dose (explosive strength falls during the second glycolytic peak). They do not explain why speed must be excluded entirely rather than reduced. Inference: it follows from their rule that high-intensity work needs a fresh, not a depressed, functional state ([[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]]).
215	
216	**When to apply** — Cyclic speed sports such as sprinting, and by the authors' mention of "team sports" for the second glycolytic peak, sports where repeated speed matters. Eric's baseline: "For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 116, Explicit, claimed again as Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: the authors program two deliberate glycolytic peaks, which goes further than the baseline; their own caution (small segments combined with speed work, a maintenance dose for explosive strength) is the part that fits the baseline best.
217	
218	**When NOT to apply** — Speed-strength and complex-technical sports keep some technique and do not separate speed so sharply ([[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]). Eric's baseline also says "staff do program it in the off-season" for glycolytic work (line 117, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)), so the conflict with line 116 is about in-season emphasis. No volumes, durations or intensities are given for either glycolytic peak.
219	
220	**Example** — The authors give the schematic only. Inference: a 200 m sprinter spends a concentrated strength block doing strength-endurance circuits and relaxed technical drills with no sprinting, starts sprint work as the block ends, and adds short speed-endurance runs only after sprint volume has peaked, with a few explosive lifts kept in each week.
221	
222	**Related** — [[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[principle--speed-strength-strength-endurance-and-speed-endurance-are-independent-qualities]], [[framework--annual-models-for-medium-and-long-duration-endurance-sports]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]]

236	
237	# Two Ways to Build a Large Mesocycle: Variant A Rises Smoothly to a Plateau; Variant B Concentrates Load First, Dips, Then Rebounds Higher
238	
239	**What it is** — In 6.12.3 (PDF pp. 385-387 / printed pp. 374-376, all checked against the page images) the authors compare two forms of mesocycle organisation (Fig 6.33, PDF p. 386).
240	
241	**A terminology warning first.** "In this chapter, *the term 'mesocycle' is reserved for what in Russian is called 'the large stage' or large mesocycle*, which extends over several months to produce a specific adaptive effect... The large mesocycle, in fact, may comprise a few conventional mesocycles and also be referred to as a phase" (italics in the original; PDF p. 385). Its duration "can vary (usually 3-5 months), since its calculation depends on the competition calendar and especially on the dates of the most important competitions" (PDF p. 387).
242	
243	**Common practice, as the authors report it.** "The literature reveals that three and four week stages are the most frequently used, where the last one week serves as a restoration week. There are combinations of two weeks with heavy loading and two weeks with moderate loading, or an alternation of weeks with high and moderate loading... all of them, depending on circumstances, can produce good results. It is very difficult to establish which of these is the most effective, since the criteria are extremely diverse" (PDF p. 385). Research has concentrated on the annual cycle and the microcycle, plus the "pre-competition training stage lasting 4-6 weeks" (PDF p. 385).
244	
245	**The two variants.**
246	- **Variant A** "displays a smooth increase in the functional indicators until it reaches a distinct plateau" and "is a traditional form of training organisation" (PDF p. 385). In Fig 6.33(b) its volume curve rises to a broad peak mid-cycle and falls, GPP peaks early and declines, and the fitness state rises steadily.
247	- **Variant B** "begins with a steady decline which is followed by a sharp increase in the functional indicators up to a level which significantly exceeds the maximum of the first variant" (PDF p. 385). It has two micro-stages: a first one of concentrated special physical preparation that "produces a steady decrease in the functional indicators," then lower-volume specialised and competition loading "designed primarily to improve technique or speed so as to stimulate supercompensation." "The volume increases and decreases more steeply than in the traditional scheme, while there is a slight rise in the intensity of loading... one can achieve the necessary volume of work only with a relatively low intensity of loading" (PDF p. 385). In Fig 6.33(c) volume rises steeply and peaks early, the fitness state stays low then climbs above it, and the shaded GPP area grows across the whole cycle.
248	
249	**Who uses which.** "Variant A is appropriate for athletes of medium qualification, as well as for qualified athletes needing to devote much time to perfecting technical skill. Variant B can be used best by qualified athletes who possess a high special physical work-capacity, can endure voluminous loading and display excellent sports technique" (PDF p. 386).
250	
251	**Why it works** — The authors' explanation for Variant B: the concentrated special loading "cause[s] extensive adaptation," and the lower-volume specialised stage that follows stimulates "supercompensation of energy resources and increase[s] special work-capacity. The stabilisation of the body at a new functional level signifies an increase in adaptive reserves" (PDF p. 385). Intensity is held low because "the concentrated volume of intense loading can seriously overstrain the body and disrupt adaptation." They also claim Variant B avoids the falling results that come from "exhausting the motor potential": "variant B leads to an increase in the athlete's special work capacity and achievements during the competition phase" (PDF p. 386). Fig 6.33 is a schematic (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999) with no data.
252	
253	**When to apply** — Choosing the shape of a several-month training phase. Variant B for qualified athletes with high work capacity and sound technique who can tolerate a planned dip; Variant A for medium-level athletes and those who still need a lot of technical work. Eric's baseline: "Undulating/non-linear periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks) is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: Eric's four-week waves are the "three and four week stages" the authors call common practice; the authors' A and B describe the longer phase those waves sit inside, so the two do not conflict.
254	
255	**When NOT to apply** — Not for athletes who cannot yet tolerate voluminous loading or whose technique is still unstable (the authors' own limit, PDF p. 386). "Mesocycle" here means a phase of 3-5 months, not the looser usage the authors note, "a period of several weeks or months consisting of a certain number of microcycles" (PDF p. 385), so the rules do not transfer to a four-week block without translation. The authors give no study for the claim that B exceeds A; the comparison rests on their adaptation theory. Both variants sit in a chapter whose models all use concentrated loading, which Issurin 2016 questions for team sports (see [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]).
256	
257	**Example** — The authors give Fig 6.33 only. Inference: a qualified jumper's 16-week autumn phase under Variant B spends the first six or seven weeks on high-volume, moderate-intensity strength and jump work with performance tests dropping, then shifts to lower-volume technique and speed work, with test results expected to climb above their start by the end.
258	
259	**Related** — [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]], [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]], [[heuristic--loading-reduction-for-the-delayed-effect-must-outlast-1-2-weeks]], [[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]

# The Programme-Objective Approach: Set a Quantified Goal First, and the Work Needed to Reach It Is the Strategy

**What it is** — "The basis of programming is the programme-objective approach, in accordance with which the contents, volume and organisation of training loads are determined by the *objectives* of the preparation (see Fig 6.8). The objectives consist of three main components: the desired improvement in performance; the appropriate changes in technical-tactical, psychological and competition preparedness; the necessary modification of special physical preparedness" (italics in the original; PDF p. 379 / printed p. 368, checked against the page image). "In practice, the selection of a programming strategy is performed by means of a logical 'if-then' approach... if one sets a specific and quantitatively defined goal, then the precise work and methods necessary to accomplish this goal constitute the appropriate strategy."

Two framing points on the same page:
- **Construction aims at economy.** Construction "involves regulating its contents to provide the effective use of loading of different primary emphasis, i.e. the organisation of the contents over time, so that the required training effect occurs with a minimal expenditure of energy" (6.12.1). Two categories of construction follow: "one based on structural organisation and the other on time management" (how loads of different emphasis are combined, and how loading is regulated within cycles and stages).
- **Level is harder than timing.** Closing section 6.11, just above the 6.12 heading: "The art of controlling the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state consists, firstly, of achieving the necessary level of conditioning and, secondly, achieving it at the required time, as dictated by the competition calendar. Research shows that achievement of the second requirement is not especially complex. However, the probability of successfully achieving the first requirement is much smaller" (PDF p. 379).

**Why it works** — The authors present it as logic rather than evidence: a quantified target makes the required work derivable. Fig 6.8, which they cite, is outside this batch. No study is cited for the claim that reaching the level is harder than timing it.

**When to apply** — Starting any plan by writing the performance target and the changes in technical and physical preparedness it requires, with numbers, before choosing exercises or a periodisation model. The eight-step sequence of 6.15 is the operational version ([[framework--eight-step-sequence-for-programming-annual-training]]). Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 32, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)). Inference: the if-then rule is the planning counterpart of Eric's testing rule, since each training element has to trace back to a stated objective.

**When NOT to apply** — The approach assumes the goal can be "quantitatively defined" and the work to reach it is known; in team sports the outcome (winning) is not a single measurable performance, and the authors do not address that. The "level is harder than timing" sentence is the authors' summary of unnamed research ("Research shows"); no study is named, so treat it as their view.

**Example** — The authors give no worked example on this page. Inference: a coach sets "standing triple jump from 9.2 m to 9.6 m by the June championship" and then derives the jump, strength and technique work and its timing from that target, rather than starting from a favourite weekly template.

**Related** — [[framework--eight-step-sequence-for-programming-annual-training]], [[framework--seven-primary-aims-of-programming-training]], [[principle--programming-is-an-art-on-principles-not-an-algorithm]], [[framework--descriptive-and-prescriptive-training-models]], [[periodization--bompa/framework--eight-training-objectives]]

# Complex (Concurrent) Training Suits Beginners and Average Athletes; for Highly Qualified Athletes the Authors Favour Single-Emphasis Workouts, Microcycles and Stages

**What it is** — The authors define the two ways of organising training: "Complex loading involves prescription of multi-faceted training regimes to achieve several different fitness objectives over the same period, whereas the concentrated loading method concentrates for a given period on producing a single major specific fitness quality via the use of a unidirectional regime of training" (PDF p. 379 / printed p. 368). "For instance, a complex workout might comprise resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting; a complex microcycle (typically a week) might employ those same training means on different days or during different sessions on the same day." Using complex means requires knowing how the means interact through "the acute and delayed after-effects of each" (PDF p. 379).

Their case against complex training for top athletes (PDF pp. 380-381 / printed pp. 369-370, all pages checked against the images):
- **The supporting research is old and used weak athletes.** The early studies (Krestovnikov, 1951; Letunov et al., 1954; Zimkin, 1956; Korobkov et al, 1960; Matveyev, 1970) found complex loading gave balanced fitness and better strength, speed and endurance than unidirectional work. The authors call these concepts "indisputable in principle," but "the research supporting these ideas was done many years ago and utilised athletes of low qualification... under modern conditions this loading would be applicable only to beginners or athletes of average qualification" (PDF p. 380).
- **Verkhoshansky's verdict.** "According to Verkhoshansky (1977), there generally appears to be little advantage for high-level athletes to utilise the complex system of training, although one should not dismiss their possible value at different stages of training with certain individuals in specific cases" (PDF p. 380).
- **Three deficiencies for highly qualified athletes.** (1) Their very high special preparedness needs "strong and relatively prolonged training influences of appropriate emphasis. Complex training does not achieve this." (2) "Complex training, with its multifaceted influence on the body, cannot create the conditions necessary for producing highly specific physical preparedness." (3) "Extensive complex loading to simultaneously perfect sport technique and special physical preparedness inevitably leads to general fatigue and deterioration of this control" (PDF p. 380). These deficiencies "are not as noticeable in athletes of average qualification."
- **Evidence for single-emphasis units.** Single-emphasis workouts make adaptation "more marked" (Handelsman & Stetsenko, 1980); sessions devoted solely to technique are "very effective in improving technical skill" (Struchkov, 1980; Mironenko, 1981; Petrovsky, 1977); single-ability sessions "exert a more profound effect on special preparedness" than multi-objective sessions (five studies cited); single-emphasis microcycles "powerfully stimulate the trainability of swimmers (Kudelin, 1980)" and strength-emphasis microcycles "significantly raise the special physical preparedness of track-and-field jumpers (Mironenko, 1981)" (PDF p. 381).
- **The resolution: complexity over time.** "*The conjugate sequence system does not reject the complex (concurrent) method as the most general principle of training, but only extends it so that it meets the requirements of conditioning highly qualified athletes.* Complexity should be understood in terms of its evolution over time, not its contents and structure at a given instant" (italics in the original; PDF p. 384 / printed p. 373). Complex preparation "is limited as a general principle for training all athletes at all stages of development."

**Why it works** — The authors' reasons are the three deficiencies above: too weak a stimulus in any one direction, too little specificity, and fatigue that degrades technical control. Their stated mechanism for the alternative is "the summation of positive, accumulated after-effects of preceding loading of different primary emphasis" (PDF p. 384). No effect sizes are given for any cited study.

**When to apply** — Deciding whether a well-trained athlete's week should mix every quality in each session or give whole sessions and whole weeks to one emphasis. Eric's baseline: "Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 182, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the baseline and the authors agree that not everything is trained hard at once; the baseline still trains other qualities "at a retention dose," closer to Issurin's multi-targeted blocks than to a single emphasis.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin.** Issurin's multi-targeted block model trains a minimal number of targets per block, not one ([[block-periodization--issurin/principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), and the library's brief of Issurin 2016 records the multi-targeted model's 28-study support against insufficient evidence for the concentrated-unidirectional model in team, combat and swimming preparation ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]], pp. 6-7, 11). Inside the book there is a caveat a few pages later: a swimming week built from single-emphasis workouts of different kinds still "typifies the complex (multi-faceted) form of training organisation" and "fails to produce a definite increase in speed, aerobic or anaerobic productivity" (PDF pp. 387-388 / printed pp. 376-377; see [[case-study--unidirectional-weekly-microcycles-swimming-and-speed-strength]]). So single-emphasis workouts alone are not enough; the authors want the emphasis held across a microcycle or stage. Unidirectional loading "is effective only if it forms part of a complex of several means of a single primary emphasis involving a variety of methods" (PDF p. 381). The argument is for highly qualified athletes; for beginners the authors keep complex training.

**Example** — The authors' own example of a complex unit: a workout of "resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting," or a week using those means on different days (PDF p. 379). Their single-emphasis examples are the swimmer and jumper microcycles of Kudelin (1980) and Mironenko (1981) (PDF p. 381).

# Concentrated Strength Loading: a Substitutable Block of Up to 2 Months, Claimed Best for Highly Qualified Athletes and to Cut Annual Strength Volume by 13-15%

**What it is** — Chapter 6 restates the concentrated method and adds claims not in the Chapter 5 entry on its conditions (PDF pp. 381-382 / printed pp. 370-371, both checked against the page images):
1. **Duration.** "The main novelty of this method consists of exerting a concentrated training influence on the body with a high volume of unidirectional loading for a limited period (of up to 2 months)" (PDF p. 381, citing Verkhoshansky, 1977). Earlier on the same page: "the primary use of unidirectional training for prolonged stages (4-12 weeks) of training can be very effective." The two figures sit a paragraph apart; 12 weeks is longer than 2 months, and the book does not reconcile them (the 4-12 weeks refers to "unidirectional training," the 2 months to "concentrated" loading).
2. **The strength block as a planning unit.** "Concentrated strength loading constitutes a relatively independent part or block of training to create a functional foundation for the subsequent enhancement of technical skill or those motor abilities which chiefly determine success in a given sport." The block's means must fit "the training specifics of that type of sport," and "The strength block should have a specific place in the annual cycle." "To achieve the principal aims of organising loading in the annual cycle, the coach must select a certain strength block or substitute one block for another, depending on the situation and the individual. Obviously, in order to do this, he needs to prepare a detailed selection of appropriate strength blocks in advance" (PDF p. 381). Concentrated strength loading matters "not only for raising the athlete's physical fitness, but also for regulating the entire complex of loading over the annual cycle in all sports."
3. **Evidence claimed.** "The effectiveness of concentrated strength loading has been confirmed by many coaches and special research in a number of speed-strength, cyclic and team sports (Varakin, 1979; Zhdanovich, 1980; Rudokene, 1981; Naraliev, 1981; Ptushkin, 1981; Verkhoshanskaya, 1982; Kabachkova et al, 1982). In particular, it has been established that this system is most appropriate for highly qualified athletes. Moreover, the use of concentrated strength loading enables the general annual volume of strength loading to be reduced (by 13-15%), when compared with the conventional approach (Mironenko, 1981; Antonova, 1982)" (PDF p. 382).
4. **Advanced stages.** "In more advanced stages, the concentrated unidirectional method of loading is the most effective way of further increasing the high level of physical fitness which athletes achieve with multi-year training," provided one finds "regimes of concentrated loading which definitely do not produce negative training effects (Verkhoshansky, 1977)" (PDF p. 382).

**Two volume-saving figures.** Chapter 5 says "the training volume over a macrocycle can be reduced by as much as 20%" with the conjugate sequence system for advanced athletes (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294; see [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]]). Chapter 6 says the "general annual volume of strength loading" falls by 13-15%. These measure different things (all training volume over a macrocycle versus annual strength volume), so they are recorded side by side, not as a contradiction.

**Why it works** — The authors give a mechanism at PDF p. 381: the concentrated influence "produces a brief, fairly stable state of incomplete restoration which is associated with the persistent and relatively prolonged disturbance of homeostasis. This triggers extensive functional changes which are prerequisites for subsequent supercompensation and the raising of the body to a higher level of special preparedness." The cited studies are named without design, sample size or effect size.

**When to apply** — Building an annual plan for qualified athletes around one or two strength blocks, each designed for the sport and kept ready to swap in or out. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract: lay out the competition calendar, key non-training dates (holidays, exam weeks), and phase-by-phase volume/intensity waves, then adapt the route as circumstances change while still reaching the same destination" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the authors' "detailed selection of appropriate strength blocks in advance" is a concrete way to make that roadmap adaptable.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin** for team sports. The book says concentrated strength loading was confirmed in "team sports" (PDF p. 382); the library's brief of Issurin 2016 records that concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports "improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance," and that Issurin judged the evidence "insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation" (brief, p. 6). See [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]. The method is stated as most appropriate for highly qualified athletes, not novices. It has costs, set out on the same page: a "brief but consistent decrease in speed-strength" ([[case-study--antonova-and-levchenko-high-strength-volume-lowers-explosive-qualities]]).

**Example** — The authors' sports examples are general (speed-strength, cyclic and team sports, PDF p. 382). Inference: a strength coach keeps three prepared strength blocks for a jumper (a general-strength block, a speed-strength block, a reactive block) and chooses which to run in the second preparation phase according to how the first block went.
