# Antonova (Women Long Jumpers) and Levchenko (Sprinters): Months of Peak Strength Volume Lowered Explosive Qualities, Which Rose Again When Loading Fell

**What it is** — Under "Problems with Concentrated Loading" the authors report two Soviet studies (PDF p. 382 / printed p. 371, checked against the page image). They open with the general cost: concentrated strength loading "leads to a brief but consistent decrease in speed-strength, which diminishes the athlete's special work-capacity and complicates the task of improving technical skills and speed of movement."
1. **Antonova (1982), women long jumpers.** The study analysed "the connection between the organisation and the volume of training loads, the changes in the force-time characteristics of the take-off in jumping, the sport results and the explosive strength." "It was found that in the months with the largest training volumes, there was a noticeable decrease in the special-strength preparedness and sporting results. However, these same qualities rose during the subsequent months of reduced loading."
2. **Levchenko (1980), sprinters.** It examined "the interdependence between the dynamics of the volume of special strength-training means, the elasticity of the muscles and the control results of the standing triple-jump of highly qualified sprinters during the spring-summer stage (15 weeks) of training." "An increase in the volume of special strength-training means results in increased muscle stiffness and decreased explosive force. Unfavourable conditions were thus created for improving technique and running speed and the likelihood of injury increased significantly."

The authors add that "voluminous strength loading is detrimental to the technique of the weightlifting movements (Khlystov, 1976; Vorobyev et al, 1978), javelin throwing (Ruvinsky, 1980) and punching speed in boxing (Filimonov, 1979)," and conclude: "Rather than negating the value of concentrated loading, these findings stress the importance of knowing when this method may be appropriate to use."

**Why it works** — The book reports correlations between volume and outcomes; it gives no sample sizes, effect sizes or statistics for either study. The only mechanism offered is Levchenko's observed rise in "muscle stiffness" with strength volume. The book does not define how stiffness or elasticity was measured.

**When to apply** — As the evidence behind expecting a temporary drop in jump and sprint qualities during high-volume strength phases, and a rebound when volume falls. The authors' remedy follows on the same page: "if concentrated loading is used, then *cybernetic periodisation* or programming based on Perceived Ratings of Effort and Ratings of Technique, as well as formal testing, can assist greatly in preventing overtraining (see 6.2.2)." Section 6.2.2 defines cybernetic periodisation as a scheme in which "the original preplanned periodisation scheme is regularly modified by subjective and objective feedback" (PDF p. 340 / printed p. 329, text layer). Eric's baseline: "Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74, Explicit). Inference: a daily jump measure is the kind of "formal testing" that would catch the drop Antonova and Levchenko describe.

**When NOT to apply** — Both groups were qualified track athletes ("highly qualified sprinters" for Levchenko; the long jumpers' level is not stated). The injury statement ("the likelihood of injury increased significantly") gives no injury counts. The book does not say whether loads were heavy or moderate, only that volume rose. This duplicates in part the Chapter 5 warning in [[claim--excess-heavy-strength-volume-impairs-speed-strength-and-technique]], which cites Kotz, Filinov and Deniskin; the Chapter 6 page adds the Antonova and Levchenko studies and spells the boxing author "Filimonov, 1979."

**Example** — The authors' own example is the Antonova finding: results fell in the highest-volume months and rose in the reduced-loading months that followed (PDF p. 382).

# Keep Technique Work in a Concentrated Strength Block: Learn Components at Low Intensity During the Block, Perfect the Whole Skill at High Intensity as the Delayed Effect Appears

**What it is** — The authors reject reading block loading as strength only: "*Although there is a primary emphasis on a specific motor quality at different stages of training, this does not mean that technique work is totally omitted during the stage of concentrated strength loading*" (italics in the original; PDF p. 382 / printed p. 371). Their rules (PDF pp. 382-383 / printed pp. 371-372, both checked against the page images):
1. **Daily technique, with freshness for the hard parts.** "One must work on improving technique daily, especially in speed-strength and complex-technical types of sports, with 'freshness' of the body being an important prerequisite for development of technique (Dyachkov, 1966; Ozolin, 1970; Ratov, 1979). Separate tasks of technical training which do not require maximum intensity of effort can be performed with the body in a lowered functional state, but the execution of other tasks under such conditions is unacceptable."
2. **Two stages of technical work in the preparatory period.** "During the first stage, one perfects those *components of technique* which need improvement and during the second, the emphasis is on executing *the sport exercise as a whole* with high intensity of effort" (italics in the original; PDF p. 383). High-intensity whole-skill work "should begin in the preparatory period, since it would be too late were it to commence in the competitive period" (PDF p. 382).
3. **During the block: motor learning at low intensity.** One should "primarily emphasize motor learning, i.e. mastering the more precise variants of technique, oriented to that specific level of speed-strength preparedness which will be provided by the concentrated loading... this task is carried out at low intensity," by "special supplementary exercises, by imitation of the rhythmic pattern (but not the tempo) and its related individual elements, and by execution of the whole sports exercise, not at full strength, but under less demanding conditions" (PDF p. 383).
4. **After the block: perfecting at high intensity.** "During the LDTE stage of strength loading, the athlete begins perfecting technique and adapting it to his increasing speed-strength preparedness. This is where one models competition conditions in training to stabilise the perfected technique of the competition exercise at the necessary high intensity of effort" (PDF p. 383).

Fig 6.32(a) (PDF p. 383, checked against the page image) draws this for speed-strength and complex-technical sports: a shaded concentrated strength block on the left, labelled "Learning" below the axis, a dotted line, then "Perfecting." The "STATE" curve (overall fitness state) drops below the zero line during the block and rises after it to the highest level at the right; the Technique and GPP curves continue through both stages. The figure has no numeric scale.

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the lowered functional state during concentrated loading ("Noting that one's functional state will be lowered during this stage, this task is carried out at low intensity," PDF p. 383) and the later rise in speed-strength, which the technique is "oriented to." They add that each cycle of technical improvement consists of "the preliminary development of the motor qualities which the athlete needs to reproduce in the near future, accompanied by the immediate accommodation of technique to that level," and that with this system "the athlete will not be unduly concerned about technique and his achievements will not stagnate" (PDF p. 383). No study is cited for the two-stage scheme itself.

**When to apply** — Any off-season strength block for a speed-strength athlete: keep a daily technique slot, load it with drills, rhythm work and sub-maximal whole movements while the block is heavy, and move full-speed, competition-like technique to the weeks after the block. The 6.14.1 model states the same rule (technique "is included at reduced intensity using the separate elements and their links," PDF p. 394 / printed p. 383). Eric's baseline: "The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 101, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: the authors' scheme does not wait for strength to be built before skill work starts; it runs low-intensity skill learning alongside the strength block, which is a different reading of "foundation" than a strict stepwise hierarchy.

**When NOT to apply** — Speed sports with a cyclic structure separate the two more sharply: "Speed work is excluded totally from the concentrated strength loading stage," though intermuscular coordination work is allowed (PDF p. 384 / printed p. 373; see [[framework--speed-sport-block-organisation-and-two-glycolytic-peaks]]). The rule concerns the authors' concentrated-block method for qualified athletes; it says nothing about technique learning in novices outside a block. The authors do not give a dose or a proportion of time for the technique slot. Section 6.10 already places technical training in the delayed-effect window ([[heuristic--time-technique-and-competition-strength-work-to-the-ldte-window]]); the 6.12.2 pages add the learning-then-perfecting split, the daily freshness rule and the low-intensity means to use inside the block. Inference: in team sports the sport coach, not the strength staff, usually owns technical practice, so the strength staff can control only the timing of their own heavy work relative to it.

**Example** — The authors give Fig 6.32(a) as their illustration, not a named athlete. Inference: a long jumper in a six-week strength block does approach-rhythm runs and short-approach jumps at moderate effort three or four days a week, then after the block moves to full-approach jumps at competition speed as speed-strength rises.

# After Large Volumes, the Delayed Training Effect Needs a Prolonged Reduction in Loading, Far Longer Than the Usual 1-2 Week Unload

**What it is** — The authors (PDF p. 383 / printed p. 372, checked against the page image): "A relatively prolonged stage of reduction in the volume of training is necessary to promote the LDTE. However, in practice, coaches usually aim to achieve large volumes of accumulated loading and do not always emphasize the role of restoration. Although they provide recuperation pauses within the microcycle and the so-called overload microcycles to provide some rest, they still do not effectively utilise prolonged reduction of loading after large volumes." Such methods are needed "not only for restoration, but also for the development and optimal use of those physiological processes which underlie adaptation. These processes occur relatively slowly and an extended period is necessary for their completion, which is far longer than the 1-2 weeks usually allocated for reduction of loading." They add a warning about extra work: "By overestimating the loading required for developing special preparedness, athletes frequently not only undertake an excessive volume of work, but also execute this volume when it is clearly contraindicated, namely when restoration is vital. Therefore, additional volumes of loading not only do not offer increased training benefits, but also become a major barrier to stimulating the restoration which is sorely needed by the body."

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is that the adaptive processes behind the LDTE "occur relatively slowly." They do not name the processes on this page or give a measured duration here. Inference: this matches the book's Chapter 6 figure of 4-12 weeks for the long-term delayed effect, cited in [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]] (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364), but this page itself gives only "far longer than the 1-2 weeks."

**When to apply** — After a concentrated, high-volume block: plan a stage of reduced volume measured in weeks, not a single deload week, and do not fill it with more volume. Speed and technique work rise during this stage in the authors' models ([[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The rule is about the period after large accumulated volumes, not routine week-to-week loading. Section 6.10 sets out the delayed effect and its timed volume cut ([[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]); this 6.12.2 page adds the critique that the usual 1-2 week reduction is too short and that extra volume blocks restoration. Tension with another library source: Bompa's step-loading paradigm uses one unloading week after three loading weeks (3:1) as the standard wave ([[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]]). The two address different situations (a routine wave versus the aftermath of a concentrated block), so this is not recorded as a contradiction, but a 3:1 deload should not be taken as enough reduction for the LDTE in the authors' sense. The authors themselves report 3- and 4-week stages with a final restoration week as the most common practice and say "all of them, depending on circumstances, can produce good results" (PDF p. 385 / printed p. 374). Reduced volume is not reduced intensity: speed work begins at the LDTE stage "together with the necessary gradual rise in the training intensity" (PDF p. 384 / printed p. 373).

**Example** — The authors give no worked case on this page. Inference: after a six-week concentrated strength block, a jumper keeps strength volume low for the following four to six weeks while jump and sprint intensity rises, instead of returning to full volume after one easy week.

# Speed Sports: No Speed Work During the Strength Block, Speed Starts as the Delayed Effect Rises, and Glycolytic Loading Has Two Peaks

**What it is** — For "speed sports with a cyclical movement structure" (Fig 6.32b caption, PDF p. 383 / printed p. 372) the authors separate strength and speed more sharply than in speed-strength sports (PDF p. 384 / printed p. 373; both pages checked against the images):
1. **Speed out of the block.** "Speed work is excluded totally from the concentrated strength loading stage. However, it is possible during this stage to perfect the athlete's motor skill, which directly determines high speed of movement." That skill is intermuscular coordination with "no tension in the muscle groups which do not directly take part in executing the motor tasks," and "This type of work is quite compatible with the athlete's decreased functional state, provided it is executed in the optimal range of intensity of effort and frequency of movement."
2. **Speed starts with the LDTE.** "Speed work begins only at the beginning of the LDTE of strength loading (when the 'State' curve rises above the time axis), together with the necessary gradual rise in the training intensity."
3. **Two anaerobic-glycolytic peaks.** High competition speed "is determined largely by specific speed-endurance." The glycolytic loading "exhibits two peaks": the first "is timed to end near the conclusion of the stage of concentrated strength loading. Specialised strength means are employed and the objective is to develop special strength-endurance which is primarily of a local nature"; the second "follows the period during which volume of speed work reaches a peak. Distance methods (in cyclic sports) or specialised means and methods (in one-on-one events and team sports) are employed... this type of work should be done in segments of small volume and combined with speed work."
4. **Protect explosive strength.** "Along with the rise in strength-endurance, explosive strength tends to decrease when the second peak of the anaerobic-glycolytic loading occurs. Therefore, in those sports where explosive strength is of great importance, it is necessary to include a sufficiently intensive, small volume of maintenance loading."

Fig 6.32(b), read from the image (PDF p. 383, no numeric scale): a shaded concentrated strength wave on the left; most curves (Vmax, S-E, Speed, STATE, An-Gly) dip or stay low during it and rise after it ends, with Vmax ending highest at the right. Individual curves are hard to follow where they cross.

**Why it works** — The authors give the reason for allowing coordination work during the block (it is compatible with a lowered functional state) and for the maintenance dose (explosive strength falls during the second glycolytic peak). They do not explain why speed must be excluded entirely rather than reduced. Inference: it follows from their rule that high-intensity work needs a fresh, not a depressed, functional state ([[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]]).

**When to apply** — Cyclic speed sports such as sprinting, and by the authors' mention of "team sports" for the second glycolytic peak, sports where repeated speed matters. Eric's baseline: "For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 116, Explicit, claimed again as Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: the authors program two deliberate glycolytic peaks, which goes further than the baseline; their own caution (small segments combined with speed work, a maintenance dose for explosive strength) is the part that fits the baseline best.

**When NOT to apply** — Speed-strength and complex-technical sports keep some technique and do not separate speed so sharply ([[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]). Eric's baseline also says "staff do program it in the off-season" for glycolytic work (line 117, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)), so the conflict with line 116 is about in-season emphasis. No volumes, durations or intensities are given for either glycolytic peak.

**Example** — The authors give the schematic only. Inference: a 200 m sprinter spends a concentrated strength block doing strength-endurance circuits and relaxed technical drills with no sprinting, starts sprint work as the block ends, and adds short speed-endurance runs only after sprint volume has peaked, with a few explosive lifts kept in each week.

# Two Ways to Build a Large Mesocycle: Variant A Rises Smoothly to a Plateau; Variant B Concentrates Load First, Dips, Then Rebounds Higher

**What it is** — In 6.12.3 (PDF pp. 385-387 / printed pp. 374-376, all checked against the page images) the authors compare two forms of mesocycle organisation (Fig 6.33, PDF p. 386).

**A terminology warning first.** "In this chapter, *the term 'mesocycle' is reserved for what in Russian is called 'the large stage' or large mesocycle*, which extends over several months to produce a specific adaptive effect... The large mesocycle, in fact, may comprise a few conventional mesocycles and also be referred to as a phase" (italics in the original; PDF p. 385). Its duration "can vary (usually 3-5 months), since its calculation depends on the competition calendar and especially on the dates of the most important competitions" (PDF p. 387).

**Common practice, as the authors report it.** "The literature reveals that three and four week stages are the most frequently used, where the last one week serves as a restoration week. There are combinations of two weeks with heavy loading and two weeks with moderate loading, or an alternation of weeks with high and moderate loading... all of them, depending on circumstances, can produce good results. It is very difficult to establish which of these is the most effective, since the criteria are extremely diverse" (PDF p. 385). Research has concentrated on the annual cycle and the microcycle, plus the "pre-competition training stage lasting 4-6 weeks" (PDF p. 385).

**The two variants.**
- **Variant A** "displays a smooth increase in the functional indicators until it reaches a distinct plateau" and "is a traditional form of training organisation" (PDF p. 385). In Fig 6.33(b) its volume curve rises to a broad peak mid-cycle and falls, GPP peaks early and declines, and the fitness state rises steadily.
- **Variant B** "begins with a steady decline which is followed by a sharp increase in the functional indicators up to a level which significantly exceeds the maximum of the first variant" (PDF p. 385). It has two micro-stages: a first one of concentrated special physical preparation that "produces a steady decrease in the functional indicators," then lower-volume specialised and competition loading "designed primarily to improve technique or speed so as to stimulate supercompensation." "The volume increases and decreases more steeply than in the traditional scheme, while there is a slight rise in the intensity of loading... one can achieve the necessary volume of work only with a relatively low intensity of loading" (PDF p. 385). In Fig 6.33(c) volume rises steeply and peaks early, the fitness state stays low then climbs above it, and the shaded GPP area grows across the whole cycle.

**Who uses which.** "Variant A is appropriate for athletes of medium qualification, as well as for qualified athletes needing to devote much time to perfecting technical skill. Variant B can be used best by qualified athletes who possess a high special physical work-capacity, can endure voluminous loading and display excellent sports technique" (PDF p. 386).

**Why it works** — The authors' explanation for Variant B: the concentrated special loading "cause[s] extensive adaptation," and the lower-volume specialised stage that follows stimulates "supercompensation of energy resources and increase[s] special work-capacity. The stabilisation of the body at a new functional level signifies an increase in adaptive reserves" (PDF p. 385). Intensity is held low because "the concentrated volume of intense loading can seriously overstrain the body and disrupt adaptation." They also claim Variant B avoids the falling results that come from "exhausting the motor potential": "variant B leads to an increase in the athlete's special work capacity and achievements during the competition phase" (PDF p. 386). Fig 6.33 is a schematic (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999) with no data.

**When to apply** — Choosing the shape of a several-month training phase. Variant B for qualified athletes with high work capacity and sound technique who can tolerate a planned dip; Variant A for medium-level athletes and those who still need a lot of technical work. Eric's baseline: "Undulating/non-linear periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week (e.g., medium-high, medium, high, low over four weeks) is stated as the personally preferred model over strict linear progression" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 106, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: Eric's four-week waves are the "three and four week stages" the authors call common practice; the authors' A and B describe the longer phase those waves sit inside, so the two do not conflict.

**When NOT to apply** — Not for athletes who cannot yet tolerate voluminous loading or whose technique is still unstable (the authors' own limit, PDF p. 386). "Mesocycle" here means a phase of 3-5 months, not the looser usage the authors note, "a period of several weeks or months consisting of a certain number of microcycles" (PDF p. 385), so the rules do not transfer to a four-week block without translation. The authors give no study for the claim that B exceeds A; the comparison rests on their adaptation theory. Both variants sit in a chapter whose models all use concentrated loading, which Issurin 2016 questions for team sports (see [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]).

**Example** — The authors give Fig 6.33 only. Inference: a qualified jumper's 16-week autumn phase under Variant B spends the first six or seven weeks on high-volume, moderate-intensity strength and jump work with performance tests dropping, then shifts to lower-volume technique and speed work, with test results expected to climb above their start by the end.

**Related** — [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]], [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]], [[heuristic--loading-reduction-for-the-delayed-effect-must-outlast-1-2-weeks]], [[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]

######## PDF 379 (printed 368)
SUPERTRAINING
Mastering the ability to effectively programme the contents of training and regulate the dynamics of the athlete’s 
fitness state during training involves eliminating all weak links in the system of managing training and thereby 
significantly increasing the probability of achieving the intended level of sporting performance.
The art of controlling the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state consists, firstly, of achieving the necessary 
level of conditioning and, secondly, achieving it at the required time, as dictated by the competition calendar. 
Research shows that achievement of the second requirement is not especially complex. However, the probability 
of successfully achieving the first requirement is much smaller.
6.12 Principles of Programming and Organising Training
The basis of programming is the programme-objective approach, in accordance with which the contents, volume 
and organisation of training loads are determined by the objectives of the preparation (see Fig 6.8). The 
objectives consist of three main components:
• the desired improvement in performance
• the appropriate changcs in technical-tactical, psychological and competition preparedness
• the necessary modification of special physical preparedness.
In practice, the selection of a programming strategy is performed by means of a logical 'if-then' approach, which 
is understood in the following way: if one sets a specific and quantitatively defined goal, then the precise work 
and methods necessary to accomplish this goal constitute the appropriate strategy.
6.12.1 Forms of Constructing Training
Construction of training involves regulating its contents to provide the effective use of loading of different 
primary emphasis, i.e. the organisation of the contents over time, so that the required training effect occurs with a 
minimal expenditure of energy.
Consequently, time and organisation are two closely interdependent variables in the planning of training. 
The contents and organisation of training are dictated by the training objectives and the characteristics of 
adaptation to the intense muscular work deemed to be necessary for the given period. The time limitation 
imposed by the competition calendar and the duration of the energy supply from the current adaptation reserves 
affects the selection of the contents and organisation of training. Actual conditions do not always satisfy the 
optimal values of these variables. Therefore, programming of training requires creative flexibility based on the 
skill to anticipate the effect of any form of training and select its optimal variant.
It is appropriate now to examine the different forms of training against a background of research into the 
characteristics of adaptation to intense exercise and the principal trends produced by the given loading in the 
dynamics of the athlete's cxercise state. Two categories of training construction may be identified: one based on 
structural organisation and the other on time management. With respect to organisation, one has to consider the 
ways of combining loading of different primary emphasis as a basic condition for achieving a large training 
effect. With respect to time, one has to consider ways of regulating the loading within definite cycles and stages, 
as determined by the periodisation of training and the competition calendar.
6.12.2 Organisational Aspects of Structuring Training
There are essentially two basic different ways of organising training, namely the complcx and the conccntrated 
loading methods. Complex loading involves prescription of multi-faceted training regimes to achieve several 
different fitness objectives over the same period, whereas the concentrated loading method concentrates for a 
given period on producing a single major specific fitness quality via the use of a unidirectional regime of training.
Complex training refers to the concurrent use of different training means in the same workout, microcycle or 
mesocycle. For instance, a complex workout might comprise resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting; a 
complex microcycle (typically a week) might employ those same training means on different days or during 
different sessions on the same day. If complex means are to be utilised, it is essential to understand fully how the 
different means and exercises interact with one another, as determined by the acute and delayed after-effects of 
each (discussed earlier in this chaptcr). In addition, the prescription of complex means depends on the individual, 
the level of proficiency of the athlete, the specific objective, and the stage of the training programme, especially 
the proximity to important competitions
368

######## PDF 380 (printed 369)
SUPERTRAINING
Complex Training
Complex training, which involves concurrent (during one workout or microcycle) and parallel (prolonged stages 
of training, up to a year) use of several training tasks and loads of different primary emphasis, is usually regarded 
is the most effective form of training construction. This is a direct result of considerable early research that 
supported the principle of complex organisation of training. The results showed that the athlete achieves balanced 
ad multi-faceted physical fitness, that development of one motor ability contributes to the development of others 
aid that multifaceted loading improves strength, speed of movement and endurance to a greater extent than 
unidirectional exercise (Krestovnikov, 1951; Letunov et al., 1954; Zimkin, 1956; Korobkov et al, 1960).
Consequendy, arguments were propounded for unifying the GPP and SPP, and combining personal qualities 
to determine training methods, independent of the athlete's level of qualification. Complex training became 
preferred over the unidirectional approach, with its inherently monotonous workouts that tend to diminish 
conditioning effectiveness and promote one-sided physical preparation.
Prolonged unidirectional work (focused on developing factors such as strength or speed) apparently causes 
the body to adapt to loading with the dominant involvement of only some of the physiological mechanisms and 
docs not create conditions for specific adaptation to competition activities. Parallel loading of different emphasis 
was shown to simultaneously improve different physiological functions in the necessary balance for various 
sports (Matveyev, 1970).
All of these concepts are indisputable in principle and are important as the most general guidelines, serving 
is the fundamentals of physical education and sport training. However, the research supporting these ideas was 
done many years ago and utilised athletes of low qualification. Had advanced athletes taken part in these studies, 
then their achievements would have been only average with respect to modem criteria. Besides this, the form of 
loading in those days was different. Therefore, under modem conditions this loading would be applicable only to 
beginners or athletes of average qualification.
According to Verkhoshansky (1977), there generally appears to be little advantage for high-level athletes to 
utilise the complex system of training, although one should not dismiss their possible value at different stages of 
training with certain individuals in specific cases. Arguments in favour of another approach may be based on 
more progressive sports practice, involving the search to overcome the major deficiencies of the complex system 
of training, in particular the following:
1. Highly qualified athletes have a very high level of special physical preparedness. To raise this significantly 
to improve sports proficiency, one must use strong and relatively prolonged training influences of 
appropriate emphasis. Complex training does not achieve this. In complex training, the distribution of the 
volume of special loading (see 6.7.4) is not able to provoke extensive adaptation of the necessary emphasis.
2. There is a definite specificity in the structure of the physical preparedness of high-level athletes. Complex 
training, with its multifaceted influence on the body, cannot create the conditions necessary for producing 
highly specific physical preparedness. Besides this, complex training at high volume accentuates the need to 
establish specific relationships between the processes which develop separate systems of the body, as well as 
between the training effects of loading of different primary emphasis.
3. Highly qualified athletes have to execute the competition activities expertly and with precise control. 
Extensive complex loading to simultaneously perfect sport technique and special physical preparedness 
inevitably leads to general fatigue and deterioration of this control.
Unidirectional Training
The above deficiencies of complex training are not as noticeable in athletes of average qualification and are much 
more obvious at the level of high proficiency where the general volume and intensity of loading is high. If one 
does not prescribe measures to eliminate these deficiencies, they can significantly diminish the success of 
training.
Consequently, it is important to determine such measures for systematically applying loading of some single 
training emphasis in separate workouts and during stages of different duration. For example, research has shown 
that the use of unidirectional loading in separate workouts makes it possible to achieve training objectives more 
effectively. Because of this, the level of adaptation in the body is more marked than when one is trying to
369

######## PDF 381 (printed 370)
SUPERTRAINING
achieve several simultaneous training objectives with means of different primary influence (Handelsman & 
Stetsenko, 1980).
It has also been shown that individual workouts devoted solely to perfecting sport technique are appropriate. 
Even when a wide variety of means and regimes of work and rest are used, these types of training session arc 
very effective in improving technical skill (Struchkov, 1980; Mironenko, 1981; Petrovsky, 1977). It has been 
shown that training sessions with the primary emphasis on developing a single motor ability (under conditions of 
a wide variety of means and methods) exert a more profound effect on special preparedness compared with 
training sessions where several objectives are pursued concurrently (Urzhensnevsky, 1969; Gorkin et al, 1973; 
Monogradov & Platonov, 1975; Fedorova et al, 1975; Chepelyev, 1980).
In addition to its value during separate workouts, unidirectional loading is also appropriate during 
microcycies (Kudelin, 1980; Mikhailova & Sokolova, 1980; Budokho et al, 1978; Mironenko, 1981). For 
example, it has been established that microcycies of a single primary emphasis (in particular, to increase speed or 
various types of endurance) powerfully stimulate the trainability of swimmers (Kudelin, 1980). Similarly, it has 
been shown that microcycies of a primarily strength emphasis significantly raise the special physical 
preparedness of track-and-field jumpers (Mironenko, 1981).
However, research shows that unidirectional loading is effective only if it forms part of a complex of several 
means of a single primary emphasis involving a variety of methods (Fedorova et al, 1975; Platonov & 
Monogradov, 1977; Vcrkhoshansky, 1977).
Considerable work has revealed that the primary use of unidirectional training for prolonged stages (4-12 
weeks) of training can be very effective. Use of a variety of means, especially when applied with a gradual 
increase in intensity, has been shown to be particularly appropriate for enhancing sporting technique, speed- 
strength, and the capacity and power of the ATP-CP and glycolytic-anaerobic energy processes (Mironenko. 
1981; Antonova, 1980; Deniskin, 1976; Levchenko, 1981; Kornelyuk, 1980).
Concentrated Loading
Thus, the method of concentrated training loads was devised for preparing highly qualified athletes, with the 
loading being concentrated during specific stages of preparation (Verkhoshansky, 1977). The main novelty of 
this method consists of exerting a concentrated training influence on the body with a high volume of 
unidirectional loading for a limited period (of up to 2 months). This concentrated influence produces a brief, 
fairly stable state of incomplete restoration which is associated with the persistent and relatively prolonged distur­
bance of homeostasis. 
This triggers extensive functional changes which are prerequisites for subsequent 
supercompensation and the raising of the body to a higher level of special preparedness. An important condition 
for the using concentrated loading is the relatively low intensity of the means, since the frequent use of these 
means already intensifies the training. The loading may be defined as concentrated if its volume in the month in 
which it is concentrated is 23-25% of the general annual volume.
It is appropriate to use concentrated loading primarily for increasing the effectiveness o f SPP, and for this 
purpose one can use loading of any primary emphasis. However, the concentration of specialised strength loading 
is of particular significance, not only for raising the athlete's physical fitness, but also for regulating the entire 
complex of loading over the annual cycle in all sports.
Concentrated strength loading constitutes a relatively independent part or block of training to create a 
functional foundation for the subsequent enhancement of technical skill or those motor abilities which chiefly 
determine success in a given sport. Hence:
• The composition of means and their organisation in strength blocks, as well as their logical connection with
other loading, should be determined by taking into account the training specifics of that type of sport.
• The strength block should have a specific place in the annual cycle, and consequently, have a beneficial
effect on the sequence of loading and the organisation of loading of other primary emphasis over time.
Here the concept of a block has a definite meaning, arising from the programming of technique. To achieve the 
principal aims of organising loading in the annual cycle, the coach must select a certain strength block or 
substitute one block for another, depending on the situation and the individual. Obviously, in order to do this, he 
needs to prepare a detailed selection of appropriate strength blocks in advance.
370

######## PDF 382 (printed 371)
SUPERTRAINING
The effectiveness of concentrated strength loading has been confirmed by many coaches and special research 
d a number of speed-strength, cyclic and team sports (Varakin, 1979; Zhdanovich, 1980; Rudokene, 1981; 
Naraliev, 1981; Ptushkin, 1981; Verkhoshanskaya, 1982; Kabachkova et al, 1982). 
In particular, it has been 
stablished that this system is most appropriate for highly qualified athletes. Moreover, the use of concentrated 
srength loading enables the general annual volume of strength loading to be reduced (by 13-15%), when 
compared with the conventional approach (Mironenko, 1981; Antonova, 1982).
Problems with Concentrated Loading
Concentrated strength loading docs have its deficiencies along with its obvious advantages. For instance, it leads 
to a brief but consistent decrease in speed-strength, which diminishes the athlete's special work-capacity and 
complicates the task of improving technical skills and speed of movement.
The connection between the organisation and the volume of training loads, the changes in the forcc-time 
characteristics of the take-off in jumping, the sport results and the explosive strength of women long jumpers was 
also analysed (Antonova, 1982). It was found that in the months with the largest training volumes, there was a 
noticeable decrease in the special-strength preparedness and sporting results. However, these same qualities rose 
during the subsequent months of reduced loading.
Another study examined the interdependence between the dynamics of the volume of special strength- 
training means, the elasticity of the muscles and the control results of the standing triple-jump of highly qualified 
sprinters during the spring-summer stage (15 weeks) of training (Levchenko, 1980). Here, it was also found that 
an increase in the volume of special strength-training means results in increased muscle stiffness and decreased 
explosive force. Unfavourable conditions were thus created for improving technique and running speed and the 
likelihood of injury increased significantly.
Thus, it is apparent that voluminous strength loading creates adverse conditions for improving skill and 
speed. Considerable research has established that voluminous strength loading is detrimental to the technique of 
the weightlifting movements (Khlystov, 1976; Vorobyev et al, 1978), javelin throwing (Ruvinsky, 1980) and 
punching speed in boxing (Filimonov, 1979). Rather than negating the value of conccntrated loading, these 
findings stress the importance of knowing when this method may be appropriate to use. 
It is important to 
remember, too, that if concentrated loading is used, then cybernetic periodisation or programming based on 
Perceived Ratings of Effort and Ratings of Technique, as well as formal testing, can assist greatly in preventing 
overtraining (see 6.2.2).
The Use of Concentrated Loading
In more advanced stages, the concentrated unidirectional method of loading is the most effective way of further 
increasing the high level of physical fitness which athletes achieve with multi-year training. In order to employ 
it, one should find ways of overcoming the above disadvantages. One way is to periodically devise regimes of 
concentrated loading which definitely do not produce negative training effects (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977).
For example, the scheme in Figure 6.32(a) presents the block-loading of concentrated strength means 
(shaded area) and the work associated with improving technique in speed-strength and complex-technical types of 
sports. It must be emphasized that the block-loading method should not be taken literally as being strictly limited 
to strength and technique training. Although there is a primary emphasis on a specific motor quality at different 
stages o f training, this does not mean that technique work is totally omitted during the stage o f concentrated 
strength loading. It is necessary to examine some features of technical preparation in order to determine the 
correct methodological approach.
One must work on improving technique daily, especially in spccd-strength and complex-technical types of 
sports, with 'freshness’ of the body being an important prerequisite for development of technique (Dyachkov, 
1966; Ozolin, 1970; Ratov, 1979). Separate tasks of technical training which do not require maximum intensity 
of effort can be performed with the body in a lowered functional state, but the execution of other tasks under such 
conditions is unacceptable. For instance, the most important aspect of technical preparation during the com­
petition stage is associated with executing the fundamental sports cxercise at high intensity under conditions that 
are close to those encountered in competition. This type of work should be done when the body is at its highest 
fractional level and should begin in the preparatory period, since it would be too late were it to commence in the 
competitive period.
371

######## PDF 383 (printed 372)
SUPERTRAINING
Thus, one may recognise two successive stages of technical training in the preparatory period. During the 
first stage, one perfects those components o f technique which need improvement and during the second, the 
emphasis is on executing the sport exercise as a whole with high intensity of effort.
Improvement in technical skill involves a multi-year, continuous learning process. The basis for this is the 
athlete's constant striving to master the skill by continuously raising his motor abilities to a higher level of special 
physical preparedness in successive cycles. Each cycle consists of the preliminary development of the motor 
qualities which the athlete needs to reproduce in the near future, accompanied by the immediate accommodation 
of technique to that level. Completion of this process marks the point where a new cycle needs to begin, so that 
two stages may be recognised for inclusion into the idealised annual cycle of training. With the use of such a 
system, the athlete will not be unduly concerned about technique and his achievements will not stagnate.
The above concepts may be explained more thoroughly by referring to Figure 6.32(a). During the stage of 
concentrated strength loading, one should primarily emphasize motor learning, i.e. mastering the more precise 
variants of technique, oriented to that specific level of speed-strength preparedness which will be provided by the 
concentrated loading. Noting that one's functional state will be lowered during this stage, this task is carried out 
at low intensity. This will be done chiefly by means of special supplementary exercises, by imitation of the 
rhythmic pattern (but not the tempo) and its related individual elements, and by execution of the whole sports 
exercise, not at full strength, but under less demanding conditions (including accentuation of individual elements, 
as discussed in 4.3). The effort is gradually intensified during execution of the whole sports exercise.
During the LDTE stage of strength loading, the athlete begins perfecting technique and adapting it to his 
increasing spced-strength preparedness. This is where one models competition conditions in training to stabilise 
the perfected technique of the competition exercise at the necessary high intensity of effort. Since perfecting of 
technique is timed for the LDTE stage of the strength loading, it is appropriate to examine this phenomenon and 
add further information to the recommendations made earlier (see 6.11).
A relatively prolonged stage of reduction in the volume of training is necessary to promote the LDTE. 
However, in practice, coaches usually aim to achieve large volumes of accumulated loading and do not always 
emphasize the role of restoration. Although they provide recuperation pauses within the microcycle and the so- 
called overload microcycles to provide some rest, they still do not effectively utilise prolonged reduction of 
loading after large volumes. However, such methods are necessary, not only for restoration, but also for the 
development and optimal use of those physiological processes which underlie adaptation. These processes occur 
relatively slowly and an extended period is necessary for their completion, which is far longer than the 1-2 weeks 
usually allocated for reduction of loading.
By overestimating the loading required for developing special preparedness, athletes frequently not only 
undertake an excessive volume of work, but also execute this volume when it is clearly contraindicated, namely 
when restoration is vital. Therefore, additional volumes of loading not only do not offer increased training 
benefits, but also become a major barrier to stimulating the restoration which is sorely needed by the body.
Figure 632 (a) Organisation of loading for speed-strength and complex-technical types of sport (b) Organisation of loading for speed 
sports with a cyclical movement structure. The shaded areas refer to concentrated strength loading, S-E = strength-endurance, An-Gly 
* anaerobic-glycolytic, Vmax = maximum velocity. In both graphs, the % change over time for all factors relative to their initial values 
is depicted. 'State1 refers to the overall fitness state of the athlete at any time. (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
A training scheme which emphasizes the development of speed is presented in Figure 6.32(b). It is distinguished 
from speed-strength sports (Fig 6.32a) in that it provides a sharper separation between concentrated strength
372

######## PDF 384 (printed 373)
SUPERTRAINING
loading (shaded area) and work on improving speed. Speed work is excluded totally from the concentrated 
strength loading stage. However, it is possible during this stage to perfect the athlete's motor skill, which directly 
determines high speed of movement.
This motor proficiency requires efficient intermuscular coordination, when there should be no tension in the 
muscle groups which do not directly take part in executing the motor tasks. This involves a specific sequence of 
jension and relaxation of the working muscle groups to perfect the general coordination structure of the given 
exercise. This type of work is quite compatible with the athlete's decreased functional state, provided it is 
executed in the optimal range of intensity of effort and frequency of movement.
Speed work begins only at the beginning of the LDTE of strength loading (when the 'State' curve rises above 
the time axis), together with the necessary gradual rise in the training intensity. At this time, both the frequency 
and the speed of movement also rise.
High speed of movement under competition conditions is determined largely by specific spced-endurance, 
which is produced at a definite level of power and capacity of the anaerobic-glycolytic energy processes. The 
accessary type of anaerobic-glycolytic loading exhibits two peaks (see Fig 6.32b):
• The first peak is timed to end near the conclusion of the stage of concentrated strength loading. Specialised 
strength means are employed and the objective is to develop special strength-cndurance which is primarily of 
a local nature.
• The second peak follows the period during which volume of speed work reaches a peak. Distance methods (in 
cyclic sports) or specialised means and methods (in one-on-one events and team sports) are employed, where 
the objective is to develop specific speed-endurance. To ensure that it does not produce a negative effect, this 
type of work should be done in segments of small volume and combined with speed work.
It should be taken into account that, along with the rise in strength-cndurance, explosive strength tends to 
decrease when the second peak of the anaerobic-glycolytic loading occurs. Therefore, in those sports where 
explosive strength is of great importance, it is necessary to include a sufficiently intensive, small volume of 
maintenance loading.
The above forms of loading organisation of different primary emphasis illustrate the departure from the 
traditional complex training principle, which consists of the parallel execution of several tasks. However, these 
forms by no means negate the value of complex preparation. They only show that the latter method is limited as 
a general principle for training all athletes at all stages of development and highlights the necessity for devising 
more effective ways of training highly qualified athletes.
Use of the Conjugate Sequence System
Recent research shows that it is appropriate to employ the conjugate sequence system of loading for highly 
qualified athletes (discussed in 5.3.3). The conjugate sequence system does not reject the complex (concurrent) 
method as the most general principle o f training, but only extends it so that it meets the requirements o f 
conditioning highly qualified athletes. Complexity should be understood in terms of its evolution over time, not 
its contents and structure at a given instant. As stated before, the chief mechanism of the training effect of such a 
method consists of the summation of positive, accumulated after-effects of preceding loading of different primary 
emphasis. Thus, the conjugate sequence system not only preserves the advantage of the complex method of 
training, but it also accentuates the specific training effect of the loading of a given emphasis. On the whole, the 
positive accumulation of preceding training effects of this form results in a more unidirectional elevation of the 
body to a higher and more stable special work capacity.
The advantage of the conjugate sequence system consists not only in providing a high and stable cumulative 
effect of loading of different primary emphasis, but also in achieving a high degree of functional effectiveness. In 
this case, the entire volume of the unidirectional loading contributes to enhancing motor potential and perfecting 
technical skill. At the same time, superfluous work is excluded, because it does not enhance trainability, but 
often hinders achievement of the planned cumulative training effect.
The conjugate sequence system should be used in the annual training cycle for organising loading of 
different primary emphasis and during separate stages for organising loading of a single primary emphasis. 
Furthermore, it should be distinguished in terms of the power and specificity of the training influence of the 
means and methods used.

influenced by factors such as external conditions, the competition calendar, type of pcriodisation, work demands

2	SUPERTRAINING
3	Mastering the ability to effectively programme the contents of training and regulate the dynamics of the athlete’s 
4	fitness state during training involves eliminating all weak links in the system of managing training and thereby 
5	significantly increasing the probability of achieving the intended level of sporting performance.
6	The art of controlling the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state consists, firstly, of achieving the necessary 
7	level of conditioning and, secondly, achieving it at the required time, as dictated by the competition calendar. 
8	Research shows that achievement of the second requirement is not especially complex. However, the probability 
9	of successfully achieving the first requirement is much smaller.
10	6.12 Principles of Programming and Organising Training
11	The basis of programming is the programme-objective approach, in accordance with which the contents, volume 
12	and organisation of training loads are determined by the objectives of the preparation (see Fig 6.8). The 
13	objectives consist of three main components:
14	• the desired improvement in performance
15	• the appropriate changcs in technical-tactical, psychological and competition preparedness
16	• the necessary modification of special physical preparedness.
17	In practice, the selection of a programming strategy is performed by means of a logical 'if-then' approach, which 
18	is understood in the following way: if one sets a specific and quantitatively defined goal, then the precise work 
19	and methods necessary to accomplish this goal constitute the appropriate strategy.
20	6.12.1 Forms of Constructing Training
21	Construction of training involves regulating its contents to provide the effective use of loading of different 
22	primary emphasis, i.e. the organisation of the contents over time, so that the required training effect occurs with a 
23	minimal expenditure of energy.
24	Consequently, time and organisation are two closely interdependent variables in the planning of training. 
25	The contents and organisation of training are dictated by the training objectives and the characteristics of 
26	adaptation to the intense muscular work deemed to be necessary for the given period. The time limitation 
27	imposed by the competition calendar and the duration of the energy supply from the current adaptation reserves 
28	affects the selection of the contents and organisation of training. Actual conditions do not always satisfy the 
29	optimal values of these variables. Therefore, programming of training requires creative flexibility based on the 
30	skill to anticipate the effect of any form of training and select its optimal variant.
31	It is appropriate now to examine the different forms of training against a background of research into the 
32	characteristics of adaptation to intense exercise and the principal trends produced by the given loading in the 
33	dynamics of the athlete's cxercise state. Two categories of training construction may be identified: one based on 
34	structural organisation and the other on time management. With respect to organisation, one has to consider the 
35	ways of combining loading of different primary emphasis as a basic condition for achieving a large training 
36	effect. With respect to time, one has to consider ways of regulating the loading within definite cycles and stages, 
37	as determined by the periodisation of training and the competition calendar.
38	6.12.2 Organisational Aspects of Structuring Training
39	There are essentially two basic different ways of organising training, namely the complcx and the conccntrated 
40	loading methods. Complex loading involves prescription of multi-faceted training regimes to achieve several 
41	different fitness objectives over the same period, whereas the concentrated loading method concentrates for a 
42	given period on producing a single major specific fitness quality via the use of a unidirectional regime of training.
43	Complex training refers to the concurrent use of different training means in the same workout, microcycle or 
44	mesocycle. For instance, a complex workout might comprise resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting; a 
45	complex microcycle (typically a week) might employ those same training means on different days or during 
46	different sessions on the same day. If complex means are to be utilised, it is essential to understand fully how the 
47	different means and exercises interact with one another, as determined by the acute and delayed after-effects of 
48	each (discussed earlier in this chaptcr). In addition, the prescription of complex means depends on the individual, 
49	the level of proficiency of the athlete, the specific objective, and the stage of the training programme, especially 
50	the proximity to important competitions

54	SUPERTRAINING
55	Complex Training
56	Complex training, which involves concurrent (during one workout or microcycle) and parallel (prolonged stages 
57	of training, up to a year) use of several training tasks and loads of different primary emphasis, is usually regarded 
58	is the most effective form of training construction. This is a direct result of considerable early research that 
59	supported the principle of complex organisation of training. The results showed that the athlete achieves balanced 
60	ad multi-faceted physical fitness, that development of one motor ability contributes to the development of others 
61	aid that multifaceted loading improves strength, speed of movement and endurance to a greater extent than 
62	unidirectional exercise (Krestovnikov, 1951; Letunov et al., 1954; Zimkin, 1956; Korobkov et al, 1960).
63	Consequendy, arguments were propounded for unifying the GPP and SPP, and combining personal qualities 
64	to determine training methods, independent of the athlete's level of qualification. Complex training became 
65	preferred over the unidirectional approach, with its inherently monotonous workouts that tend to diminish 
66	conditioning effectiveness and promote one-sided physical preparation.
67	Prolonged unidirectional work (focused on developing factors such as strength or speed) apparently causes 
68	the body to adapt to loading with the dominant involvement of only some of the physiological mechanisms and 
69	docs not create conditions for specific adaptation to competition activities. Parallel loading of different emphasis 
70	was shown to simultaneously improve different physiological functions in the necessary balance for various 
71	sports (Matveyev, 1970).
72	All of these concepts are indisputable in principle and are important as the most general guidelines, serving 
73	is the fundamentals of physical education and sport training. However, the research supporting these ideas was 
74	done many years ago and utilised athletes of low qualification. Had advanced athletes taken part in these studies, 
75	then their achievements would have been only average with respect to modem criteria. Besides this, the form of 
76	loading in those days was different. Therefore, under modem conditions this loading would be applicable only to 
77	beginners or athletes of average qualification.
78	According to Verkhoshansky (1977), there generally appears to be little advantage for high-level athletes to 
79	utilise the complex system of training, although one should not dismiss their possible value at different stages of 
80	training with certain individuals in specific cases. Arguments in favour of another approach may be based on 
81	more progressive sports practice, involving the search to overcome the major deficiencies of the complex system 
82	of training, in particular the following:
83	1. Highly qualified athletes have a very high level of special physical preparedness. To raise this significantly 
84	to improve sports proficiency, one must use strong and relatively prolonged training influences of 
85	appropriate emphasis. Complex training does not achieve this. In complex training, the distribution of the 
86	volume of special loading (see 6.7.4) is not able to provoke extensive adaptation of the necessary emphasis.
87	2. There is a definite specificity in the structure of the physical preparedness of high-level athletes. Complex 
88	training, with its multifaceted influence on the body, cannot create the conditions necessary for producing 
89	highly specific physical preparedness. Besides this, complex training at high volume accentuates the need to 
90	establish specific relationships between the processes which develop separate systems of the body, as well as 
91	between the training effects of loading of different primary emphasis.
92	3. Highly qualified athletes have to execute the competition activities expertly and with precise control. 
93	Extensive complex loading to simultaneously perfect sport technique and special physical preparedness 
94	inevitably leads to general fatigue and deterioration of this control.
95	Unidirectional Training
96	The above deficiencies of complex training are not as noticeable in athletes of average qualification and are much 
97	more obvious at the level of high proficiency where the general volume and intensity of loading is high. If one 
98	does not prescribe measures to eliminate these deficiencies, they can significantly diminish the success of 
99	training.
100	Consequently, it is important to determine such measures for systematically applying loading of some single 
101	training emphasis in separate workouts and during stages of different duration. For example, research has shown 
102	that the use of unidirectional loading in separate workouts makes it possible to achieve training objectives more 
103	effectively. Because of this, the level of adaptation in the body is more marked than when one is trying to
104	369
105	
106	######## PDF 381 (printed 370)
107	SUPERTRAINING
108	achieve several simultaneous training objectives with means of different primary influence (Handelsman & 
109	Stetsenko, 1980).
110	It has also been shown that individual workouts devoted solely to perfecting sport technique are appropriate. 
111	Even when a wide variety of means and regimes of work and rest are used, these types of training session arc 
112	very effective in improving technical skill (Struchkov, 1980; Mironenko, 1981; Petrovsky, 1977). It has been 
113	shown that training sessions with the primary emphasis on developing a single motor ability (under conditions of 
114	a wide variety of means and methods) exert a more profound effect on special preparedness compared with 
115	training sessions where several objectives are pursued concurrently (Urzhensnevsky, 1969; Gorkin et al, 1973; 
116	Monogradov & Platonov, 1975; Fedorova et al, 1975; Chepelyev, 1980).
117	In addition to its value during separate workouts, unidirectional loading is also appropriate during 
118	microcycies (Kudelin, 1980; Mikhailova & Sokolova, 1980; Budokho et al, 1978; Mironenko, 1981). For 
119	example, it has been established that microcycies of a single primary emphasis (in particular, to increase speed or 
120	various types of endurance) powerfully stimulate the trainability of swimmers (Kudelin, 1980). Similarly, it has 
121	been shown that microcycies of a primarily strength emphasis significantly raise the special physical 
122	preparedness of track-and-field jumpers (Mironenko, 1981).
123	However, research shows that unidirectional loading is effective only if it forms part of a complex of several 
124	means of a single primary emphasis involving a variety of methods (Fedorova et al, 1975; Platonov & 
125	Monogradov, 1977; Vcrkhoshansky, 1977).
126	Considerable work has revealed that the primary use of unidirectional training for prolonged stages (4-12 
127	weeks) of training can be very effective. Use of a variety of means, especially when applied with a gradual 
128	increase in intensity, has been shown to be particularly appropriate for enhancing sporting technique, speed- 
129	strength, and the capacity and power of the ATP-CP and glycolytic-anaerobic energy processes (Mironenko. 
130	1981; Antonova, 1980; Deniskin, 1976; Levchenko, 1981; Kornelyuk, 1980).
131	Concentrated Loading
132	Thus, the method of concentrated training loads was devised for preparing highly qualified athletes, with the 
133	loading being concentrated during specific stages of preparation (Verkhoshansky, 1977). The main novelty of 
134	this method consists of exerting a concentrated training influence on the body with a high volume of 
135	unidirectional loading for a limited period (of up to 2 months). This concentrated influence produces a brief, 
136	fairly stable state of incomplete restoration which is associated with the persistent and relatively prolonged distur­
137	bance of homeostasis. 
138	This triggers extensive functional changes which are prerequisites for subsequent 
139	supercompensation and the raising of the body to a higher level of special preparedness. An important condition 
140	for the using concentrated loading is the relatively low intensity of the means, since the frequent use of these 
141	means already intensifies the training. The loading may be defined as concentrated if its volume in the month in 
142	which it is concentrated is 23-25% of the general annual volume.
143	It is appropriate to use concentrated loading primarily for increasing the effectiveness o f SPP, and for this 
144	purpose one can use loading of any primary emphasis. However, the concentration of specialised strength loading 
145	is of particular significance, not only for raising the athlete's physical fitness, but also for regulating the entire 
146	complex of loading over the annual cycle in all sports.
147	Concentrated strength loading constitutes a relatively independent part or block of training to create a 
148	functional foundation for the subsequent enhancement of technical skill or those motor abilities which chiefly 
149	determine success in a given sport. Hence:
150	• The composition of means and their organisation in strength blocks, as well as their logical connection with
151	other loading, should be determined by taking into account the training specifics of that type of sport.
152	• The strength block should have a specific place in the annual cycle, and consequently, have a beneficial
153	effect on the sequence of loading and the organisation of loading of other primary emphasis over time.
154	Here the concept of a block has a definite meaning, arising from the programming of technique. To achieve the 
155	principal aims of organising loading in the annual cycle, the coach must select a certain strength block or 
156	substitute one block for another, depending on the situation and the individual. Obviously, in order to do this, he 
157	needs to prepare a detailed selection of appropriate strength blocks in advance.
158	370
159	
160	######## PDF 382 (printed 371)
161	SUPERTRAINING
162	The effectiveness of concentrated strength loading has been confirmed by many coaches and special research 
163	d a number of speed-strength, cyclic and team sports (Varakin, 1979; Zhdanovich, 1980; Rudokene, 1981; 
164	Naraliev, 1981; Ptushkin, 1981; Verkhoshanskaya, 1982; Kabachkova et al, 1982). 
165	In particular, it has been 
166	stablished that this system is most appropriate for highly qualified athletes. Moreover, the use of concentrated 
167	srength loading enables the general annual volume of strength loading to be reduced (by 13-15%), when 
168	compared with the conventional approach (Mironenko, 1981; Antonova, 1982).
169	Problems with Concentrated Loading
170	Concentrated strength loading docs have its deficiencies along with its obvious advantages. For instance, it leads 
171	to a brief but consistent decrease in speed-strength, which diminishes the athlete's special work-capacity and 
172	complicates the task of improving technical skills and speed of movement.
173	The connection between the organisation and the volume of training loads, the changes in the forcc-time 
174	characteristics of the take-off in jumping, the sport results and the explosive strength of women long jumpers was 
175	also analysed (Antonova, 1982). It was found that in the months with the largest training volumes, there was a 
176	noticeable decrease in the special-strength preparedness and sporting results. However, these same qualities rose 
177	during the subsequent months of reduced loading.
178	Another study examined the interdependence between the dynamics of the volume of special strength- 
179	training means, the elasticity of the muscles and the control results of the standing triple-jump of highly qualified 
180	sprinters during the spring-summer stage (15 weeks) of training (Levchenko, 1980). Here, it was also found that 
181	an increase in the volume of special strength-training means results in increased muscle stiffness and decreased 
182	explosive force. Unfavourable conditions were thus created for improving technique and running speed and the 
183	likelihood of injury increased significantly.
184	Thus, it is apparent that voluminous strength loading creates adverse conditions for improving skill and 
185	speed. Considerable research has established that voluminous strength loading is detrimental to the technique of 
186	the weightlifting movements (Khlystov, 1976; Vorobyev et al, 1978), javelin throwing (Ruvinsky, 1980) and 
187	punching speed in boxing (Filimonov, 1979). Rather than negating the value of conccntrated loading, these 
188	findings stress the importance of knowing when this method may be appropriate to use. 
189	It is important to 
190	remember, too, that if concentrated loading is used, then cybernetic periodisation or programming based on 
191	Perceived Ratings of Effort and Ratings of Technique, as well as formal testing, can assist greatly in preventing 
192	overtraining (see 6.2.2).
193	The Use of Concentrated Loading
194	In more advanced stages, the concentrated unidirectional method of loading is the most effective way of further 
195	increasing the high level of physical fitness which athletes achieve with multi-year training. In order to employ 
196	it, one should find ways of overcoming the above disadvantages. One way is to periodically devise regimes of 
197	concentrated loading which definitely do not produce negative training effects (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977).
198	For example, the scheme in Figure 6.32(a) presents the block-loading of concentrated strength means 
199	(shaded area) and the work associated with improving technique in speed-strength and complex-technical types of 
200	sports. It must be emphasized that the block-loading method should not be taken literally as being strictly limited 
201	to strength and technique training. Although there is a primary emphasis on a specific motor quality at different 
202	stages o f training, this does not mean that technique work is totally omitted during the stage o f concentrated 
203	strength loading. It is necessary to examine some features of technical preparation in order to determine the 
204	correct methodological approach.
205	One must work on improving technique daily, especially in spccd-strength and complex-technical types of 
206	sports, with 'freshness’ of the body being an important prerequisite for development of technique (Dyachkov, 
207	1966; Ozolin, 1970; Ratov, 1979). Separate tasks of technical training which do not require maximum intensity 
208	of effort can be performed with the body in a lowered functional state, but the execution of other tasks under such 
209	conditions is unacceptable. For instance, the most important aspect of technical preparation during the com­
210	petition stage is associated with executing the fundamental sports cxercise at high intensity under conditions that 
211	are close to those encountered in competition. This type of work should be done when the body is at its highest 
212	fractional level and should begin in the preparatory period, since it would be too late were it to commence in the 
213	competitive period.
214	371
215

217	SUPERTRAINING
218	Thus, one may recognise two successive stages of technical training in the preparatory period. During the 
219	first stage, one perfects those components o f technique which need improvement and during the second, the 
220	emphasis is on executing the sport exercise as a whole with high intensity of effort.
221	Improvement in technical skill involves a multi-year, continuous learning process. The basis for this is the 
222	athlete's constant striving to master the skill by continuously raising his motor abilities to a higher level of special 
223	physical preparedness in successive cycles. Each cycle consists of the preliminary development of the motor 
224	qualities which the athlete needs to reproduce in the near future, accompanied by the immediate accommodation 
225	of technique to that level. Completion of this process marks the point where a new cycle needs to begin, so that 
226	two stages may be recognised for inclusion into the idealised annual cycle of training. With the use of such a 
227	system, the athlete will not be unduly concerned about technique and his achievements will not stagnate.
228	The above concepts may be explained more thoroughly by referring to Figure 6.32(a). During the stage of 
229	concentrated strength loading, one should primarily emphasize motor learning, i.e. mastering the more precise 
230	variants of technique, oriented to that specific level of speed-strength preparedness which will be provided by the 
231	concentrated loading. Noting that one's functional state will be lowered during this stage, this task is carried out 
232	at low intensity. This will be done chiefly by means of special supplementary exercises, by imitation of the 
233	rhythmic pattern (but not the tempo) and its related individual elements, and by execution of the whole sports 
234	exercise, not at full strength, but under less demanding conditions (including accentuation of individual elements, 
235	as discussed in 4.3). The effort is gradually intensified during execution of the whole sports exercise.
236	During the LDTE stage of strength loading, the athlete begins perfecting technique and adapting it to his 
237	increasing spced-strength preparedness. This is where one models competition conditions in training to stabilise 
238	the perfected technique of the competition exercise at the necessary high intensity of effort. Since perfecting of 
239	technique is timed for the LDTE stage of the strength loading, it is appropriate to examine this phenomenon and 
240	add further information to the recommendations made earlier (see 6.11).
241	A relatively prolonged stage of reduction in the volume of training is necessary to promote the LDTE. 
242	However, in practice, coaches usually aim to achieve large volumes of accumulated loading and do not always 
243	emphasize the role of restoration. Although they provide recuperation pauses within the microcycle and the so- 
244	called overload microcycles to provide some rest, they still do not effectively utilise prolonged reduction of 
245	loading after large volumes. However, such methods are necessary, not only for restoration, but also for the 
246	development and optimal use of those physiological processes which underlie adaptation. These processes occur 
247	relatively slowly and an extended period is necessary for their completion, which is far longer than the 1-2 weeks 
248	usually allocated for reduction of loading.
249	By overestimating the loading required for developing special preparedness, athletes frequently not only 
250	undertake an excessive volume of work, but also execute this volume when it is clearly contraindicated, namely 
251	when restoration is vital. Therefore, additional volumes of loading not only do not offer increased training 
252	benefits, but also become a major barrier to stimulating the restoration which is sorely needed by the body.
253	Figure 632 (a) Organisation of loading for speed-strength and complex-technical types of sport (b) Organisation of loading for speed 
254	sports with a cyclical movement structure. The shaded areas refer to concentrated strength loading, S-E = strength-endurance, An-Gly 
255	* anaerobic-glycolytic, Vmax = maximum velocity. In both graphs, the % change over time for all factors relative to their initial values 
256	is depicted. 'State1 refers to the overall fitness state of the athlete at any time. (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
257	A training scheme which emphasizes the development of speed is presented in Figure 6.32(b). It is distinguished 
258	from speed-strength sports (Fig 6.32a) in that it provides a sharper separation between concentrated strength
