216	# Annual Model for Explosive-Strength Sports: Two Mesocycles, Two Concentrated Strength Blocks, the Second Smaller in Volume and Higher in Intensity
217	
218	**What it is** — The authors' prescriptive model for sports "requiring explosive strength" (PDF p. 394 / printed p. 383; Fig 6.39 on PDF p. 395 / printed p. 384; both pages checked against the page images, the figure also at 300 dpi). The text gives these rules:
219	1. **Bi-cyclic structure.** "This model involves bi-cyclic periodisation of training and includes two mesocycles aimed at optimally developing the body's current adaptation reserves and achieving the planned level of special-strength preparedness at the most important competitions." The fitness model tracks "absolute, explosive and starting strength indicators, the highest values of which are achieved at the end of each mesocycle" (PDF p. 394).
220	2. **Strength blocks against a background of speed and technique.** "The organisation of loading provides for exploiting the LDTE of the block of strength work in each mesocycle against a background of the fundamental speed and technical training. The basic principle is block loading with means of different primary emphasis." Technique is "not excluded during the strength loading block. However, such work is included at reduced intensity using the separate elements and their links (see 2.1.2), as well as the rhythmic patterns of individual phases" (PDF p. 394). LDTE is the book's long-term delayed training effect of concentrated strength loading.
221	3. **Second block: less volume, more intensity.** "The second strength block imposes a smaller volume, although the general loading intensity is higher than in the first block. Since the second block is executed against a background of the adaptation occurring in the first mesocycle, the LDTE will be preserved during the second competitive stage. It is unnecessary at this time to further increase the volume of strength work, which can be used exclusively for preparing the neuromuscular system before the subsequent training that emphasizes technique or competitive readiness" (PDF p. 394).
222	4. **Block contents.** The blocks follow "the principle of preserving the training potential of the loading by means of the conjugate sequence system (5.3.3)" (PDF p. 394). The section just before 6.14.1 shows what a speed-strength block holds: "Jumping > Weights exercises > Plyometrics," "not sharply separated by time intervals, but substituted continuously for one another, ensuring that intensity and functional indicators are monitored carefully to avoid overtraining" (PDF p. 394; Fig 6.38, Verkhoshansky 1977). In Fig 6.38 the three overlapping volume waves are A jumps (early, small), B weights exercises (middle, the largest) and C plyometric depth jumps (late, small); read from the image, no numeric axis.
223	5. **GPP.** "Within each block, they offer variety and aid restoration after high volume strength loading, while at the LDTE stage, the GPP assists restoration after intense specialised loading... The largest relative volume of GPP means occurs during the competitive periods" (PDF p. 394). See [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]].
224	
225	**Fig 6.39, read from the image (all month values "about"; no vertical scale).** The time axis runs 11 months (the 6.14 conventions: "Each model consists of about 11 months, since, on average, one month is allotted for the final transition period," PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379). Phases: I (1st preparation) about months 1-4, II (1st competition) about month 5, III (2nd preparation) about months 6-8, IV (2nd competition) about months 9-11. The phase boundaries and dashed lines do not fall exactly on the month ticks (phase I ends late in month 4; phase III ends during month 8). Block 1 is a tall shaded rectangle over about months 1-3; block 2 is a shorter rectangle over about months 6-7, roughly two thirds of block 1's height, matching the text's "smaller volume." Upper panel: all three strength curves (Starting, Explosive, Maximum) fall during block 1 after a small early bump in the two upper curves, rise to a first peak at about months 4-5 (around the phase I/II boundary), dip again during block 2 (about months 6-7), then climb through phase IV to their highest values at month 11. The two upper curves cross at about months 8-9, so only the right-edge order is certain: Starting Strength ends highest, then Explosive Strength, then Maximum Strength. Lower panel: Technique rises inside block 1, falls during block 2, then rises to its highest level at about months 9-10 and declines toward month 11. The GPP and Speed curves cross several times and cannot be told apart reliably in the image; the text is the source for GPP being highest in the competitive periods.
226	
227	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the LDTE: the concentrated block lowers the athlete's state, and the gain appears afterward, so technique and speed work is timed for the period after the block. For concentrated loading in general they state a mechanism at PDF p. 381 / printed p. 370 (checked against the page image): it "produces a brief, fairly stable state of incomplete restoration which is associated with the persistent and relatively prolonged disturbance of homeostasis. This triggers extensive functional changes which are prerequisites for subsequent supercompensation." The second block can be smaller because it runs "against a background of the adaptation occurring in the first mesocycle" (PDF p. 394). No data are shown for this model; Fig 6.39 is a schematic credited to Siff & Verkhoshansky (1999).
228	
229	**When to apply** — Planning a year for an explosive-strength sport with two clearly separated competition phases: put the large strength block early in the first preparation phase, a smaller and more intense block early in the second preparation phase, keep technique work going at reduced intensity inside each block, and shift to technique, speed and competition readiness as the delayed effect appears. Eric's baseline: "In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: football has one long competition phase, not two, so the model maps onto the football year only partly: a large block in the winter off-season and a smaller, more intense block in the summer before fall camp would follow the model's block sizes, with phase IV standing in for the season. The authors do not discuss football or weekly competition.
230	
231	**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin.** Every model in 6.14 uses the concentrated block: "All models in this chapter use the principle of concentrated special strength loading, which elicits the LDTE" (PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379, checked against the page image). The library's brief of Issurin 2016 records that concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports "improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance," and that Issurin judged the evidence "insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation" (brief, p. 6), and saw the model as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality (p. 11); see [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]. American football is a team sport. Other limits: the model is drawn for "highly qualified athletes" (the concentrated method "was devised for preparing highly qualified athletes," PDF p. 381); the block rectangles are not literal ("The use of rectangular blocks should not create the impression that the concentrated loads are applied suddenly at peak intensity," PDF p. 391 / printed p. 380); and stage boundaries "can vary somewhat" with the real calendar (PDF p. 391). Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule" (line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: that rule fits the model's phase IV, where the strength block is over, but the model gives no in-season strength dose, and the baseline's game week ("lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game," line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)) is a microcycle rule the annual model does not address.
232	
233	**Example** — The authors give the model, not a worked year (Fig 6.39, PDF p. 395). Inference: for a jumper with indoor and outdoor seasons, block 1 would sit in the first three months of autumn preparation with the jumps, weights and depth-jump sequence inside it, the indoor season would fall about month 5, block 2 would run about months 6-7 at less volume and more intensity, and the main outdoor competitions would fall in months 9-11.
234	
235	**Related** — [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[heuristic--sequence-jumps-then-barbell-then-depth-jumps-across-stages]], [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]], [[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]], [[heuristic--follow-a-concentrated-block-with-moderate-volume-explosive-work]], [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]], [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]], [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]]

250	# Annual Models for Endurance Sports: Bi-Cyclic With Two Strength Blocks for Medium Duration, Monocyclic With Two Strength Blocks for Long Duration
251	
252	**What it is** — Two prescriptive models from 6.14.2 and 6.14.3 (PDF pp. 395-397 / printed pp. 384-386; text and Figs 6.40 and 6.41 checked against the page images; Fig 6.46 on PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389).
253	
254	**Medium-duration endurance (bi-cyclic, Fig 6.40).**
255	- Two mesocycles and two competition stages; in the first "one need not compete at the fundamental distance," but can compete "at other distances," which "simultaneously serve as control estimates of the athlete's level of aerobic and anaerobic capacity" (PDF p. 395).
256	- "Explosive strength peaks at the beginning of the second competition stage, after which it decreases, together with the rise in the volume of intense (anaerobic-glycolytic) cyclic work." Anaerobic capacity and strength-endurance "reach their highest levels during the most important competitive stage (10th - 11th months)" (PDF p. 395).
257	- Aerobic loading predominates in the first preparatory stage; "during the second stage the work is chiefly at the OBLA (onset of blood lactate accumulation) level"; aerobic volume rises again in the second competition stage "to promote restoration." Speed work (ATP-CP) and speed-endurance (glycolytic) are timed for the LDTE stage, "i.e. the development of speed precedes that of speed-endurance." Overall sequence: "General endurance > Speed > Speed-endurance" (PDF p. 395).
258	- Strength block contents: "The first block emphasizes the development of explosive strength and local muscular endurance, while the second emphasizes mainly local muscular endurance" (PDF p. 396 / printed p. 385).
259	- Fig 6.40, read by eye: block 1 over about months 2-4 (taller), block 2 over about months 6-7 (shorter); phases I about months 1-4, II about month 5, III about months 6-8, IV about months 9-11. For a large mesocycle (Fig 6.46, PDF pp. 399-400), aerobic training "covers the first half of the large mesocycle during which the GPP and concentrated strength loading take place," then speed, then specialised endurance, with competitions as a main way to develop it.
260	
261	**Long-duration endurance (monocyclic, Fig 6.41).**
262	- "Competition in long duration events requires a long preparatory period (up to 6 months) for creating stable adaptation to preserve the special work-capacity for some 4-5 months during the competitive period" (PDF p. 396).
263	- Stable results come "if the increase in loading during the preparatory period occurs gradually (a mean monthly increase of 7-14%), if there is not a sharp drop in the volume of loading during the competitive period, and if the portion of loading in the zone of anaerobic energy production is not increased (Gilyazova, 1978)" (PDF p. 396). See [[claim--prolonged-competition-period-volume-cuts-lower-special-work-capacity]].
264	- "Within a monocycle of periodisation, it provides a two-stage organisation of strength and speed training": "The first block contains general conditioning strength work, while the second block emphasizes the development of local muscular endurance," carrying work capacity "right up to the important competitions in the 10th and 11th months" (PDF p. 396).
265	- Fig 6.41, read by eye: phase I about months 1-6, phase II about months 6-11; block 1 over about months 2-3, block 2 over about months 6-7. Aerobic capacity peaks around the start of the competition period and then eases, as the text says ("maximum aerobic productivity at the beginning of the competition period, and some decrease," PDF p. 397).
266	
267	**Why it works** — Both models rest on the LDTE of concentrated strength blocks and on timing speed and speed-endurance after them. The only cited data are Gilyazova (1978) for the monocyclic loading conditions; the figures are schematics (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
268	
269	**When to apply** — Annual planning for middle-distance (medium) or long-distance (long) endurance athletes who use strength blocks. Not a football model; the medium-duration sequence "General endurance > Speed > Speed-endurance" is the transferable idea. Eric's baseline: "A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once" and "priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 115, Explicit; the two phrases are joined by a dash in the baseline). Inference: both models pick one energy-system emphasis per stage in that spirit.
270	
271	**When NOT to apply** — Long-duration sports are given a monocycle, while the 6.13 aims call for "at least two large mesocycles... even in sports which traditionally... use monocyclic periodisation" (PDF p. 389); see [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]] for this internal conflict. The models are for qualified athletes and carry the same Issurin 2016 challenge to concentrated loading as the other 6.14 models ([[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]). Fig 6.46's caption says "A is the block of concentrated strength loading," but the figure prints "GPP" under A and "Strength Load" under B; which wave is the strength block is unclear.
272	
273	**Example** — The authors give the schematics only. Inference: an 800 m runner competes at 400 m and 1500 m in the first competition stage as control tests, then runs the main 800 m season in months 10-11 after a smaller second block focused on local muscular endurance.
274

# Two Large Mesocycles a Year, the Second Peaking Higher: the Authors Question Monocyclic Periodisation but Keep It for Long-Duration Endurance

**What it is** — "Research shows that it is appropriate to use two large mesocycles in the annual cycle to promote supercompensation of the current adaptation reserves (Figure 6.34). In this case, the athlete's state displays two large peaks, with the second one producing the higher special work-capacity (i.e. fitness state). This further corroborates the value of this form of bi-cyclic organisation of annual preparation which was empirically worked out and applied successfully long ago in several sports" (PDF p. 387 / printed p. 376, checked against the page image). "Consequently, unquestioning adherence to monocyclic periodisation in a number of sports is not justified, and it is advisable that coaches re-examine this tradition carefully." Bi-cyclic periodisation may also suit sports that traditionally use monocyclic forms (skiing, Ogoltsov, 1979; middle-distance running, Turin, 1980; Sirenko, 1980) or tri-cyclic forms (boxing, Nikiforov & Viktorov, 1978; swimming, Vaitsekhovsky, 1981). "In a number of team sports and one-on-one events, tri-cyclic periodisation may have to be used, as dictated by the competition calendar, whereas in long-duration endurance sports, monocyclic periodisation is usually recommended" (PDF p. 387).

The first primary aim of programming (6.13) repeats it: "It is appropriate to fit at least two large mesocycles into the annual cycle, even in sports which traditionally have one main competitive period and use monocyclic periodisation" (PDF p. 389 / printed p. 378, checked against the page image). The practical principles add: "the optimal period for enhancing the current adaptation reserves is about 20 weeks for the most efficient loading of highly qualified athletes," and "the first mesocycle should always be considered as the foundation for the second" (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389, checked against the page image).

Fig 6.34 (PDF p. 387, read from the image, no numeric scale): two shaded strength-loading waves, V1 and V2. The fitness-state curve dips during V1, rises to a peak between the waves, dips again during V2, and then climbs to a level above the first peak at the right edge.

**Contested inside the book.** Aim 1 says "at least two large mesocycles... even in sports which traditionally... use monocyclic periodisation" (PDF p. 389), but the same chapter says "in long-duration endurance sports, monocyclic periodisation is usually recommended" (PDF p. 387) and gives a monocyclic model for them with "one competitive stage" (PDF p. 396 / printed p. 385). The authors partly reconcile this: the monocyclic endurance model still contains "a two-stage organisation of strength and speed training" with two strength blocks (PDF p. 396). See [[framework--annual-models-for-medium-and-long-duration-endurance-sports]].

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is supercompensation of the "current adaptation reserves" and the claim that the second mesocycle builds on the first. They cite no data for the second peak being higher beyond "research shows" and long empirical use.

**When to apply** — Sports with two main competition periods, or one long one where an intermediate peak is useful. Eric's baseline: "In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: if the winter-spring and summer off-season phases are treated as the two large mesocycles, the authors' rule that the second builds on the first and peaks higher fits a fall season with a November priority window; the authors do not discuss football.

**When NOT to apply** — **Also contested by Issurin** on the length and number of training units. Issurin's training stage "should be about two months," and the number of stages "usually varies from four to seven" a season ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]], Block Periodization PDF pp. 38-40), against the authors' two large mesocycles of usually 3-5 months (PDF p. 387) and "about 20 weeks" to enhance the adaptation reserves (PDF p. 400). Bompa's cycle types as taught by Evans reserve the bicycle for "ADVANCED OR ELITE ATHLETES" and the monocycle for novice and junior athletes ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]]); the authors' models are likewise for qualified athletes. Long-duration endurance sports stay monocyclic in the authors' own scheme.

**Example** — The authors' illustration is Fig 6.34 and the bi-cyclic models of 6.14.1 and 6.14.2 ([[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]). Inference: a middle-distance runner with an indoor season in winter and the main outdoor championship in late summer runs two large mesocycles of about four to five months each, the first ending at the indoor meets.

**Related** — [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[framework--mesocycle-variants-smooth-rise-versus-concentrated-dip-and-rebound]], [[heuristic--set-mesocycle-boundaries-by-main-competition-dates]], [[framework--tricyclic-annual-model-for-individual-and-one-on-one-sports]], [[framework--annual-models-for-medium-and-long-duration-endurance-sports]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]], [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]]

# Weekly Microcycles for Swimmers and Speed-Strength Athletes: a Mixed Week of Single-Emphasis Workouts Gave Volume but No Clear Supercompensation; Single-Emphasis Weeks Showed 72-Hour Restoration Patterns

**What it is** — The authors present three weekly microcycles (PDF pp. 387-389 / printed pp. 376-378; all pages and figures checked against the page images). They call the microcycle "the basic units of training construction" and say the traditional complex microcycle cannot carry the volume a large mesocycle needs (PDF p. 387).

1. **A mixed week for highly qualified swimmers (Fig 6.35, PDF p. 388).** The week was built from the restoration time each workout type needs. The bars read: day 1 aerobic, day 2 speed, day 3 complex (lower bar), day 4 anaerobic, day 5 aerobic, day 6 complex (lower bar), day 7 empty. The "trend of restoration" curve, which "combines the separate effects on restoration for the aerobic, anaerobic and speed components," wavers around a flat line with its deepest dip around days 2-3. The authors' verdict: "despite the uni-directional character of individual workouts, the microcycle as the whole typifies the complex (multi-faceted) form of training organisation. The body cannot simultaneously differentiate between and accumulate specific reactions to every type of daily loading... this form of microcycle construction enables one to achieve a large volume of loading, but the absence of any marked supercompensation (as revealed by the trend of restoration curve) shows that it fails to produce a definite increase in speed, aerobic or anaerobic productivity" (PDF pp. 387-388).
2. **Single-emphasis swimming weeks (Fig 6.36, PDF p. 388; caption credits "Kubelin, 1980," the text and PDF p. 381 spell it "Kudelin").** Each week has three aerobic (or three anaerobic) workouts on days 1, 3 and 6, with speed-strength, complex and speed-endurance workouts on days 2, 4 and 5, and day 7 empty. Text: after the aerobic week "there was a significant depression of aerobic potential (VO2 max), the restoration of which was observed over a 72 hour period. At the same time, anaerobic potential, assessed by a swimming test of 4 x 50m, restored quickly and exceeded its initial level. In the second case, restoration of anaerobic productivity took longer and exceeded its initial level after 72 hours. It is interesting that, during this time, aerobic potential rose over a 12 hour span and then diminished."
   Figure values (read by eye, "about"): aerobic week, VO2 max starts about 87% of initial, crosses 100% at about 36 h and reaches about 106-107% by 72 h; the curve labelled "Training effect" starts about 93%, reaches 100% by about 12-24 h and sits about 101-102% at 72 h. Anaerobic week, VO2 max jumps to about 112-113% by about 12 h and falls to about 106% by 72 h; "Training effect" starts about 96% and crosses 100% at about 30-36 h, reaching about 102-103% at 72 h.
3. **A speed-strength week (Fig 6.37, PDF p. 389, Mironenko 1979).** Bars: day 1 technique (medium), day 2 speed-strength (medium), day 3 speed-strength (high), day 4 complex (low), day 5 speed-strength (medium), day 6 speed-strength (high), day 7 empty. The text says these microcycles combine "workouts with large and moderate volumes of strength loading" with "workouts with an emphasis on technical and complex training" (PDF pp. 388-389).

The authors close: "the microcycles used years ago have become the weakest link in the programming of training. Naturally, the preceding examples still do not eliminate those insufficiencies, although they point the way in which scientific research should be directed" (PDF p. 389).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason for the mixed week's failure is that the body "cannot simultaneously differentiate between and accumulate specific reactions to every type of daily loading" (PDF p. 387). For the single-emphasis weeks they report the restoration curves without explaining them.

**When to apply** — Designing a loading week where one quality should be pushed: concentrate workouts of one emphasis in the week and expect roughly three days for the stressed quality to come back above baseline in the swimmers' data. Eric's baseline: "The in-season game week: Sunday off; Monday heavy lift; Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice, with a lighter lift Wednesday; lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)). Inference: the swimmers' VO2 max took about 72 h to recover after an aerobic-emphasis week, the same window Eric leaves before kickoff; this is a coincidence of numbers from a different sport and quality, not support for the football rule.

**When NOT to apply** — **Unclear spots.** The text says anaerobic productivity "exceeded its initial level after 72 hours" in the anaerobic week, but the figure's "Training effect" curve crosses 100% at about 30-36 h; the figure also labels that curve "Training effect," not anaerobic potential, so which curve is the 4 x 50 m test is inferred from the text. The text says aerobic potential "rose over a 12 hour span and then diminished," but the figure shows it still about 6% above initial at 72 h. No sample sizes, athlete numbers or units for the "training load" bars are given. These are elite swimmers and a Soviet-era report; the speed-strength week has no outcome data at all.

**Example** — The authors' own example is the Kudelin swimmer data above (PDF p. 388).

# In the Concentrated-Loading Models, GPP Is Mainly a Low-Intensity Restoration Tool, and Its Largest Relative Share Falls in the Competitive Periods

**What it is** — In these models general physical preparation (GPP) is assigned a restorative job rather than a fitness-building one. For mesocycle Variant B (PDF p. 386 / printed p. 375, checked against the page image): "The basic purpose of this GPP is to facilitate the transition to activities which differ from the special work and thereby promote restoration. The GPP means solve the problem of restoring work-capacity during extensive concentrated loading and during appearance of the LDTE, being used for restoration, especially after high intensity technique and speed work. On the whole, the GPP means are executed at low intensity. However, to prepare the body to switch to training to develop speed and technical skill during the stage of reduced concentrated loading, the intensity of the GPP means is increased slightly." For the explosive-strength annual model (PDF p. 394 / printed p. 383, checked against the page image): "Within each block, they offer variety and aid restoration after high volume strength loading, while at the LDTE stage, the GPP assists restoration after intense specialised loading. It should always be remembered that this procedure constitutes part of pedagogical restoration, which facilitates recovery alongside other methods such as sports massage (see 8.5). The largest relative volume of GPP means occurs during the competitive periods." In the medium-duration endurance model the aerobic work plays the same role in the second competition stage: "There is an increase in the volume of aerobic loading again during the second competition stage, its role being to promote restoration" (PDF p. 395 / printed p. 384).

**Why it works** — The authors' stated reason is switching: GPP moves the athlete to "activities which differ from the special work and thereby promote restoration" (PDF p. 386). They give no physiological mechanism for why a change of activity speeds recovery and cite no study for it here. Inference: this is the active-rest idea applied to block planning.

**When to apply** — Inside a concentrated strength block, and after high-intensity technique or speed sessions: use low-intensity general work as the recovery filler rather than adding more special work, and raise its intensity slightly as the block ends and speed and technique work begins. In Fig 6.33(c) (PDF p. 386) the shaded GPP area for Variant B rises steadily across the whole mesocycle, while in Variant A's panel (b) GPP peaks early and then declines (read from the image; no numeric scale).

**When NOT to apply** — The authors do not give a dose, a modality list or an intensity figure beyond "low." GPP in this sense is not the general base-building of a novice's preparatory period; the models are for qualified athletes. Inference: whether general work restores or adds fatigue depends on what it is, and a hard conditioning session labelled GPP would not fit the authors' "low intensity" condition.

**Example** — The authors name sports massage as a companion method (PDF p. 394) but give no worked session. Inference: after a full-speed sprint and technique day during the delayed-effect stage, an easy swim, mobility circuit or light bike session the next morning fills the GPP slot.

**Related** — [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[framework--mesocycle-variants-smooth-rise-versus-concentrated-dip-and-rebound]], [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]], [[framework--annual-models-for-medium-and-long-duration-endurance-sports]]

# Seven Primary Aims for Programming the Training of Highly Qualified Athletes

**What it is** — The authors condense 6.12 into seven aims that "become the definitive rules of programming" for "highly qualified athletes under modern conditions" (PDF p. 389 / printed p. 378, and PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379, both checked against the page images). Paraphrased with the key wording:
1. **Exploit the current adaptation reserves.** Plan the mesocycles so "the special work capacity peaks at the time of the most important competitions," fitting "at least two large mesocycles into the annual cycle, even in sports which traditionally have one main competitive period."
2. **Preserve the training potential of the loading** by "systematically increasing the intensity and specificity of the training influence, according to the rise in work capacity," using the conjugate sequence system (5.3.3).
3. **Concentrate extensive, specialised unidirectional loading** "of optimal intensity, frequency and duration," especially special strength loading as "a relatively independent block" that creates "a functional base for the subsequent special preparation."
4. **Exploit the LDTE of concentrated strength loading** to regulate "the general volume of loading in the annual cycle" and to create "favourable conditions for improving technique, speed and competitive preparedness."
5. **Block-load means of different primary emphasis** to "effectively utilise intrinsically incompatible loading regimes (e.g. emphasizing strength, technique or speed), eliminate or minimise negative interaction between loads of different primary emphasis, and devise combinations which provide sequential accumulation of the partial training effects."
6. **Lead with special physical preparation (SPP):** "training where SPP precedes in-depth technique or speed work."
7. **Model competition activity:** reproduce "training work that typifies competitive conditions, especially regarding execution of sporting actions at the high intensity which is encountered in competition."

The authors attach a condition: "adherence to these aims will lead to success only if all the preceding preparation has been systematic and the athlete has achieved well-balanced technical and special physical preparedness. To achieve these aims, one must institute measures that take into account actual conditions, the individual characteristics of the athlete and the specifics of the sport" (PDF p. 390).

**Why it works** — The authors present the aims as conclusions from the preceding sections ("The above findings may be expressed as a number of general aims," PDF p. 389) and give no separate mechanism. Each aim's support is in its own section: concentrated loading ([[claim--concentrated-strength-loading-limited-period-qualified-athletes-and-volume-saving]]), the conjugate sequence ([[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]]), two mesocycles ([[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]]).

**When to apply** — As a checklist when reviewing an annual plan for an advanced athlete: does each phase have one main emphasis, are incompatible qualities separated into blocks, does SPP come before the heavy technique and speed work, and is there competition-like work at competition intensity? Eric's baseline: "Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 182, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: this matches aim 5 closely.

**When NOT to apply** — The aims are written for highly qualified athletes, and the authors make them conditional on systematic, well-balanced earlier preparation; they are not a plan for beginners. Aim 1's "even in sports which traditionally have one main competitive period" conflicts with the chapter's monocyclic recommendation for long-duration endurance (see [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]]). Aims 3-5 rest on the concentrated-unidirectional model that Issurin 2016 judged under-supported for team, combat and swimming preparation ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]); that challenge is recorded on the model entries, not set on this list.

**Example** — The authors' worked illustrations of the aims are the annual models of 6.14 ([[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]). Inference: in a jumper's plan, aims 3 and 6 put the strength block first, aim 4 times technique for the weeks after it, and aim 7 adds full-approach jumps under meet conditions in the later preparatory weeks.

**Related** — [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[claim--concentrated-strength-loading-limited-period-qualified-athletes-and-volume-saving]], [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]], [[principle--technical-mastery-needs-competition-intensity-practice]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[block-periodization--issurin/principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]]

# Sports Modelling: a Descriptive Model of the Sport Feeds a Prescriptive Model of the Athlete's State and the Loading Programme

**What it is** — The authors split the models needed to design programmes into two classes (PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379, checked against the page image):
- **The descriptive model** "furnishes qualitative details of the motor qualities and fitness factors needed for proficiency in a given sport, as well as desirable quantitative kinanthropometric, kinesiological, physiological and biomechanical details which characterise movement at all stages of that sport." Examples of its contents: "movement patterns, velocities and accelerations at different joint angles or stages of an event, reaction time, 'lactate threshold' (OBLA), relative muscle strength, body proportions, agonist/antagonist muscle strength ratios and timing of segments of important movements."
- **The prescriptive model** "represents a simplified analogue of the actual training process, omitting some details, but preserving the essential information concerning its composition and structure. It describes the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state and the systems of organising annual training." Its core is a model of the athlete's state that "diagramatically expresses the optimal changes in the most important indicators of special work capacity over time" and "determines the specific periods when one should plan to achieve peak levels." It "draws strongly on the data furnished by the descriptive model."
- Each can be **qualitative** (the dynamics of the functional indicators, the main training contents and how components connect) or **quantitative** ("all numerical aspects of the training... such as calculation of volume, intensity, duration of stages and loading distribution in different intensity zones").

Conventions for the 6.14 annual models (PDF pp. 390-391 / printed pp. 379-380, checked against the page images): months are not named because summer and winter sports are covered; "Each model consists of about 11 months, since, on average, one month is allotted for the final transition period"; each model pairs a fitness-state diagram with a loading diagram; "One can use any method that enables one to measure the values of these indicators"; "All models in this chapter use the principle of concentrated special strength loading, which elicits the LDTE"; the rectangular blocks are schematic, since "the actual loading follows a concentrated wave pattern which gradually reaches a peak, then subsides in volume"; and stage boundaries "can vary somewhat" with the real calendar.

On measurement: "It is of little value to identify which energy systems, types of fitness or movement patterns are involved in a sport unless accurate numerical determinations are regularly made of each of these factors. Even then, we have to remember that the body is not simply a machine in which input and output are deterministically related, but an organism whose behaviour displays non-linearity and fairly random deviations... Nevertheless, without this information, long-term programming becomes imprecise" (PDF p. 391, checked against the page image). The descriptive-modelling passage names the "Multifactorial Fitness Profile (MFP) discussed later... (Ch 7)" and says "Many years of Russian research have produced models for every type of sport" (PDF pp. 390-391). Inference: the passage reads as Siff's framing of the Russian material.

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is control: modelling "makes it possible to manage the organisational complexity of sports activities and devise a practical scheme for describing and controlling the training process" (PDF p. 390), and norms "enable the coach to identify any weaknesses in the state of the athlete and thereby modify the training programme" (PDF p. 391).

**When to apply** — Before writing an annual plan: build or borrow a descriptive model of what the sport demands, with numbers, then draw the planned course of the key indicators across the year and the loading that should produce it. Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 32, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)). Inference: the descriptive model is one way to state those questions in advance, so each test in the battery is tied to a factor the model says matters.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves warn that the body is non-linear and deviates "fairly random[ly]" from quantitative prediction, so a model is a guide, not a forecast. Their example norms (Tables 6.6-6.12) come from Soviet track-and-field and weightlifting populations of the 1970s and 1980s and are "not... all-embracing models" (PDF p. 391; the sentence is printed with a double negative, "None of these examples should not be regarded as all-embracing models"). No football descriptive model is given.

**Example** — The authors' own examples are the model-characteristic tables, including weightlifters' muscle and fat proportions and PWC170 by weight class (Table 6.6, Stepanova et al, 1983, PDF p. 391) and 100 m sprinter models ([[case-study--tabachnik-100m-sprinter-model-characteristics]]).

# Tabachnik's Model Characteristics for 10.0 s Men and 11.0 s Women 100 m Sprinters: Speed, Relative Strength and Jump Targets

**What it is** — Two tables from Tabachnik (1979) give the profile a sprinter should reach to run 10.0 s (men) or 11.0 s (women) (PDF p. 392 / printed p. 381; every value below checked against the page image).

**Table 6.8** (men 10.0 s / women 11.0 s):
- General data: initial 100 m time 11.62 / 13.0 s; age of beginning sprinting 14.6 / 14.1 years; years of sprinting 8.4 / 8.3.
- Speed indicators: simple motor reaction time 0.110 / 0.121; starting reaction time 0.136 / 0.149; total starting time 0.37 / 0.40 s; 5 m from low start 1.18 / 1.32; 30 m from low start 3.80 / 4.25; 50 m from low start 5.70 / 6.15; last 50 m of 100 m 4.45 / 5.00 s.
- Relative muscular strength (relative to bodymass): trunk extension 2.80 / 2.60; trunk flexion 1.20 / 1.15; knee extension 2.20 / 2.00; knee flexion 1.10 / 1.05; hip extension 3.10 / 2.80; hip flexion 1.20 / 1.05; ankle plantarflexion 3.00 / 2.80.
- Speed-strength: standing long jump 3.20 / 2.80 m; standing triple jump 10.0 / 8.40 m; ten-step jump from standing start 36.0 / 32.0 m.

**Table 6.9** (section times by goal, seconds): for a 10.0 s goal, 15 m 1.16-1.18, 30 m 3.70-3.80, first 50 m 5.60-5.70, second 50 m 4.30-4.40, last 10 m 0.900; for 10.9 s, 15 m 1.30-1.32, 30 m 4.20-4.30, first 50 m 6.00-6.10, second 50 m 4.80-4.90, last 10 m 0.990 (goals 10.2, 10.5 and 10.7 s lie between).

The tables sit among the authors' examples of descriptive modelling, alongside middle-distance (Tables 6.7, 6.10, Maximenko 1979), javelin (Table 6.11, Konstantinov 1978) and juvenile sprinter norms (Table 6.12, Alabin & Yushkevitch 1978) (PDF pp. 392-393).

**Why it works** — The book gives no derivation, sample or method for the norms, and does not say how the relative-strength values were measured (the units are "relative to bodymass" only). The authors' general claim is that such norms "enable the coach to identify any weaknesses in the state of the athlete" (PDF p. 391 / printed p. 380).

**When to apply** — As a reference for what a world-class sprint profile looked like in this Soviet model, and as a template for building one's own position-specific norm table. Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 32, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)). Inference: a table like this only earns a place if each row answers a programming question for the roster.

**When NOT to apply** — **Internal inconsistencies, recorded as printed.** In Table 6.8 the men's 50 m from a low start (5.70 s) plus the last 50 m (4.45 s) sum to 10.15 s, not 10.0 s; Table 6.9 gives 4.30-4.40 s for the second 50 m at a 10.0 s goal, faster than Table 6.8's 4.45 s. Women's 6.15 + 5.00 = 11.15 s against an 11.0 s goal. The sources may define the splits differently, but the book does not say. Hand timing and 1970s testing methods are not described, so the values do not convert directly to modern electronic timing. These are elite sprinters, not football players; the relative-strength values come from an unspecified test and cannot be compared with force-plate or 1RM data.

**Example** — The authors' own example is the table itself. Inference: a coach reading the standing triple jump target (10.0 m for 10.0 s men) would check whether a sprinter with fast 30 m times but a short triple jump lacks the speed-strength the model expects.

# Annual Model for Explosive-Strength Sports: Two Mesocycles, Two Concentrated Strength Blocks, the Second Smaller in Volume and Higher in Intensity

**What it is** — The authors' prescriptive model for sports "requiring explosive strength" (PDF p. 394 / printed p. 383; Fig 6.39 on PDF p. 395 / printed p. 384; both pages checked against the page images, the figure also at 300 dpi). The text gives these rules:
1. **Bi-cyclic structure.** "This model involves bi-cyclic periodisation of training and includes two mesocycles aimed at optimally developing the body's current adaptation reserves and achieving the planned level of special-strength preparedness at the most important competitions." The fitness model tracks "absolute, explosive and starting strength indicators, the highest values of which are achieved at the end of each mesocycle" (PDF p. 394).
2. **Strength blocks against a background of speed and technique.** "The organisation of loading provides for exploiting the LDTE of the block of strength work in each mesocycle against a background of the fundamental speed and technical training. The basic principle is block loading with means of different primary emphasis." Technique is "not excluded during the strength loading block. However, such work is included at reduced intensity using the separate elements and their links (see 2.1.2), as well as the rhythmic patterns of individual phases" (PDF p. 394). LDTE is the book's long-term delayed training effect of concentrated strength loading.
3. **Second block: less volume, more intensity.** "The second strength block imposes a smaller volume, although the general loading intensity is higher than in the first block. Since the second block is executed against a background of the adaptation occurring in the first mesocycle, the LDTE will be preserved during the second competitive stage. It is unnecessary at this time to further increase the volume of strength work, which can be used exclusively for preparing the neuromuscular system before the subsequent training that emphasizes technique or competitive readiness" (PDF p. 394).
4. **Block contents.** The blocks follow "the principle of preserving the training potential of the loading by means of the conjugate sequence system (5.3.3)" (PDF p. 394). The section just before 6.14.1 shows what a speed-strength block holds: "Jumping > Weights exercises > Plyometrics," "not sharply separated by time intervals, but substituted continuously for one another, ensuring that intensity and functional indicators are monitored carefully to avoid overtraining" (PDF p. 394; Fig 6.38, Verkhoshansky 1977). In Fig 6.38 the three overlapping volume waves are A jumps (early, small), B weights exercises (middle, the largest) and C plyometric depth jumps (late, small); read from the image, no numeric axis.
5. **GPP.** "Within each block, they offer variety and aid restoration after high volume strength loading, while at the LDTE stage, the GPP assists restoration after intense specialised loading... The largest relative volume of GPP means occurs during the competitive periods" (PDF p. 394). See [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]].

**Fig 6.39, read from the image (all month values "about"; no vertical scale).** The time axis runs 11 months (the 6.14 conventions: "Each model consists of about 11 months, since, on average, one month is allotted for the final transition period," PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379). Phases: I (1st preparation) about months 1-4, II (1st competition) about month 5, III (2nd preparation) about months 6-8, IV (2nd competition) about months 9-11. The phase boundaries and dashed lines do not fall exactly on the month ticks (phase I ends late in month 4; phase III ends during month 8). Block 1 is a tall shaded rectangle over about months 1-3; block 2 is a shorter rectangle over about months 6-7, roughly two thirds of block 1's height, matching the text's "smaller volume." Upper panel: all three strength curves (Starting, Explosive, Maximum) fall during block 1 after a small early bump in the two upper curves, rise to a first peak at about months 4-5 (around the phase I/II boundary), dip again during block 2 (about months 6-7), then climb through phase IV to their highest values at month 11. The two upper curves cross at about months 8-9, so only the right-edge order is certain: Starting Strength ends highest, then Explosive Strength, then Maximum Strength. Lower panel: Technique rises inside block 1, falls during block 2, then rises to its highest level at about months 9-10 and declines toward month 11. The GPP and Speed curves cross several times and cannot be told apart reliably in the image; the text is the source for GPP being highest in the competitive periods.

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the LDTE: the concentrated block lowers the athlete's state, and the gain appears afterward, so technique and speed work is timed for the period after the block. For concentrated loading in general they state a mechanism at PDF p. 381 / printed p. 370 (checked against the page image): it "produces a brief, fairly stable state of incomplete restoration which is associated with the persistent and relatively prolonged disturbance of homeostasis. This triggers extensive functional changes which are prerequisites for subsequent supercompensation." The second block can be smaller because it runs "against a background of the adaptation occurring in the first mesocycle" (PDF p. 394). No data are shown for this model; Fig 6.39 is a schematic credited to Siff & Verkhoshansky (1999).

**When to apply** — Planning a year for an explosive-strength sport with two clearly separated competition phases: put the large strength block early in the first preparation phase, a smaller and more intense block early in the second preparation phase, keep technique work going at reduced intensity inside each block, and shift to technique, speed and competition readiness as the delayed effect appears. Eric's baseline: "In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: football has one long competition phase, not two, so the model maps onto the football year only partly: a large block in the winter off-season and a smaller, more intense block in the summer before fall camp would follow the model's block sizes, with phase IV standing in for the season. The authors do not discuss football or weekly competition.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin.** Every model in 6.14 uses the concentrated block: "All models in this chapter use the principle of concentrated special strength loading, which elicits the LDTE" (PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379, checked against the page image). The library's brief of Issurin 2016 records that concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports "improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance," and that Issurin judged the evidence "insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation" (brief, p. 6), and saw the model as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality (p. 11); see [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]. American football is a team sport. Other limits: the model is drawn for "highly qualified athletes" (the concentrated method "was devised for preparing highly qualified athletes," PDF p. 381); the block rectangles are not literal ("The use of rectangular blocks should not create the impression that the concentrated loads are applied suddenly at peak intensity," PDF p. 391 / printed p. 380); and stage boundaries "can vary somewhat" with the real calendar (PDF p. 391). Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule" (line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: that rule fits the model's phase IV, where the strength block is over, but the model gives no in-season strength dose, and the baseline's game week ("lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game," line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)) is a microcycle rule the annual model does not address.

**Example** — The authors give the model, not a worked year (Fig 6.39, PDF p. 395). Inference: for a jumper with indoor and outdoor seasons, block 1 would sit in the first three months of autumn preparation with the jumps, weights and depth-jump sequence inside it, the indoor season would fall about month 5, block 2 would run about months 6-7 at less volume and more intensity, and the main outdoor competitions would fall in months 9-11.

**Related** — [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[heuristic--sequence-jumps-then-barbell-then-depth-jumps-across-stages]], [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]], [[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]], [[heuristic--follow-a-concentrated-block-with-moderate-volume-explosive-work]], [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]], [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]], [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]]

# Annual Models for Endurance Sports: Bi-Cyclic With Two Strength Blocks for Medium Duration, Monocyclic With Two Strength Blocks for Long Duration

**What it is** — Two prescriptive models from 6.14.2 and 6.14.3 (PDF pp. 395-397 / printed pp. 384-386; text and Figs 6.40 and 6.41 checked against the page images; Fig 6.46 on PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389).

**Medium-duration endurance (bi-cyclic, Fig 6.40).**
- Two mesocycles and two competition stages; in the first "one need not compete at the fundamental distance," but can compete "at other distances," which "simultaneously serve as control estimates of the athlete's level of aerobic and anaerobic capacity" (PDF p. 395).
- "Explosive strength peaks at the beginning of the second competition stage, after which it decreases, together with the rise in the volume of intense (anaerobic-glycolytic) cyclic work." Anaerobic capacity and strength-endurance "reach their highest levels during the most important competitive stage (10th - 11th months)" (PDF p. 395).
- Aerobic loading predominates in the first preparatory stage; "during the second stage the work is chiefly at the OBLA (onset of blood lactate accumulation) level"; aerobic volume rises again in the second competition stage "to promote restoration." Speed work (ATP-CP) and speed-endurance (glycolytic) are timed for the LDTE stage, "i.e. the development of speed precedes that of speed-endurance." Overall sequence: "General endurance > Speed > Speed-endurance" (PDF p. 395).
- Strength block contents: "The first block emphasizes the development of explosive strength and local muscular endurance, while the second emphasizes mainly local muscular endurance" (PDF p. 396 / printed p. 385).
- Fig 6.40, read by eye: block 1 over about months 2-4 (taller), block 2 over about months 6-7 (shorter); phases I about months 1-4, II about month 5, III about months 6-8, IV about months 9-11. For a large mesocycle (Fig 6.46, PDF pp. 399-400), aerobic training "covers the first half of the large mesocycle during which the GPP and concentrated strength loading take place," then speed, then specialised endurance, with competitions as a main way to develop it.

**Long-duration endurance (monocyclic, Fig 6.41).**
- "Competition in long duration events requires a long preparatory period (up to 6 months) for creating stable adaptation to preserve the special work-capacity for some 4-5 months during the competitive period" (PDF p. 396).
- Stable results come "if the increase in loading during the preparatory period occurs gradually (a mean monthly increase of 7-14%), if there is not a sharp drop in the volume of loading during the competitive period, and if the portion of loading in the zone of anaerobic energy production is not increased (Gilyazova, 1978)" (PDF p. 396). See [[claim--prolonged-competition-period-volume-cuts-lower-special-work-capacity]].
- "Within a monocycle of periodisation, it provides a two-stage organisation of strength and speed training": "The first block contains general conditioning strength work, while the second block emphasizes the development of local muscular endurance," carrying work capacity "right up to the important competitions in the 10th and 11th months" (PDF p. 396).
- Fig 6.41, read by eye: phase I about months 1-6, phase II about months 6-11; block 1 over about months 2-3, block 2 over about months 6-7. Aerobic capacity peaks around the start of the competition period and then eases, as the text says ("maximum aerobic productivity at the beginning of the competition period, and some decrease," PDF p. 397).

**Why it works** — Both models rest on the LDTE of concentrated strength blocks and on timing speed and speed-endurance after them. The only cited data are Gilyazova (1978) for the monocyclic loading conditions; the figures are schematics (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).

**When to apply** — Annual planning for middle-distance (medium) or long-distance (long) endurance athletes who use strength blocks. Not a football model; the medium-duration sequence "General endurance > Speed > Speed-endurance" is the transferable idea. Eric's baseline: "A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once" and "priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 115, Explicit; the two phrases are joined by a dash in the baseline). Inference: both models pick one energy-system emphasis per stage in that spirit.

**When NOT to apply** — Long-duration sports are given a monocycle, while the 6.13 aims call for "at least two large mesocycles... even in sports which traditionally... use monocyclic periodisation" (PDF p. 389); see [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]] for this internal conflict. The models are for qualified athletes and carry the same Issurin 2016 challenge to concentrated loading as the other 6.14 models ([[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]). Fig 6.46's caption says "A is the block of concentrated strength loading," but the figure prints "GPP" under A and "Strength Load" under B; which wave is the strength block is unclear.

**Example** — The authors give the schematics only. Inference: an 800 m runner competes at 400 m and 1500 m in the first competition stage as control tests, then runs the main 800 m season in months 10-11 after a smaller second block focused on local muscular endurance.

**Related** — [[claim--prolonged-competition-period-volume-cuts-lower-special-work-capacity]], [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[framework--speed-sport-block-organisation-and-two-glycolytic-peaks]], [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]], [[principle--local-muscular-endurance-adaptation-is-specific-to-the-trained-muscles]]

147	Two types of model are distinguished: qualitative and quantitative. The qualitative model describes the 
148	dynamics of the athlete's state (the functional indicators), the most important parameters of the contents (such as 
149	strength, endurance and speed-strength training) and the interconnections between the components of training 
150	(e.g. concentrated loads, preparatory phases, microcycies and mesocycles). The quantitative model contains all 
151	numerical aspects of the training in microcycies, mesocycles and macrocycles, such as calculation of volume, 
152	intensity, duration of stages and loading distribution in different intensity zones (see 6.2.2). Before specific 
153	models are analysed, it is useful to present some of the general information concerning them:

155	model consists of about 11 months, since, on average, one month is allotted for the final transition period.

157	dynamics of the athlete's state (the functional indicators, e.g. as shown in upper diagram of Fig 6.39) and a 
158	model of the programme of loading (e.g. lower diagram in Fig 6.39). The scheme of training construction in 
159	each sport group is based on that periodisation regime of annual training which best characterises it.
160	3. The model of the dynamics o f the athlete's fitness state includes the most important functional indicators of 
161	special work capacity. One can use any method that enables one to measure the values of these indicators.
162	4. All models in this chapter use the principle of concentrated special strength loading, which elicits the LDTE. 
163	The strength loading is represented by blocks which arc timed to occupy specific stages of the annual cycle.
164	5. By describing the qualitative features of training organisation, the models present the most desirable trend 
165	in the distribution of the volume of loading of different emphasis over the annual cycle and the variation of

172	peak intensity according to some step function; the actual loading follows a concentrated wave pattern which 
173	gradually reaches a peak, then subsides in volume (as in Fig 6.38).
174	6. The boundaries of the stages and dates of the major competitions in the given models are based on the most 
175	typical schemes of events in each sport. However, if the actual calendar is taken into account, they can vary 
176	somewhat so as to fulfill the general principles of loading organisation.
177	Examples of Descriptive Modelling
178	It would require a large separate volume for cach sport to present the most important qualitative and quantitative 
179	factors which constitute a thorough descriptive model in every ease. However, it is useful to select a few 
180	examples of the types of information that feature in such a model.
181	For instance, kinanthropometric data in weightlifting would include the bodymass-height, strength-bodymass 
182	and strength-age relationships discussed in Section 3.3. Other useful information may be obtained from lean 
183	muscle mass or bodyfat ratios, and physical work capacity (PWC170) measurements (Table 6.6).
184	Many years of Russian research have produced models for every type of sport which offer information not 
185	only on the sport specific movements, but also on any supplementary exercises or tests that arc of importance in a 
186	given sport. These norms enable the coach to identify any weaknesses in the state of the athlete and thereby 
187	modify the training programme to improve results.

189	sport unless accurate numerical determinations are regularly made of each of these factors. Even then, we have to 
190	remember that the body is not simply a machine in which input and output are deterministically related, but an 
191	organism whose behaviour displays non-linearity and fairly random deviations form what one may expect on the 
192	basis of quantitative measurements. Nevertheless, without this information, long-term programming becomes 
193	imprecise with little hope of producing consistent, reasonably predictable growth of results. It is useful to study

635	The Composition of the Concentrated Loading Volume
636	As mentioned earlier, the rectangular blocks used in the diagrams of the training models to depict stages of 
637	concentrated loading are not intended to show their precise form or contents. Each block represents concentrated 
638	loading of a primary emphasis, which does not necessarily utilise only one means of training. For instance, a 
639	concentrated block intended to increase speed-strength may consist of several different resistance and jumping 
640	means and methods introduced in a specific conjugate sequence.
641	In Figure 6.38, methods with a successively greater training effect are sequenced within the concentrated 
642	loading stage, thus: Jumping > Weights exercises > Plyometrics. These exercises are not sharply separated by 
643	time intervals, but substituted continuously for one another, ensuring that intensity and functional indicators arc 
644	monitored carefully to avoid overtraining.
645	Figure 6.38 Structure and contents of exercises within a typical concentrated loading volume for speed-strength sports. A - jumps, B= 
646	weights exercises, C ■ plyometric depth jumps. (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
647	It is now appropriate to examine principal prescriptive models of the systems of constructing training in the 
648	annual cycle for a number of sport groups.
649	6.14.1 A Model for Sports requiring Explosive Strength
650	This model involves bi-cyclic periodisation of training and includes two mesocycles aimed at optimally 
651	developing the body's current adaptation reserves and achieving the planned level of special-strength 
652	preparedness at the most important competitions (Fig 6.39). The model of the dynamics of the athlete’s fitness 
653	state (upper diagram) shows the optimal trend in the changes of the absolute, explosive and starting strength 
654	indicators, the highest values of which are achieved at the end of each mesocycle.
655	The organisation of loading provides for exploiting the LDTE of the block of strength work in each 
656	mcsocycle against a background of the fundamental speed and technical training. The basic principle is block 
657	loading with means of different primary emphasis, which creates favourable conditions for in-depth improvement 
658	of technique and uni-directional preparation for competition. As stated before, technique work is not excluded 
659	during the strength loading block. However, such work is included at reduced intensity using the separate 
660	elements and their links (sec 2.1.2), as well as the rhythmic patterns of individual phases.
661	The second strength block imposes a smaller volume, although the general loading intensity is higher than in 
662	the first block. Since the second block is executed against a background of the adaptation occurring in the first 
663	mesocycle, the LDTE will be preserved during the second competitive stage. It is unnecessary at this time to 
664	further increase the volume of strength work, which can be used exclusively for preparing the neuromuscular 
665	system before the subsequent training that emphasizes technique or competitive readiness. The contents and the 
666	organisation of the strength loading blocks are based on the principle of preserving the training potential of the 
667	loading by means of the conjugate sequence system (5.3.3).
668	The means of GPP have a specific purpose. Within each block, they offer variety and aid restoration after 
669	high volume strength loading, while at the LDTE stage, the GPP assists restoration after intense specialised 
670	loading. It should always be remembered that this procedure constitutes part of pedagogical restoration, which 
671	facilitates recovery alongside other methods such as sports massage (see 8.5). The largest relative volume of 
672	GPP means occurs during the competitive periods.
673	383
674	
675	######## PDF 395 (printed 384)
676	SUPERTRAINING
677	Figure 6.39 A model of constructing the training for sports requiring explosive effort. I = the 1st preparation phase, II = the 1st 
678	competition phase. III = the 2nd preparauon phase. IV = the 2nd competition phase. The shaded blocks represent the stages of 
679	concentrated special strength loading to promote the subsequent LDTE. (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
680	6.14.2 A Model for Medium Duration Endurance Sports
681	The model is based on bi-cyclic periodisation and consists of two mesocyclcs designed for optimally developing 
682	the current adaptation reserves (Fig 6.40). There are two competition stages in the annual cycle and one need not 
683	compete at the fundamental distance during the first stage. Here, it is important to maintain the trend towards 
684	intensifying the training, in order to increase the current adaptation reserves. One can achieve this by competing 
685	at other distances in competition, which will simultaneously serve as control estimates of the athlete’s level of 
686	aerobic and anaerobic capacity.
687	The model of the dynamics of the athlete's state promotes twin-peaked changes in aerobic and anaerobic 
688	capacity. The dynamics of the special strength preparedness arc expressed in the form of an accelerated increase 
689	in general strength-endurance and special endurance for repetitive production of explosive force (i.e. explosive 
690	strength-endurance) during the second competitive stage, as well as by the planned rise in maximum strength.
691	Explosive strength peaks at the beginning of the second competition stage, after which it decreases, together 
692	with the rise in the volume of intense (anaerobic-glycolytic) cyclic work. The fundamental functional indicators, 
693	namely anaerobic capacity and strength-endurance, reach their highest levels during the most important 
694	competitive stage (10th - 11th months).
695	This organisation of loading combines two strength blocks concurrently with special 
696	aerobic-anaerobic 
697	work, where the ratio of aerobic to anaerobic work changes over the annual cycle. There is a predominance of 
698	aerobic loading during the first preparatory stage; during the second stage the work is chiefly at the OBLA (onset 
699	of blood lactate accumulation) level. There is an increase in the volume of aerobic loading again during the 
700	second competition stage, its role being to promote restoration. Speed work (primarily in the ATP-CP zone) and 
701	the development of speed-endurance (chiefly in the anaerobic-glycolytic zone) are timed for the stage where one 
702	realises the LDTE of the strength loading, i.e. the development of speed precedes that of speed-endurance.
703	Thus, the general strategy of loading organisation in the annual cycle is based on the following sequence of 
704	enhancing special work capacity: General endurance > Speed > Speed-endurance, the orientation of the training 
705	process being towards the systematic development of strength and speed-cndurance during the stage when there 
706	are important competitions.

SUPERTRAINING
competitive preparedness. The necessary contents, volume and organisation of training and competition 
loading are determined on the basis of this training emphasis. The central trait of the mesocycle is the 
execution of all the intermediate tasks associated with special physical, technical and competition preparation.
Thus, the large mesocycle is a relatively independent part of the annual cycle which integrates the fundamental 
forms and skills of training prescribed for all the microcycies. The duration of the large mesocycle can vary 
(usually 3-5 months), since its calculation depends on the competition calendar and especially on the dates of the 
most important competitions.
Research shows that it is appropriate to use two large mesocycles in the annual cycle to promote 
supercompensation of the current adaptation reserves (Figure 6.34). In this case, the athlete's state displays two 
large peaks, with the second one producing the higher special work-capacity (i.e. fitness state). This further 
corroborates the value of this form of bi-cyclic organisation of annual preparation which was empirically worked 
out and applied successfully long ago in several sports.
Consequently, unquestioning adherence to monocyclic periodisation in a number of sports is not justified, 
and it is advisable that coaches re-examine this tradition carefully. Bi-cyclic periodisation may also be applied in 
several different types of sport which traditionally employ other forms of periodisation, in particular monocyclic 
forms in skiing (Ogoltsov, 1979) and middle-distancc running (Turin, 1980; Sirenko, 1980), as well as tri-cyclical 
forms in boxing (Nikiforov & Viktorov, 1978) and swimming (Vaitsekhovsky, 1981). In a number of team sports 
and one-on-one events, tri-cyclic periodisation may have to be used, as dictated by the competition calendar, 
whereas in long-duration endurance sports, monocyclic periodisation is usually recommended.
Figure 634 Organisation of annual training with two mesocycles o f strength loading (SifF & Vcrkhoshansky, 1999).
The principles of programming and organising training in the annual cycle will be discussed later, but it is 
relevant now to examine the microcycle more carefully.
In planning large mesocycles, the problem of fitting in the necessary volume of work arises, which 
complicates the structuring the microcycle. In this respect, all traditional schemes of constructing a microcycle 
with complex training to achieve several simultaneous training objectives and increase specific work capacity at 
the beginning of a new microcycle do not satisfy these requirements. It is necessary to seek new forms of 
constructing microcycies which permit the use of high volumes of loading, including unidirectional regimes. It is 
important to note that microcycies are the basic units of training construction, whose function is to utilise those 
parts of the volume which help them to comply with the objectives and general strategy of the mesocycle.
It is relevant now to examine the currently scant experimental findings which suggest ways of solving these 
problems. It has been established that large unidirectional loading sharply reduces the capability of displaying 
those qualities and abilities which facilitate the effective and safe execution of training programmes. At the same 
time, athletes who exhibit a high work capacity generally achieve it by means of other training systems 
(Monogarov& Platonov, 1975; Fedorova et al, 1975; Chepclyev, 1980; Platonov, 1980).
For example, a week's cycle was devised (Fig 6.35), which took into account the length of restoration periods 
needed by highly qualified swimmers after high volume unidirectional workouts. The scheme was intended to 
achieve a generally high volume of loading using a systematic combination of workouts of different magnitude 
and emphasis which took into account the duration of the accompanying restoration processes.
It should be noted that, despite the uni-directional character of individual workouts, the microcyclc as the 
whole typifies the complex (multi-faceted) form o f training organisation. The body cannot simultaneously 
differentiate between and accumulate specific reactions to every type of daily loading and respond to them with 
generalised reactions which contain separate proportions of adaptation to each of the different training influences. 
Therefore, this form of microcycle construction enables one to achieve a large volume of loading, but the absence
376
