14	
15	# In a Long Monocyclic Competition Period, a Prolonged Cut in Loading Volume Lowers Fitness; Competition Plus Small Special Loads Cannot Maintain It
16	
17	**What it is** — In the long-duration endurance model (PDF p. 396 / printed p. 385, checked against the page image): "It has been established that the prolonged reduction in the volume of loading during the competition period (with monocyclic periodisation) leads to re-adaptation at a lower level, which is reflected in the drop of non-specific trainability. Competition and special supplementary loading (with limited volumes) cannot stimulate further development or even maintain special work-capacity. Thus, it is appropriate to periodically increase the volume of competition and special assistance loading (Baranovsky, 1969; Kryazh, 1969; Muzis, 1970; Zhikharevich, 1976)." The paired condition from Gilyazova (1978) is that stable results need "not a sharp drop in the volume of loading during the competitive period" and a gradual preparatory increase ("a mean monthly increase of 7-14%") (PDF p. 396).
18	
19	**Why it works** — The authors' explanation is "re-adaptation at a lower level": the body adapts down to the reduced load. They give no physiological detail and no data beyond the four citations.
20	
21	**When to apply** — Long competition periods (the model's is "some 4-5 months," PDF p. 396) in which the athlete would otherwise only compete and do light maintenance: build in periodic increases in special and assistance volume. Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Also: "In-season programming deliberately waves volume and intensity even when the practice schedule looks repetitive week to week, specifically to avoid training monotony for the athlete" (line 181, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the authors' warning is against a *prolonged* volume cut in a long season; the baseline's in-season waving, and the bye-week "speed and strength top-up" (line 187, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q17)), are the kind of periodic volume increase the authors call for. A football season of games is shorter than the model's 4-5 month competition period, and the sport is not an endurance sport.
22	
23	**When NOT to apply** — The statement is made for long-duration endurance sports under monocyclic periodisation; the authors do not extend it to strength or team sports. It does not mean intensity can be dropped. In the explosive-strength model the second strength block deliberately carries less volume than the first ("It is unnecessary at this time to further increase the volume of strength work," PDF p. 394 / printed p. 383), so the rule applies to special and competition loading in endurance sport, not to every quality in every sport.
24	
25	**Example** — The authors give no worked case. Inference: a marathoner in a five-month racing season returns every few weeks to a higher-volume week of race-pace and assistance work instead of only racing and easy running between races.
26	
27	**Related** — [[framework--annual-models-for-medium-and-long-duration-endurance-sports]], [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]]

41	
42	# Tri-Cyclic Model for Individual and One-on-One Sports: Three Mesocycles for SPP, Technical Mastery and Competition Readiness, Each With Its Own Strength Block
43	
44	**What it is** — 6.14.4 (PDF p. 397 / printed p. 386, checked against the page image; Fig 6.42 on PDF p. 398 / printed p. 387, checked against the image): "The tri-cyclic model is intended primarily for individual and one-on-one sports (Fig 6.42). It comprises three mesocycles, with preparatory and competitive micro-stages. The first stage is oriented chiefly towards special physical preparation; the second, to perfecting technical mastery, and the third, to readiness for the major competitions." The third stage "can be increased by shortening the duration of the second stage," and "In certain cases a bi-cyclic model of training can be employed with this group of sports."
45	- **Athlete-state model:** maximum aerobic productivity in the second stage, then some decrease; "Maximum strength rises uniformly, while strength-endurance accelerates more during the third stage. Explosive strength reaches a maximum at the beginning of the second and at the end of the third stages."
46	- **Three strength blocks:** the first "to develop maximum and explosive strength; the second, to develop strength-endurance; the third, chiefly to increase explosive strength and create conditions for exploiting the LDTE of the strength loading during the fundamental competition phase."
47	- **Energy-system pairing:** "The first and third blocks of strength work are executed in combination with special work in the mixed (aerobic-anaerobic) zone of energy production, while the second is combined with work in the anaerobic (ATP-CP and anaerobic-glycolytic) zone. The fundamental volume of speed and technical-tactical preparation is executed against a background of the LDTE elicited by the blocks of strength work."
48	- **Fig 6.42, read by eye:** phases I about months 1-4, II about months 5-8, III about months 9-11. Block 1 about months 1-3 (tallest), block 2 about months 5-6, block 3 about months 9-10 (shortest). The labels at the right edge of the upper panel read, top to bottom, Explosive strength, Anaerobic capacity, Aerobic capacity, Strength-endurance, with Maximum strength lowest and rising nearly linearly. Shorter mesocycles of this kind "should not shift achieving the objective of optimal enhancement of the current adaptation reserves (CAR) to the next stage" (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389).
49	
50	**Why it works** — The authors give the structure, not a mechanism beyond the LDTE of each strength block. No data are shown; the figure is credited to Siff & Verkhoshansky (1999).
51	
52	**When to apply** — Individual and combat sports with three main competition periods, such as the boxing and swimming examples the authors cite for tri-cyclic forms (PDF p. 387 / printed p. 376), and team sports where "tri-cyclic periodisation may have to be used, as dictated by the competition calendar" (PDF p. 387). Eric's baseline: "The head coach's system of play and roster identity (e.g., a "home run hitters" lineup vs. a "steal bases" lineup) is treated as a direct input into whether a team's programming leans toward maximal strength or toward speed/power emphasis" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 188, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the model's block contents (maximum, endurance, explosive) are the kind of lever that input would set.
53	
54	**When NOT to apply** — **Issurin 2016 challenge (combat sports).** The library's brief of Issurin 2016 records that concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports improved some fitness measures without reported effects on practice or competitive performance, and that Issurin judged the evidence insufficient for broad use in "high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation" (brief, p. 6; [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]). This entry keeps `supported` because the tri-cyclic layout itself is not what Issurin challenges; the challenge is to the concentrated blocks inside it, recorded on [[claim--concentrated-strength-loading-limited-period-qualified-athletes-and-volume-saving]]. The model assumes three distinct competition peaks; it is not a template for a weekly-competition season.
55	
56	**Example** — The authors give the schematic only. Inference: a wrestler with a winter national championship, a spring continental event and a late-summer world championship runs a maximum-strength block in autumn, a strength-endurance block in late winter with anaerobic work, and a short explosive block before the summer peak.
57	
58	**Related** — [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[heuristic--set-mesocycle-boundaries-by-main-competition-dates]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]], [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]

72	
73	# Follow a High-Volume, Low-Intensity Concentrated Block With Moderate-Volume Explosive Work to Enlarge the Delayed Training Effect
74	
75	**What it is** — Under the heading "More Advanced Use of Concentrated Loading" (PDF p. 397 / printed p. 386, checked against the page image) the authors modify the separated-block models of 6.14: "in speed-strength sports, the magnitude of the delayed training effect (LDTE) may be enhanced further if the concentrated loading is followed by specialised work of moderate volume, which includes higher power or more explosive muscle contraction regimes, such as jumps, plyometrics and maximal attempts." The loads overlap: "There is an overlapping of the different training volumes, which peak smoothly in each case to ensure optimal increase in the LDTE" (PDF p. 398 / printed p. 387). In the bi-cyclic version, "stages A and C refer to concentrated periods of high volume, low intensity work and stages B and D to moderate volumes of specialised, higher intensity speed-strength work. This scheme has been recommended to ensure continuous increase in special strength over a long period (Verkhoshansky, 1978)" (PDF p. 398).
76	
77	The figures, read from the page images (no numeric axes):
78	- **Fig 6.43** (PDF p. 398, monocyclic large mesocycle): a tall wave A in the preparatory phase, a smaller wave B starting as A falls and peaking at about the start of the competition phase. The speed-strength curve sags while A is high, then rises through B and keeps rising into the competition phase.
79	- **Fig 6.44** (PDF p. 399 / printed p. 388, bi-cyclic): tall A, small B, tall C, small D in sequence. Speed-strength dips during A, rises during B, flattens or dips slightly during C, and rises again after it to its highest level at the right.
80	- **Fig 6.45** (PDF p. 399, a large mesocycle for speed-strength sports): the text says "the concentrated strength loading block occupies the first half of the large mesocycle, following the groundwork laid by general physical preparation (GPP) and the peak amount of aerobic work... Technique and speed training occupies the second half." The figure shows an aerobic-work curve peaking early, a large shaded wave over the first half, a second shaded wave over the second half labelled "Technique and Speed," and a fitness-state curve that dips then rises to its highest point at the right.
81	
82	**Why it works** — The authors give a principle rather than a measured mechanism: overlapping loads that "peak smoothly" serve the LDTE, and "the inclusion of regular passive and active restoration periods between stages of greater loading is important to facilitate development of the LDTE" (PDF p. 398). They also argue for putting the bulk of strength work early: "Since large volumes of strength and technique training generally are incompatible, the greatest quantity of strength work should be done during the preparatory period, with more emphasis being placed on technique work during the competitive phase when the LDTE rises markedly" (PDF p. 399). No data are shown; the figures are schematics credited to Siff & Verkhoshansky (1999).
83	
84	**When to apply** — Speed-strength athletes coming out of a high-volume strength block: bring in moderate volumes of jumps, plyometrics and maximal attempts as the block tapers, rather than dropping straight to technique and speed alone. The authors say the boundaries are loose: "stage B does not necessarily begin where shown, but may commence far earlier, while stage A may tail off right near the end of phase B" (PDF p. 398; "phase B" is printed as such). The authors tie this to Matveyev's "non-discreteness of the preparatory and competitive phases": "it is sometimes perfectly appropriate to have elements of each intermingled in various 'doses'" (PDF p. 398). Eric's baseline: "Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: the A-then-B wave is one way to stage that shift within one off-season.
85	
86	**When NOT to apply** — The scheme is stated for speed-strength sports. It assumes the A stage is "high volume, low intensity," consistent with the low-intensity condition for concentrated loading ([[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]]); an A stage built from heavy, intense lifting is a different situation the authors do not cover. **Unclear figure labels:** the caption of Fig 6.45 says "A is the block of concentrated strength loading, while B and C refer to the types of training identified in the diagram," but in the figure the label "GPP" sits under wave A and "Strength Load" sits under wave B (PDF p. 399). Fig 6.46 has the same mismatch (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389). Which wave is the strength block cannot be settled from the page. No dose for the B stage is given beyond "moderate volume."
87	
88	**Example** — The authors give the schematics only. Inference: after a four-week block of high-volume, moderate-load squats, pulls and loaded jumps, a jumper adds two short weekly sessions of bounding, a few depth jumps and one or two near-maximal lifts, with that work peaking about when the first competitions begin.
89	
90	**Related** — [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]], [[heuristic--sequence-jumps-then-barbell-then-depth-jumps-across-stages]], [[principle--sequentially-introduce-means-of-greater-training-effect]], [[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]], [[heuristic--loading-reduction-for-the-delayed-effect-must-outlast-1-2-weeks]]

104	
105	# Technical Mastery Comes Only From Practice at Competition-Like Intensity; Skill Learned at Low Intensity Does Not Usually Transfer to Maximal Efforts
106	
107	**What it is** — The authors (PDF p. 399 / printed p. 388, checked against the page image): "technical mastery can be acquired only through practice with high intensity loading which simulates competition conditions. Proficiency gained under conditions of low stimulation and intensity do not usually transfer successfully to the maximal effort situations of top-level competition. This is relevant to the use of visualisation to perfect sporting movements; this technique is not very successful if it does not offer mental simulation of the movements, the feelings and the competitive circumstances under which the movements have to be displayed. Practice only makes perfect if one practises all components of the performance process under the conditions which mimic those of the sporting event as closely as possible." The same idea appears as the seventh primary aim, "Modelling competition activities" at "the high intensity which is encountered in competition" (PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379), and in the medium-endurance model: "*competitions, of course, constitute the most specific form of special preparation in any sport*" (italics in the original; PDF p. 399).
108	
109	**Why it works** — The authors state the rule without a mechanism or a cited study on this page. Inference: it is the book's specificity principle applied to skill; the book's own criteria for when training matches the sport are in [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]] (section 4.3).
110	
111	**When to apply** — Deciding when and how hard to practise the competition skill: the low-intensity technique work done during a strength block ([[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]]) is preparation, and the skill must later be practised at full intensity under competition-like conditions, starting in the preparatory period (the authors: "it would be too late were it to commence in the competitive period," PDF p. 382 / printed p. 371). For mental rehearsal, include the feel and the competitive setting, not just the movement pattern. Eric's baseline: "The Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky), matching amplitude/direction of movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production, and regime of muscular work to the sport skill, governs whether an exercise actually transfers, rather than surface resemblance to the sport" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 103, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)).
112	
113	**When NOT to apply** — The same chapter allows and recommends low-intensity technique work during concentrated loading for learning components (PDF p. 383), so the rule is about where mastery is finished, not a ban on low-intensity practice. The authors say "do not usually transfer," not never. Inference: for novices learning a movement for the first time, low-intensity practice is the normal starting point; the authors' context here is "top-level competition."
114	
115	**Example** — The authors' own example is visualisation that rehearses only the movement shape and so "is not very successful" (PDF p. 399). Inference: a shot-putter who only drills the glide at half speed in the off-season and first throws at full effort in meets would be expected to see the technique break down under maximal effort.
116	
117	**Related** — [[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]], [[principle--training-effort-must-match-or-exceed-sport-effort-judged-by-movement-speed]], [[framework--seven-primary-aims-of-programming-training]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]
118	=================== heuristic--set-mesocycle-boundaries-by-main-competition-dates.md
119	---
120	type: library-entry
121	kind: heuristic
122	domain: strength-and-conditioning

124	chapter: "6.14.5"
125	topic: mesocycle boundaries and calendar
126	category: [annual-plan, competition-calendar, mesocycle, periodization, recovery]

130	---
131	
132	# Set Mesocycle Boundaries Only by the Main Competition Dates, Treat the First Mesocycle as the Foundation for the Second, and Recuperate After Each Competitive Stage
133	
134	**What it is** — The authors' four practical principles for when the calendar and adaptation pull against each other (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389, checked against the page image). The conflict: "the dates of the main competitions may change radically, while the dates of traditional competitions remain the same. A worse situation arises if the competition season is extended and the length of the preparatory stages is shortened."
135	1. "Organisation of training should provide favourable conditions for promoting functional adaptation of the body within the constraints of the competition calendar. The calendar should be co-ordinated with the periods and duration of the mesocycles."
136	2. "The optimal period for enhancing the current adaptation reserves is about 20 weeks for the most efficient loading of highly qualified athletes." It "can be increased or decreased over a small range, which requires an appropriate increase or decrease in the concentration of loading. It is important in this case not to exceed the optimal time limit, since excessive intensification of training can disrupt adaptation."
137	3. "To determine the boundaries of the mesocycles, one should be guided only by the dates of the main competitions. This rule should not be broken for any reason, including the desire to demonstrate impressive results at the beginning of the season."
138	4. "The loading of the preparatory phase is more specialised and intense during the second mesocycle than the first. Therefore, the first mesocycle should always be considered as the foundation for the second. The interests of intermediate competitions should not alter this objective."
139	
140	Then, in italics in the original: "*one should be aware of the detrimental effect that competitive loading has on the athlete's state*, since it leads to serious exhaustion of nervous energy. Therefore, during the transition to the next mesocycle, it is necessary to include a recuperation period, the duration of which is determined individually, depending on the difficulty of the competitive stage" (PDF p. 400).
141	
142	**Why it works** — The authors' reason for rules 2 and 3 is the "current adaptation reserves": there is an optimal time over which they can be raised, and stretching or squeezing it changes how concentrated the loading must be. They give no study for the 20-week figure on this page ("It has already been mentioned," referring back to earlier sections outside this batch). The recuperation rule rests on the "serious exhaustion of nervous energy" from competition, without data.
143	
144	**When to apply** — Drawing an annual plan: place the main competitions first, cut the year into mesocycles from those dates, and do not move the boundaries to chase early-season results or to serve minor meets. Eric's baseline: "In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: under rule 3, November and the postseason would set the boundary of the final mesocycle, and early-season games would be treated as the authors' "intermediate competitions," which "should not alter this objective."
145	
146	**When NOT to apply** — Rule 3's "should not be broken for any reason" is the authors' strongest wording in the section, but it assumes one or two main competitions; in a sport with a weekly game, every game counts, and the rule does not say how to weight them. The 20-week figure is for "highly qualified athletes." The recuperation period has no stated length. Issurin's competing structure uses stages of "about two months" ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]); see [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]].
147	
148	**Example** — The authors' own example of the problem is a season that is "extended" while "the length of the preparatory stages is shortened" (PDF p. 400). Inference: a jumper whose national championship moves three weeks earlier shortens the second mesocycle by concentrating its loading more, rather than shifting the boundary to keep a full block before an early-season invitational.
149	
150	**Related** — [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]], [[framework--eight-step-sequence-for-programming-annual-training]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[framework--tricyclic-annual-model-for-individual-and-one-on-one-sports]], [[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--nine-step-annual-program-construction-sequence]]
151	=================== framework--eight-step-sequence-for-programming-annual-training.md
152	---
153	type: library-entry
154	kind: framework
155	domain: strength-and-conditioning
156	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
157	chapter: "6.15"
158	topic: annual programming sequence
159	category: [annual-plan, programming, periodization, planning-process, testing]
160	confidence: supported

162	created: 2026-10-03
163	---
164	
165	# Verkhoshansky's Eight-Step Sequence for Programming the Annual Cycle, From Target Results Down to the Microcycles
166	
167	**What it is** — The authors recommend "the following sequence of logical operations, where each calculation is made by taking into account the calculation made in the preceding operation (Verkhoshansky, 1985)" (PDF p. 401 / printed p. 390, checked against the page image). The eight steps, with their key wording:
168	1. **Determine the progress in results and the dates.** "The calculations rely on a predictive model of the dynamics of the sport results relative to the competition calendar," based on "a multi-faceted objective assessment of the athlete's potential" and what is "realistically feasible in the current year at his level of mastery."
169	2. **Determine the needed changes in special physical preparedness and technical-tactical proficiency,** expressed as "specific goals, relative to the functional indicators and the characteristics of technical proficiency which must be achieved in the important competitions." "Subjective ratings of perceived effort (RPE) can be very useful in offering further guidance."
170	3. **Build quantitative models of the fitness state across the year** "so that these indicators peak in the main competitions."
171	4. **Select the training means and methods** by "assessing the training potential of the means and methods."
172	5. **Calculate the general volume of loading for all means,** based on "the accumulated effect of the loading in all preceding stages."
173	6. **Divide the year into mesocycles,** using "the competition calendar and the dates necessary for optimal increase of the body's current adaptation reserves."
174	7. **Calculate the distribution of loading over the year,** expressed as "the quantitative dynamics of the loading imposed by the fundamental training means."
175	8. **Organise loading over the mesocycle,** as "a detailed training programme giving the specific distribution of loading during each of the microcycles," based on "the characteristics of the LDTE of concentrated strength loading." "Provision should always be made available for introducing contingency changes in programmes, necessitated by unforeseen incidents such as injuries, changes in competitive timetables and personal disasters."
176	
177	The authors frame the difficulty first: "Its complexity, however, lies not so much in the quantity of calculations as in the insufficient basis for choosing and quantitatively determining the main operations. Therefore in practice, even experienced coaches need to make tentative computations which may have a low probability of producing a correct prognosis" (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389, checked against the page image).
178	
179	**Why it works** — The sequence is a top-down dependency chain: each step uses the one before. The authors give no evidence that following it improves results; it is a planning procedure.
180	
181	**When to apply** — Building or auditing an annual plan. Compare it with two other procedures in the library: Issurin's nine steps start from the competition calendar and end with obligatory correction after review ([[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--nine-step-annual-program-construction-sequence]]); Evans's ten steps start with a sport and position profile ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]]). Verkhoshansky's starts from the predicted result and the fitness changes needed to reach it, and only divides the year into mesocycles at step 6. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: step 8's contingency provision is the authors' version of that flexibility.
182	
183	**When NOT to apply** — The authors concede the operations rest on an "insufficient basis" and may have "a low probability of producing a correct prognosis" (PDF p. 400). Step 1 assumes a predictive model of performance exists; in team sports there is no single result to predict. The procedure is written for individual athletes and their competitions.
184	
185	**Example** — The authors give no worked plan in 6.15. Inference: for a triple jumper, step 1 sets a target of a 40 cm improvement at the national championship in month 10, step 2 converts it to target values for the standing triple jump and approach speed, and steps 6-8 then divide the year into two mesocycles and write the weekly loading.
186	
187	**Related** — [[framework--descriptive-and-prescriptive-training-models]], [[heuristic--set-mesocycle-boundaries-by-main-competition-dates]], [[framework--four-documents-for-programming-and-controlling-training]], [[principle--programme-objective-approach-quantified-goals-dictate-training]], [[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--nine-step-annual-program-construction-sequence]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]]

201	
202	# Manage Training by Testing Once or Twice a Month Under Constant Conditions and Comparing Results With Targets Each Month
203	
204	**What it is** — The authors define management as "control over the course of training and its prescription, based on a comparison of the actual dynamics of training with previous target standards," correcting course "by changing the appropriate parameters of the loading" (PDF p. 402 / printed p. 391, checked against the page image). Their guidelines (Verkhoshansky, 1985):
205	1. "One should first select the most informative fitness characteristics in order to assess the special physical preparedness, technical proficiency and psychological state of the athlete," using "special laboratory methods, control exercises (pedagogical tests) or functional sporting or standardised field tests."
206	2. "Control over the course of training can only be effective if one regularly analyses the dynamics of the athlete's state. When doing this, (a) testing should be done regularly once or twice a month, independent of the periodisation and structure of the training stages, (b) the testing procedure should not be excessively demanding on the time and energy of the athlete, (c) the testing conditions must be kept constant to exclude the possibility of random factors affecting the results, and (d) the testing must have functional relevance."
207	3. "Management requires a systematic comparison (over monthly periods) of the actual results and target goals of the training. If there is a discrepancy, it is necessary to carefully analyse the situation, determine the cause for such a discrepancy and revise the training programme."
208	
209	**Why it works** — The authors' logic is feedback control: without regular comparison against targets, deviations go unnoticed. They give no evidence for the once-or-twice-a-month frequency.
210	
211	**When to apply** — Setting up a testing calendar for a programme with written targets. Eric's baseline agrees on criteria (b) to (d): "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 34, Explicit) and "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention" (line 30, Explicit). On frequency it goes further for readiness: "Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker" (line 74, Explicit), with a Wednesday decision read: "Wednesdays, the thresholds should be individualized" (line 75, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a)). Inference: the two operate at different scales; the authors' monthly tests track progress toward annual targets, while daily jumps track short-term readiness, a level the authors treat separately as "largely random and at times unpredictable" acute changes (PDF p. 378 / printed p. 367, section 6.11, text layer).
212	
213	**When NOT to apply** — The monthly schedule is "independent of the periodisation," so a test may fall in the middle of a concentrated block, when the authors expect indicators to be depressed ([[framework--mesocycle-variants-smooth-rise-versus-concentrated-dip-and-rebound]]); a low result then is planned, not a discrepancy. The authors do not say how big a gap counts as a discrepancy. Inference: Eric's practice of judging change against a rolling baseline and SWC (line 75) answers that question in a way the book does not.
214	
215	**Example** — The authors give no worked case. Inference: a jumps group tests standing triple jump and 30 m from a flying start on the first Monday of each month, same surface, same warm-up, same time of day, and compares each result with the month's target from the annual model.
216	
217	**Related** — [[framework--four-documents-for-programming-and-controlling-training]], [[framework--eight-step-sequence-for-programming-annual-training]], [[framework--descriptive-and-prescriptive-training-models]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]], [[performance-technology-and-leadership/old-bull-performance-course--old-bull/principle--protocol-drift-undermines-comparability]]

231	
232	# Four Coaching Documents: a Diagrammatic Annual Model, a Quantitative Model, a Mesocycle Programme and an Individual Long-Term Chart That Also Records How the Athlete Feels
233	
234	**What it is** — The authors call record keeping "the simplest part of management" and "a source of unique material": "*the keeping of meticulous training records*. This is very simple and it is surprising that many coaches have not taken it seriously enough until recently" (italics in the original; PDF p. 402 / printed p. 391, checked against the page image). Many coaches have "a dismissive attitude towards detailed documentation... relying on their preference for intuition and standard traditional methods," but documentation "is not simply a supplementary responsibility... but an important attribute of professional management upon which the success of his athletes' preparation is largely dependent," and "offers a scientific, objective way of determining efficient training methods which lead to continuous progress and a decrease in overtraining and injury." The four recommended documents (PDF pp. 402-403 / printed pp. 391-392, both checked against the page images):
235	1. **A principal model of the annual training,** "in diagrammatic form, for example, as in Figures 6.39-6.42." It "provides a good school for the coach's professional thinking and at the same time the graphic form of the model makes it easy for the coach to convey his ideas to pupils. The extent to which they understand his ideas will largely determine the success of the training."
236	2. **A quantitative model of the training scheme,** for the individual or group, with the planned dynamics of the key indicators against the calendar and "the general annual volume of loading for all of the training means and its distribution by months." "The annual cycle of training known to be successful with qualified athletes can serve as a model."
237	3. **A programme for the mesocycle of preparation,** "worked out on the basis of weekly cycles." "These are the fundamental working documents which the coach uses to organise and control the training."
238	4. **The individualised long-term chart,** describing "the long-term dynamics (volume and intensity) of the training load executed with the fundamental means, as well as the corresponding changes in the functional indicators which reflect the athlete's fitness state and sporting results," used "chiefly for the analysis of its effectiveness and for making recommendations for future planning."
239	
240	On subjective data: "It is important to record not only the quantitative indicators of athletic state, but also the athlete's own perceptions of how he feels daily in executing the prescribed training exercises, alongside observations of general state of health and motivation. Often, the onset of a cold, reduced appetite, mood changes or altered sleep patterns may be more informative than mathematical calculations in detecting overtraining timeously. Finally, the chart would always make provision for contingency training to cope with the unexpected or unplanned, such as soreness, injury or illness" (PDF p. 403).
241	
242	**Why it works** — The authors' reasons are analysis and communication: the long-term chart lets the coach judge what worked, and the diagram lets athletes understand the plan. They cite no study.
243	
244	**When to apply** — Setting up a programme's record system: one picture of the year, one numerical plan, weekly mesocycle sheets, and a per-athlete chart that pairs load with test results. Eric's baseline: "Data collection is judged on cost versus insight" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 30, Explicit). Inference: the long-term chart is the authors' tool for judging that insight after the fact.
245	
246	**When NOT to apply** — **Tension with Eric's baseline on daily self-report.** The authors recommend daily records of how the athlete feels, mood, appetite and sleep. Eric's baseline: "Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal" (line 89, Explicit). The same baseline line keeps surveys "in return-to-play scenarios and with athletes managing chronic health conditions." Inference: the authors assume an individual coach-athlete relationship where the coach observes these signs; a roster-wide app survey is a different collection method, and the baseline's experience is evidence about that method, not about the signs themselves. The authors' claim that such signs "may be more informative than mathematical calculations" is unsupported on the page.
247	
248	**Example** — The authors point to Figs 6.39-6.42 as examples of the principal model (PDF p. 402). Inference: the long-term chart for a sprinter would plot monthly sprint and jump volume against monthly 30 m and standing triple jump results over several years, with notes on illness and injury.
249	
250	**Related** — [[heuristic--test-monthly-under-constant-conditions-and-compare-with-targets]], [[framework--eight-step-sequence-for-programming-annual-training]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[framework--descriptive-and-prescriptive-training-models]]

252	---

264	
265	# Programming Is an Art Based on Principles, Not a Rigid Order or an Algorithm; One-Variable Short Studies Mislead It
266	
267	**What it is** — The chapter's closing section (PDF p. 403 / printed p. 392, checked against the page image): "it is unacceptable to understand programming as the following of some instructions which prescribe a rigid order in the organisation of training. Furthermore, it is also senseless to view it as the creation of a precise algorithm, as is done in chess. Programming in sport is an art based on specific principles, which allows the coach creative initiative in making the final decisions." The authors call the chapter "only the first steps," and leave to the coach "the sequence of loading in the mesocycles and their composition in the microcycles, as well as rational ways of combining the contents of these microcycles into a system... It is the role of the coach to solve such problems."
268	
269	They also criticise the research base: "it is impossible to solve these problems by observing only physiological and biochemical mechanisms. It is impossible to separate, as is customary, the role of the motor processes from the mechanisms of energy production... The pitfalls of such a separation become apparent when one attempts to extract some practical recommendations from studies which change one variable at a time in an experiment of unrealistically short duration or limited complexity, using a sample of athletes of diverse levels of qualification." The research they call for: "the study of the characteristics of long-term and compensatory adaptation to intense exercise and observation of the principal trends in the dynamics of the athlete's state during prolonged training stages."
270	
271	The same stance opens 6.12.1: "Actual conditions do not always satisfy the optimal values of these variables. Therefore, programming of training requires creative flexibility based on the skill to anticipate the effect of any form of training and select its optimal variant" (PDF p. 379 / printed p. 368, checked against the page image).
272	
273	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is complexity: training effects depend on "the specific type of sport, the chosen loading, the period of training, the athlete's level of qualification and individual characteristics," which no fixed algorithm covers. They give no evidence for the claim itself.
274	
275	**When to apply** — Reading any model in this chapter, including the annual models, as principles to adapt, not templates to copy; and weighing short, single-variable studies on mixed-level samples with caution when they are offered as programming rules. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's baseline: "The coach's eye and objective data work in sequence: the eye flags, data investigates" (line 33, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q6)).
276	
277	**When NOT to apply** — Not a licence to ignore numbers: the same chapter asks for quantitative models, monthly testing and detailed records ([[framework--four-documents-for-programming-and-controlling-training]], [[heuristic--test-monthly-under-constant-conditions-and-compare-with-targets]]). The critique of one-variable studies is the authors' view; the book's own Soviet sources are often reported without design details, so the critique cuts both ways. Inference: a controlled short study is weak evidence for a season plan, but an uncontrolled long observation is weak evidence for cause.
278	
279	**Example** — The authors give no case. Inference: a coach who reads a six-week trial in recreationally trained students showing that one exercise order beats another treats it as a hint to test in his own athletes, not as a rule for a varsity programme.
280

# In a Long Monocyclic Competition Period, a Prolonged Cut in Loading Volume Lowers Fitness; Competition Plus Small Special Loads Cannot Maintain It

**What it is** — In the long-duration endurance model (PDF p. 396 / printed p. 385, checked against the page image): "It has been established that the prolonged reduction in the volume of loading during the competition period (with monocyclic periodisation) leads to re-adaptation at a lower level, which is reflected in the drop of non-specific trainability. Competition and special supplementary loading (with limited volumes) cannot stimulate further development or even maintain special work-capacity. Thus, it is appropriate to periodically increase the volume of competition and special assistance loading (Baranovsky, 1969; Kryazh, 1969; Muzis, 1970; Zhikharevich, 1976)." The paired condition from Gilyazova (1978) is that stable results need "not a sharp drop in the volume of loading during the competitive period" and a gradual preparatory increase ("a mean monthly increase of 7-14%") (PDF p. 396).

**Why it works** — The authors' explanation is "re-adaptation at a lower level": the body adapts down to the reduced load. They give no physiological detail and no data beyond the four citations.

**When to apply** — Long competition periods (the model's is "some 4-5 months," PDF p. 396) in which the athlete would otherwise only compete and do light maintenance: build in periodic increases in special and assistance volume. Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Also: "In-season programming deliberately waves volume and intensity even when the practice schedule looks repetitive week to week, specifically to avoid training monotony for the athlete" (line 181, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the authors' warning is against a *prolonged* volume cut in a long season; the baseline's in-season waving, and the bye-week "speed and strength top-up" (line 187, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q17)), are the kind of periodic volume increase the authors call for. A football season of games is shorter than the model's 4-5 month competition period, and the sport is not an endurance sport.

**When NOT to apply** — The statement is made for long-duration endurance sports under monocyclic periodisation; the authors do not extend it to strength or team sports. It does not mean intensity can be dropped. In the explosive-strength model the second strength block deliberately carries less volume than the first ("It is unnecessary at this time to further increase the volume of strength work," PDF p. 394 / printed p. 383), so the rule applies to special and competition loading in endurance sport, not to every quality in every sport.

**Example** — The authors give no worked case. Inference: a marathoner in a five-month racing season returns every few weeks to a higher-volume week of race-pace and assistance work instead of only racing and easy running between races.

**Related** — [[framework--annual-models-for-medium-and-long-duration-endurance-sports]], [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]]

# Tri-Cyclic Model for Individual and One-on-One Sports: Three Mesocycles for SPP, Technical Mastery and Competition Readiness, Each With Its Own Strength Block

**What it is** — 6.14.4 (PDF p. 397 / printed p. 386, checked against the page image; Fig 6.42 on PDF p. 398 / printed p. 387, checked against the image): "The tri-cyclic model is intended primarily for individual and one-on-one sports (Fig 6.42). It comprises three mesocycles, with preparatory and competitive micro-stages. The first stage is oriented chiefly towards special physical preparation; the second, to perfecting technical mastery, and the third, to readiness for the major competitions." The third stage "can be increased by shortening the duration of the second stage," and "In certain cases a bi-cyclic model of training can be employed with this group of sports."
- **Athlete-state model:** maximum aerobic productivity in the second stage, then some decrease; "Maximum strength rises uniformly, while strength-endurance accelerates more during the third stage. Explosive strength reaches a maximum at the beginning of the second and at the end of the third stages."
- **Three strength blocks:** the first "to develop maximum and explosive strength; the second, to develop strength-endurance; the third, chiefly to increase explosive strength and create conditions for exploiting the LDTE of the strength loading during the fundamental competition phase."
- **Energy-system pairing:** "The first and third blocks of strength work are executed in combination with special work in the mixed (aerobic-anaerobic) zone of energy production, while the second is combined with work in the anaerobic (ATP-CP and anaerobic-glycolytic) zone. The fundamental volume of speed and technical-tactical preparation is executed against a background of the LDTE elicited by the blocks of strength work."
- **Fig 6.42, read by eye:** phases I about months 1-4, II about months 5-8, III about months 9-11. Block 1 about months 1-3 (tallest), block 2 about months 5-6, block 3 about months 9-10 (shortest). The labels at the right edge of the upper panel read, top to bottom, Explosive strength, Anaerobic capacity, Aerobic capacity, Strength-endurance, with Maximum strength lowest and rising nearly linearly. Shorter mesocycles of this kind "should not shift achieving the objective of optimal enhancement of the current adaptation reserves (CAR) to the next stage" (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389).

**Why it works** — The authors give the structure, not a mechanism beyond the LDTE of each strength block. No data are shown; the figure is credited to Siff & Verkhoshansky (1999).

**When to apply** — Individual and combat sports with three main competition periods, such as the boxing and swimming examples the authors cite for tri-cyclic forms (PDF p. 387 / printed p. 376), and team sports where "tri-cyclic periodisation may have to be used, as dictated by the competition calendar" (PDF p. 387). Eric's baseline: "The head coach's system of play and roster identity (e.g., a "home run hitters" lineup vs. a "steal bases" lineup) is treated as a direct input into whether a team's programming leans toward maximal strength or toward speed/power emphasis" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 188, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the model's block contents (maximum, endurance, explosive) are the kind of lever that input would set.

**When NOT to apply** — **Issurin 2016 challenge (combat sports).** The library's brief of Issurin 2016 records that concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports improved some fitness measures without reported effects on practice or competitive performance, and that Issurin judged the evidence insufficient for broad use in "high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation" (brief, p. 6; [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]). This entry keeps `supported` because the tri-cyclic layout itself is not what Issurin challenges; the challenge is to the concentrated blocks inside it, recorded on [[claim--concentrated-strength-loading-limited-period-qualified-athletes-and-volume-saving]]. The model assumes three distinct competition peaks; it is not a template for a weekly-competition season.

**Example** — The authors give the schematic only. Inference: a wrestler with a winter national championship, a spring continental event and a late-summer world championship runs a maximum-strength block in autumn, a strength-endurance block in late winter with anaerobic work, and a short explosive block before the summer peak.

**Related** — [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[heuristic--set-mesocycle-boundaries-by-main-competition-dates]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]], [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]

# Follow a High-Volume, Low-Intensity Concentrated Block With Moderate-Volume Explosive Work to Enlarge the Delayed Training Effect

**What it is** — Under the heading "More Advanced Use of Concentrated Loading" (PDF p. 397 / printed p. 386, checked against the page image) the authors modify the separated-block models of 6.14: "in speed-strength sports, the magnitude of the delayed training effect (LDTE) may be enhanced further if the concentrated loading is followed by specialised work of moderate volume, which includes higher power or more explosive muscle contraction regimes, such as jumps, plyometrics and maximal attempts." The loads overlap: "There is an overlapping of the different training volumes, which peak smoothly in each case to ensure optimal increase in the LDTE" (PDF p. 398 / printed p. 387). In the bi-cyclic version, "stages A and C refer to concentrated periods of high volume, low intensity work and stages B and D to moderate volumes of specialised, higher intensity speed-strength work. This scheme has been recommended to ensure continuous increase in special strength over a long period (Verkhoshansky, 1978)" (PDF p. 398).

The figures, read from the page images (no numeric axes):
- **Fig 6.43** (PDF p. 398, monocyclic large mesocycle): a tall wave A in the preparatory phase, a smaller wave B starting as A falls and peaking at about the start of the competition phase. The speed-strength curve sags while A is high, then rises through B and keeps rising into the competition phase.
- **Fig 6.44** (PDF p. 399 / printed p. 388, bi-cyclic): tall A, small B, tall C, small D in sequence. Speed-strength dips during A, rises during B, flattens or dips slightly during C, and rises again after it to its highest level at the right.
- **Fig 6.45** (PDF p. 399, a large mesocycle for speed-strength sports): the text says "the concentrated strength loading block occupies the first half of the large mesocycle, following the groundwork laid by general physical preparation (GPP) and the peak amount of aerobic work... Technique and speed training occupies the second half." The figure shows an aerobic-work curve peaking early, a large shaded wave over the first half, a second shaded wave over the second half labelled "Technique and Speed," and a fitness-state curve that dips then rises to its highest point at the right.

**Why it works** — The authors give a principle rather than a measured mechanism: overlapping loads that "peak smoothly" serve the LDTE, and "the inclusion of regular passive and active restoration periods between stages of greater loading is important to facilitate development of the LDTE" (PDF p. 398). They also argue for putting the bulk of strength work early: "Since large volumes of strength and technique training generally are incompatible, the greatest quantity of strength work should be done during the preparatory period, with more emphasis being placed on technique work during the competitive phase when the LDTE rises markedly" (PDF p. 399). No data are shown; the figures are schematics credited to Siff & Verkhoshansky (1999).

**When to apply** — Speed-strength athletes coming out of a high-volume strength block: bring in moderate volumes of jumps, plyometrics and maximal attempts as the block tapers, rather than dropping straight to technique and speed alone. The authors say the boundaries are loose: "stage B does not necessarily begin where shown, but may commence far earlier, while stage A may tail off right near the end of phase B" (PDF p. 398; "phase B" is printed as such). The authors tie this to Matveyev's "non-discreteness of the preparatory and competitive phases": "it is sometimes perfectly appropriate to have elements of each intermingled in various 'doses'" (PDF p. 398). Eric's baseline: "Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: the A-then-B wave is one way to stage that shift within one off-season.

**When NOT to apply** — The scheme is stated for speed-strength sports. It assumes the A stage is "high volume, low intensity," consistent with the low-intensity condition for concentrated loading ([[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]]); an A stage built from heavy, intense lifting is a different situation the authors do not cover. **Unclear figure labels:** the caption of Fig 6.45 says "A is the block of concentrated strength loading, while B and C refer to the types of training identified in the diagram," but in the figure the label "GPP" sits under wave A and "Strength Load" sits under wave B (PDF p. 399). Fig 6.46 has the same mismatch (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389). Which wave is the strength block cannot be settled from the page. No dose for the B stage is given beyond "moderate volume."

**Example** — The authors give the schematics only. Inference: after a four-week block of high-volume, moderate-load squats, pulls and loaded jumps, a jumper adds two short weekly sessions of bounding, a few depth jumps and one or two near-maximal lifts, with that work peaking about when the first competitions begin.

**Related** — [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]], [[heuristic--sequence-jumps-then-barbell-then-depth-jumps-across-stages]], [[principle--sequentially-introduce-means-of-greater-training-effect]], [[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]], [[heuristic--loading-reduction-for-the-delayed-effect-must-outlast-1-2-weeks]]

# Technical Mastery Comes Only From Practice at Competition-Like Intensity; Skill Learned at Low Intensity Does Not Usually Transfer to Maximal Efforts

**What it is** — The authors (PDF p. 399 / printed p. 388, checked against the page image): "technical mastery can be acquired only through practice with high intensity loading which simulates competition conditions. Proficiency gained under conditions of low stimulation and intensity do not usually transfer successfully to the maximal effort situations of top-level competition. This is relevant to the use of visualisation to perfect sporting movements; this technique is not very successful if it does not offer mental simulation of the movements, the feelings and the competitive circumstances under which the movements have to be displayed. Practice only makes perfect if one practises all components of the performance process under the conditions which mimic those of the sporting event as closely as possible." The same idea appears as the seventh primary aim, "Modelling competition activities" at "the high intensity which is encountered in competition" (PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379), and in the medium-endurance model: "*competitions, of course, constitute the most specific form of special preparation in any sport*" (italics in the original; PDF p. 399).

**Why it works** — The authors state the rule without a mechanism or a cited study on this page. Inference: it is the book's specificity principle applied to skill; the book's own criteria for when training matches the sport are in [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]] (section 4.3).

**When to apply** — Deciding when and how hard to practise the competition skill: the low-intensity technique work done during a strength block ([[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]]) is preparation, and the skill must later be practised at full intensity under competition-like conditions, starting in the preparatory period (the authors: "it would be too late were it to commence in the competitive period," PDF p. 382 / printed p. 371). For mental rehearsal, include the feel and the competitive setting, not just the movement pattern. Eric's baseline: "The Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky), matching amplitude/direction of movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production, and regime of muscular work to the sport skill, governs whether an exercise actually transfers, rather than surface resemblance to the sport" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 103, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)).

**When NOT to apply** — The same chapter allows and recommends low-intensity technique work during concentrated loading for learning components (PDF p. 383), so the rule is about where mastery is finished, not a ban on low-intensity practice. The authors say "do not usually transfer," not never. Inference: for novices learning a movement for the first time, low-intensity practice is the normal starting point; the authors' context here is "top-level competition."

**Example** — The authors' own example is visualisation that rehearses only the movement shape and so "is not very successful" (PDF p. 399). Inference: a shot-putter who only drills the glide at half speed in the off-season and first throws at full effort in meets would be expected to see the technique break down under maximal effort.

**Related** — [[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]], [[principle--training-effort-must-match-or-exceed-sport-effort-judged-by-movement-speed]], [[framework--seven-primary-aims-of-programming-training]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]

# Set Mesocycle Boundaries Only by the Main Competition Dates, Treat the First Mesocycle as the Foundation for the Second, and Recuperate After Each Competitive Stage

**What it is** — The authors' four practical principles for when the calendar and adaptation pull against each other (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389, checked against the page image). The conflict: "the dates of the main competitions may change radically, while the dates of traditional competitions remain the same. A worse situation arises if the competition season is extended and the length of the preparatory stages is shortened."
1. "Organisation of training should provide favourable conditions for promoting functional adaptation of the body within the constraints of the competition calendar. The calendar should be co-ordinated with the periods and duration of the mesocycles."
2. "The optimal period for enhancing the current adaptation reserves is about 20 weeks for the most efficient loading of highly qualified athletes." It "can be increased or decreased over a small range, which requires an appropriate increase or decrease in the concentration of loading. It is important in this case not to exceed the optimal time limit, since excessive intensification of training can disrupt adaptation."
3. "To determine the boundaries of the mesocycles, one should be guided only by the dates of the main competitions. This rule should not be broken for any reason, including the desire to demonstrate impressive results at the beginning of the season."
4. "The loading of the preparatory phase is more specialised and intense during the second mesocycle than the first. Therefore, the first mesocycle should always be considered as the foundation for the second. The interests of intermediate competitions should not alter this objective."

Then, in italics in the original: "*one should be aware of the detrimental effect that competitive loading has on the athlete's state*, since it leads to serious exhaustion of nervous energy. Therefore, during the transition to the next mesocycle, it is necessary to include a recuperation period, the duration of which is determined individually, depending on the difficulty of the competitive stage" (PDF p. 400).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason for rules 2 and 3 is the "current adaptation reserves": there is an optimal time over which they can be raised, and stretching or squeezing it changes how concentrated the loading must be. They give no study for the 20-week figure on this page ("It has already been mentioned," referring back to earlier sections outside this batch). The recuperation rule rests on the "serious exhaustion of nervous energy" from competition, without data.

**When to apply** — Drawing an annual plan: place the main competitions first, cut the year into mesocycles from those dates, and do not move the boundaries to chase early-season results or to serve minor meets. Eric's baseline: "In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: under rule 3, November and the postseason would set the boundary of the final mesocycle, and early-season games would be treated as the authors' "intermediate competitions," which "should not alter this objective."

**When NOT to apply** — Rule 3's "should not be broken for any reason" is the authors' strongest wording in the section, but it assumes one or two main competitions; in a sport with a weekly game, every game counts, and the rule does not say how to weight them. The 20-week figure is for "highly qualified athletes." The recuperation period has no stated length. Issurin's competing structure uses stages of "about two months" ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]); see [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]].

**Example** — The authors' own example of the problem is a season that is "extended" while "the length of the preparatory stages is shortened" (PDF p. 400). Inference: a jumper whose national championship moves three weeks earlier shortens the second mesocycle by concentrating its loading more, rather than shifting the boundary to keep a full block before an early-season invitational.

**Related** — [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]], [[framework--eight-step-sequence-for-programming-annual-training]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[framework--tricyclic-annual-model-for-individual-and-one-on-one-sports]], [[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--nine-step-annual-program-construction-sequence]]

# Verkhoshansky's Eight-Step Sequence for Programming the Annual Cycle, From Target Results Down to the Microcycles

**What it is** — The authors recommend "the following sequence of logical operations, where each calculation is made by taking into account the calculation made in the preceding operation (Verkhoshansky, 1985)" (PDF p. 401 / printed p. 390, checked against the page image). The eight steps, with their key wording:
1. **Determine the progress in results and the dates.** "The calculations rely on a predictive model of the dynamics of the sport results relative to the competition calendar," based on "a multi-faceted objective assessment of the athlete's potential" and what is "realistically feasible in the current year at his level of mastery."
2. **Determine the needed changes in special physical preparedness and technical-tactical proficiency,** expressed as "specific goals, relative to the functional indicators and the characteristics of technical proficiency which must be achieved in the important competitions." "Subjective ratings of perceived effort (RPE) can be very useful in offering further guidance."
3. **Build quantitative models of the fitness state across the year** "so that these indicators peak in the main competitions."
4. **Select the training means and methods** by "assessing the training potential of the means and methods."
5. **Calculate the general volume of loading for all means,** based on "the accumulated effect of the loading in all preceding stages."
6. **Divide the year into mesocycles,** using "the competition calendar and the dates necessary for optimal increase of the body's current adaptation reserves."
7. **Calculate the distribution of loading over the year,** expressed as "the quantitative dynamics of the loading imposed by the fundamental training means."
8. **Organise loading over the mesocycle,** as "a detailed training programme giving the specific distribution of loading during each of the microcycles," based on "the characteristics of the LDTE of concentrated strength loading." "Provision should always be made available for introducing contingency changes in programmes, necessitated by unforeseen incidents such as injuries, changes in competitive timetables and personal disasters."

The authors frame the difficulty first: "Its complexity, however, lies not so much in the quantity of calculations as in the insufficient basis for choosing and quantitatively determining the main operations. Therefore in practice, even experienced coaches need to make tentative computations which may have a low probability of producing a correct prognosis" (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The sequence is a top-down dependency chain: each step uses the one before. The authors give no evidence that following it improves results; it is a planning procedure.

**When to apply** — Building or auditing an annual plan. Compare it with two other procedures in the library: Issurin's nine steps start from the competition calendar and end with obligatory correction after review ([[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--nine-step-annual-program-construction-sequence]]); Evans's ten steps start with a sport and position profile ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]]). Verkhoshansky's starts from the predicted result and the fitness changes needed to reach it, and only divides the year into mesocycles at step 6. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: step 8's contingency provision is the authors' version of that flexibility.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors concede the operations rest on an "insufficient basis" and may have "a low probability of producing a correct prognosis" (PDF p. 400). Step 1 assumes a predictive model of performance exists; in team sports there is no single result to predict. The procedure is written for individual athletes and their competitions.

**Example** — The authors give no worked plan in 6.15. Inference: for a triple jumper, step 1 sets a target of a 40 cm improvement at the national championship in month 10, step 2 converts it to target values for the standing triple jump and approach speed, and steps 6-8 then divide the year into two mesocycles and write the weekly loading.

**Related** — [[framework--descriptive-and-prescriptive-training-models]], [[heuristic--set-mesocycle-boundaries-by-main-competition-dates]], [[framework--four-documents-for-programming-and-controlling-training]], [[principle--programme-objective-approach-quantified-goals-dictate-training]], [[block-periodization--issurin/heuristic--nine-step-annual-program-construction-sequence]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--ten-step-process-for-building-an-annual-plan]]

# Manage Training by Testing Once or Twice a Month Under Constant Conditions and Comparing Results With Targets Each Month

**What it is** — The authors define management as "control over the course of training and its prescription, based on a comparison of the actual dynamics of training with previous target standards," correcting course "by changing the appropriate parameters of the loading" (PDF p. 402 / printed p. 391, checked against the page image). Their guidelines (Verkhoshansky, 1985):
1. "One should first select the most informative fitness characteristics in order to assess the special physical preparedness, technical proficiency and psychological state of the athlete," using "special laboratory methods, control exercises (pedagogical tests) or functional sporting or standardised field tests."
2. "Control over the course of training can only be effective if one regularly analyses the dynamics of the athlete's state. When doing this, (a) testing should be done regularly once or twice a month, independent of the periodisation and structure of the training stages, (b) the testing procedure should not be excessively demanding on the time and energy of the athlete, (c) the testing conditions must be kept constant to exclude the possibility of random factors affecting the results, and (d) the testing must have functional relevance."
3. "Management requires a systematic comparison (over monthly periods) of the actual results and target goals of the training. If there is a discrepancy, it is necessary to carefully analyse the situation, determine the cause for such a discrepancy and revise the training programme."

**Why it works** — The authors' logic is feedback control: without regular comparison against targets, deviations go unnoticed. They give no evidence for the once-or-twice-a-month frequency.

**When to apply** — Setting up a testing calendar for a programme with written targets. Eric's baseline agrees on criteria (b) to (d): "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 34, Explicit) and "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention" (line 30, Explicit). On frequency it goes further for readiness: "Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker" (line 74, Explicit), with a Wednesday decision read: "Wednesdays, the thresholds should be individualized" (line 75, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a)). Inference: the two operate at different scales; the authors' monthly tests track progress toward annual targets, while daily jumps track short-term readiness, a level the authors treat separately as "largely random and at times unpredictable" acute changes (PDF p. 378 / printed p. 367, section 6.11, text layer).

**When NOT to apply** — The monthly schedule is "independent of the periodisation," so a test may fall in the middle of a concentrated block, when the authors expect indicators to be depressed ([[framework--mesocycle-variants-smooth-rise-versus-concentrated-dip-and-rebound]]); a low result then is planned, not a discrepancy. The authors do not say how big a gap counts as a discrepancy. Inference: Eric's practice of judging change against a rolling baseline and SWC (line 75) answers that question in a way the book does not.

**Example** — The authors give no worked case. Inference: a jumps group tests standing triple jump and 30 m from a flying start on the first Monday of each month, same surface, same warm-up, same time of day, and compares each result with the month's target from the annual model.

**Related** — [[framework--four-documents-for-programming-and-controlling-training]], [[framework--eight-step-sequence-for-programming-annual-training]], [[framework--descriptive-and-prescriptive-training-models]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]], [[performance-technology-and-leadership/old-bull-performance-course--old-bull/principle--protocol-drift-undermines-comparability]]

# Four Coaching Documents: a Diagrammatic Annual Model, a Quantitative Model, a Mesocycle Programme and an Individual Long-Term Chart That Also Records How the Athlete Feels

**What it is** — The authors call record keeping "the simplest part of management" and "a source of unique material": "*the keeping of meticulous training records*. This is very simple and it is surprising that many coaches have not taken it seriously enough until recently" (italics in the original; PDF p. 402 / printed p. 391, checked against the page image). Many coaches have "a dismissive attitude towards detailed documentation... relying on their preference for intuition and standard traditional methods," but documentation "is not simply a supplementary responsibility... but an important attribute of professional management upon which the success of his athletes' preparation is largely dependent," and "offers a scientific, objective way of determining efficient training methods which lead to continuous progress and a decrease in overtraining and injury." The four recommended documents (PDF pp. 402-403 / printed pp. 391-392, both checked against the page images):
1. **A principal model of the annual training,** "in diagrammatic form, for example, as in Figures 6.39-6.42." It "provides a good school for the coach's professional thinking and at the same time the graphic form of the model makes it easy for the coach to convey his ideas to pupils. The extent to which they understand his ideas will largely determine the success of the training."
2. **A quantitative model of the training scheme,** for the individual or group, with the planned dynamics of the key indicators against the calendar and "the general annual volume of loading for all of the training means and its distribution by months." "The annual cycle of training known to be successful with qualified athletes can serve as a model."
3. **A programme for the mesocycle of preparation,** "worked out on the basis of weekly cycles." "These are the fundamental working documents which the coach uses to organise and control the training."
4. **The individualised long-term chart,** describing "the long-term dynamics (volume and intensity) of the training load executed with the fundamental means, as well as the corresponding changes in the functional indicators which reflect the athlete's fitness state and sporting results," used "chiefly for the analysis of its effectiveness and for making recommendations for future planning."

On subjective data: "It is important to record not only the quantitative indicators of athletic state, but also the athlete's own perceptions of how he feels daily in executing the prescribed training exercises, alongside observations of general state of health and motivation. Often, the onset of a cold, reduced appetite, mood changes or altered sleep patterns may be more informative than mathematical calculations in detecting overtraining timeously. Finally, the chart would always make provision for contingency training to cope with the unexpected or unplanned, such as soreness, injury or illness" (PDF p. 403).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasons are analysis and communication: the long-term chart lets the coach judge what worked, and the diagram lets athletes understand the plan. They cite no study.

**When to apply** — Setting up a programme's record system: one picture of the year, one numerical plan, weekly mesocycle sheets, and a per-athlete chart that pairs load with test results. Eric's baseline: "Data collection is judged on cost versus insight" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 30, Explicit). Inference: the long-term chart is the authors' tool for judging that insight after the fact.

**When NOT to apply** — **Tension with Eric's baseline on daily self-report.** The authors recommend daily records of how the athlete feels, mood, appetite and sleep. Eric's baseline: "Daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out across multiple sports via the AMS app starting summer 2022, were abandoned after roughly one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers the survey rewarded; the data looked clean but carried no real signal" (line 89, Explicit). The same baseline line keeps surveys "in return-to-play scenarios and with athletes managing chronic health conditions." Inference: the authors assume an individual coach-athlete relationship where the coach observes these signs; a roster-wide app survey is a different collection method, and the baseline's experience is evidence about that method, not about the signs themselves. The authors' claim that such signs "may be more informative than mathematical calculations" is unsupported on the page.

**Example** — The authors point to Figs 6.39-6.42 as examples of the principal model (PDF p. 402). Inference: the long-term chart for a sprinter would plot monthly sprint and jump volume against monthly 30 m and standing triple jump results over several years, with notes on illness and injury.

**Related** — [[heuristic--test-monthly-under-constant-conditions-and-compare-with-targets]], [[framework--eight-step-sequence-for-programming-annual-training]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[framework--descriptive-and-prescriptive-training-models]]
