# Programming Is an Art Based on Principles, Not a Rigid Order or an Algorithm; One-Variable Short Studies Mislead It

**What it is** — The chapter's closing section (PDF p. 403 / printed p. 392, checked against the page image): "it is unacceptable to understand programming as the following of some instructions which prescribe a rigid order in the organisation of training. Furthermore, it is also senseless to view it as the creation of a precise algorithm, as is done in chess. Programming in sport is an art based on specific principles, which allows the coach creative initiative in making the final decisions." The authors call the chapter "only the first steps," and leave to the coach "the sequence of loading in the mesocycles and their composition in the microcycles, as well as rational ways of combining the contents of these microcycles into a system... It is the role of the coach to solve such problems."

They also criticise the research base: "it is impossible to solve these problems by observing only physiological and biochemical mechanisms. It is impossible to separate, as is customary, the role of the motor processes from the mechanisms of energy production... The pitfalls of such a separation become apparent when one attempts to extract some practical recommendations from studies which change one variable at a time in an experiment of unrealistically short duration or limited complexity, using a sample of athletes of diverse levels of qualification." The research they call for: "the study of the characteristics of long-term and compensatory adaptation to intense exercise and observation of the principal trends in the dynamics of the athlete's state during prolonged training stages."

The same stance opens 6.12.1: "Actual conditions do not always satisfy the optimal values of these variables. Therefore, programming of training requires creative flexibility based on the skill to anticipate the effect of any form of training and select its optimal variant" (PDF p. 379 / printed p. 368, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is complexity: training effects depend on "the specific type of sport, the chosen loading, the period of training, the athlete's level of qualification and individual characteristics," which no fixed algorithm covers. They give no evidence for the claim itself.

**When to apply** — Reading any model in this chapter, including the annual models, as principles to adapt, not templates to copy; and weighing short, single-variable studies on mixed-level samples with caution when they are offered as programming rules. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's baseline: "The coach's eye and objective data work in sequence: the eye flags, data investigates" (line 33, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q6)).

**When NOT to apply** — Not a licence to ignore numbers: the same chapter asks for quantitative models, monthly testing and detailed records ([[framework--four-documents-for-programming-and-controlling-training]], [[heuristic--test-monthly-under-constant-conditions-and-compare-with-targets]]). The critique of one-variable studies is the authors' view; the book's own Soviet sources are often reported without design details, so the critique cuts both ways. Inference: a controlled short study is weak evidence for a season plan, but an uncontrolled long observation is weak evidence for cause.

**Example** — The authors give no case. Inference: a coach who reads a six-week trial in recreationally trained students showing that one exercise order beats another treats it as a hint to test in his own athletes, not as a rule for a varsity programme.

**Related** — [[framework--eight-step-sequence-for-programming-annual-training]], [[framework--descriptive-and-prescriptive-training-models]], [[principle--motor-system-leads-cardiorespiratory-adaptation-do-not-separate-them]], [[principle--programme-objective-approach-quantified-goals-dictate-training]]

# Issurin 2016 — Benefits and limitations of block-periodized preparation

> **Citation**
> Issurin, V. B. (2016). Benefits and limitations of block periodized training approaches to athletes' preparation: A review. *Sports Medicine, 46*(3), 329–338. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0425-5

## Why it was promoted

This review distinguishes concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block models and provides a useful conceptual vocabulary for discussing concentrated workloads and sequencing.

## Research question

What benefits, limitations, and sport-context boundaries are reported for two versions of block-periodized athlete preparation?

## Population and context

- The review emphasizes elite, subelite, and well-trained athletes across endurance, team, combat, dual, jumping, and strength/power settings. [p. 11]
- It also discusses a smaller number of recreational-athlete studies.
- It is a training-theory review, not evidence specific to collegiate American football.

## Study design and methods

- Narrative review contrasting concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block-periodization models.
- The article summarizes prior studies in tables but does not report a systematic search, eligibility process, formal risk-of-bias appraisal, or meta-analysis.
- Consequently, the stated number and direction of supportive studies should be interpreted as an author-curated synthesis rather than a pooled comparative estimate.

## Key findings

- Concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance. [p. 6]
- In an elite-swimmer example, specific strength and anaerobic capacity improved but swimming performance improved in only two of three athletes. [p. 6]
- The author judged the concentrated-unidirectional evidence insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation. [p. 6]
- The review reports support from 28 studies for multi-targeted block programs, but the designs, populations, outcomes, and comparator quality varied. [p. 11]
- The concentrated-unidirectional model was presented as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality and as restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities. [p. 11]
- Whose model is whose: the concentrated-unidirectional (CU) model is Verkhoshansky's; the multi-targeted model with 28-study support is Issurin's own A-T-R block model. [pp. 6-7, 11] So this review does not dispute Issurin's 2008 book; it repeats the book's critique of traditional planning. The real 2008-2016 difference is on lower-level athletes: the book (p. 33) says they do fine with medium concentration, while this review says "no evidence that amateur athletes have any serious restrictions" with highly concentrated block workloads. [p. 11] (Clarified 2026-09-27 during the Flint review of Issurin's book, checked against the paper pages.)

## Limitations and applicability

- Non-systematic study selection and absent risk-of-bias assessment create a substantial risk of selective emphasis.
- Fitness improvements are not interchangeable with sport-specific performance, availability, or competitive outcomes. [p. 6]
- Training models were not consistently isolated from total volume, intensity, exercise choice, coaching, or athlete history.
- Evidence spans dissimilar sports and training levels; it does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American football.
- The strong conclusion favoring multi-targeted block periodization is the author's synthesis and should not be treated as settled comparative evidence. [p. 11]

## Practitioner interpretation

Use block periodization as a planning hypothesis: concentrate compatible emphases when competition structure and athlete needs justify it, while maintaining the qualities and technical exposure that cannot safely decay. Judge the plan by sport-specific performance, availability, and individual response—not by the periodization label. Compare it prospectively with the program's own prior practice where feasible.

## Evidence map

| Claim | Locator | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| Review scope and distinction between two models | p. 4 | narrative framing |
| Concentrated-unidirectional evidence and performance gaps | p. 6 | narrative synthesis |
| Multi-targeted evidence claim and applicability boundaries | p. 11 | narrative synthesis/limitation |

## Related knowledge

- [[periodization]] — annual and phase planning
- [[training-load-concentration]] — sequencing compatible emphases
- [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]]: Supertraining 5.3.3's system of successive concentrated blocks; it cites this review's limits for team, combat and swimming preparation as the case against using that system there

The real 2008-2016 difference is on lower-level athletes: the book (p. 33) says they do fine with medium concentration, while this review says "no evidence that amateur athletes have any serious restrictions" with highly concentrated block workloads. [p. 11] (Clarified 2026-09-27 during the Flint review of Issurin's book, checked against the paper pages.)

## Limitations and applicability

- Non-systematic study selection and absent risk-of-bias assessment create a substantial risk of selective emphasis.
- Fitness improvements are not interchangeable with sport-specific performance, availability, or competitive outcomes. [p. 6]
- Training models were not consistently isolated from total volume, intensity, exercise choice, coaching, or athlete history.
- Evidence spans dissimilar sports and training levels; it does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American football.
- The strong conclusion favoring multi-targeted block periodization is the author's synthesis and should not be treated as settled comparative evidence. [p. 11]

## Practitioner interpretation

Use block periodization as a planning hypothesis: concentrate compatible emphases when competition structure and athlete needs justify it, while maintaining the qualities and technical exposure that cannot safely decay. Judge the plan by sport-specific performance, availability, and individual response—not by the periodization label. Compare it prospectively with the program's own prior practice where feasible.

chapter: "5.3.3"
**What it is** — The authors warn: "The system is not without its dangers, since concentrated loading is very stressful and, besides increasing the potential for overtraining, it can decrease motor qualities such as speed-strength. After a phase of emphasis on heavy strength training, there may be an increase in muscle stiffness and a loss of explosive strength, sporting skill or speed." Their rule, italicised in the original: "a diminished loading and restorative period has to be observed after a given concentrated loading phase to allow the body to supercompensate to the desired level of preparedness." The timing: "The gains elicited, for instance, by 4-8 week concentrated blocks of strength, speed-strength or speed training, may occur most commonly after a latency period of 1-3 weeks, so it is essential for the athlete not to lose patience and hasten into the next concentrated phase without adequate restoration. Not only does premature imposition of concentrated loading suppress the delayed training effect of the previous stage, but it also lowers the effectiveness of future training" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors' reason: "the conjugate sequence system is based on exploitation of the delayed training effect" (PDF p. 305 / printed p. 294), so the next block must start once that effect has appeared, not before. No physiological mechanism is given in this section. Inference: the authors frame the restorative period as supercompensation; the two-factor (fitness-fatigue) reading in this library would describe the same pattern as fatigue clearing to reveal fitness, and the book does not choose between them here.
**When to apply** — After any 4-8 week block that concentrates on one quality, plan a lower-load period before the next concentrated block. Inference: judge the block's result after the 1-3 week latency, not on the last day of loading. Eric's baseline: "An annual plan is treated as a flexible roadmap, not a fixed contract" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 183, Inferred). Inference: the 1-3 week latency is a reason to leave slack between blocks in that roadmap, so a delayed gain is not cut short by the next block.

chapter: "6.10"
**What it is** — The authors report "a steady decrease in speed-strength preparedness during individual training stages of different length (from 5-12 weeks)" caused by "voluminous strength loading," after which "speed-strength returns to its initial level and significantly exceeds it" (Nikitin 1977; Mironenko 1979; Antonova 1982; Levchenko 1982). Because this "does not agree with established ideas which stipulate a continuous rise in special physical preparedness" and "is not accompanied by marked signs of overtraining," it became "a subject of special study" (PDF p. 374 / printed p. 363, checked against the page image). They then state a dose-response rule: "The volume of the training load has a definite optimum level for each athlete, above or below which the body reacts with diminished response." "If the volume of loading is lower than the optimum level, special work-capacity decreases after some initial rise. If the volume of loading significantly exceeds this level, a steady decrease in special work-capacity occurs which, however, rises intensely during the carefully-timed reduction in the volume. This intense rise in special work-capacity is the phenomenon known as the long-term delayed training effect (LDTE)" (same page).

Their characterisation (Fig 6.31, PDF pp. 374-375 / printed pp. 363-364, checked against the page images), points 1, 2 and 4:
1. "Concentration of strength loading is the basic condition for the beginning of the LDTE."
2. "The lower the speed-strength levels fall (within an optimal range) during the concentration of strength loading stage, the higher they rise in the subsequent LDTE phase (graphs of F1 and F2). Excessive concentration of strength loading leads to a more significant drop in speed-strength and disruption of adaptation (graph F3)." In the figure, F3 dips lowest and only creeps back toward the baseline by the end of T2; F1 and F2 end above it.
4. "A subsequent moderate volume of general developmental work, combined with special work of gradually increasing intensity contributes to eliciting the LDTE."

Points 3 (non-intensive means) and 5 (T2 about equal to T1, observed 4-12 weeks, individualised) are already quoted in [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]] and [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]].

=========== heuristic--time-technique-and-competition-strength-work-to-the-ldte-window.md
chapter: "6.10"
**What it is** — Three linked rules from 6.10:
1. **Strength first, technique in the rebound.** "high-volume strength loads are detrimental to one's current level of speed-strength fitness and, consequently, to technical preparation. To avoid this, it is advisable in training high level athletes to structure the programme so that strength work precedes and does not interfere with technical training. Technical training should take place in the presence of the delayed training effect of the concentrated volume of strength work, i.e. when there is recovery of work capacity and an increase in the level of speed-strength." Technique then "rapidly adjusts to the athlete's higher level of specialised work capacity and there is much less likelihood of reinforcing errors" from the "lowered functional state, caused by high-volume loads" (PDF p. 376 / printed p. 365, checked against the page image).
2. **Do not add volume while the effect emerges.** "The volume of training work, therefore, should not be increased during the period of emergence of the LDTE" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364, checked against the page image).
3. **Competition period.** "One should be especially cautious with strength loading during the competition period. At this time, intensive and short-term strength work can be used in a small volume to tone the neuromuscular system during competition preparation, as well as to maintain the achieved level of speed-strength preparedness if the length of the competition period exceeds the duration of the LDTE of strength loading" (PDF pp. 375-376 / printed pp. 364-365).

The authors also state that "the competitive action executed with maximal physical exertion represents the most specific of all the special training means," to be viewed "simultaneously as a highly intense means of strength training," so a strength programme should rise in intensity and be "combined with technique training so as to peak concurrently with the competitive act" (PDF p. 376). They give "the dominant role" in the strength-technique interaction to "special physical preparation, both in the yearly cycle and in long-term training" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasons: a strength-depressed state reinforces technical errors, while a higher work capacity lets the athlete "concentrate his effort more effectively, increase range of movement, decrease the time of execution of movements, improve his stability, improve the strength of muscular control over all movements and increase his resistance to fatigue" (PDF p. 376). For rule 2 they report that during emergence "it is relatively easy and painless for the body to change to intensive loading, but it will react negatively to extensive work," seen as "slowed or even decreased growth of speed-strength" (PDF p. 375).
**When to apply** — After a concentrated strength block, schedule the heaviest technical emphasis for the weeks when speed-strength is coming back up, and hold volume flat through that period. In a long competition period, keep a small dose of intense, brief strength work. Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is 'maintain intensity, reduce volume'" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: rule 3 says the same thing for the competition period. Eric's baseline: the in-season week has "lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game" (line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)). Inference: that sits with rule 3's "small volume" and "short-term" strength work; the authors

# Review: Supertraining Chapter 6d (6.12-6.17), 25 entries

Reviewer: Claude Opus (independent, instructed to falsify). Date: 2026-10-03.
Scope: the 25 files in `staging/_scope_supertraining_ch6d.txt`, folder `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/`.
Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`, PDF idx 379-403 (printed 368-392), plus PDF 305, 340, 375 and 378 for cross-references. PDF idx = printed + 11.

Method: text layer for every quote (all 25 entries' quotes compared against it); page images at 200 dpi for PDF 379-403; Fig 6.39 at 300 dpi plus 450-dpi crops of both panels (`_renders/r6d_p395_upper.png`, `_renders/r6d_p395_lower.png`); Fig 6.32(b) at 450 dpi (`_renders/r6d_p383_figb.png`); PDF 392 and 393 (Tables 6.7-6.12) read from the images. Italics checked with a font-span scan (PDF 379, 382, 384, 385, 399, 400, 402: every "italics in the original" claim is correct). Every "Eric's baseline:" quote checked against `docs/method-baseline.md` lines 30, 32, 33, 34, 74, 75, 89, 101, 103, 105, 106, 115, 116, 117, 181, 182, 183, 185, 186, 187, 188: all quotes, line numbers and tags are correct. The Issurin 2016 brief (`research-papers/issurin-2016-...md`), the Issurin stage entry, and the Evans/Bompa cycle-types entry were opened, and every quote from them matches. All wikilinks in the 25 files resolve. Em dashes appear only in the six section headers of each file.

Counts: **14 GO, 11 FIX, 0 NO-GO.**

## Per-entry verdicts

| File | Verdict | Problem (entry vs source, with page) | Exact correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| principle--programme-objective-approach-quantified-goals-dictate-training | GO | None found. | Checked: the three objective components, the "if-then" sentence, 6.12.1 "minimal expenditure of energy" and "structural organisation... time management", and the 6.11 closing "probability... much smaller", all at PDF 379 / p.368; *objectives* is italic (span check); baseline line 32 quote and tag. |
| claim--complex-training-falls-short-for-highly-qualified-athletes | FIX | (1) The "Contested by Issurin" paragraph sets Issurin against the claim, but the brief it cites says the 2016 review "repeats the book's critique of traditional planning." Issurin agrees that traditional complex training falls short for elite athletes. He disputes the remedy (one target per block versus a minimal number). The brief also records Issurin 2016 saying "no evidence that amateur athletes have any serious restrictions" with highly concentrated workloads (brief, p. 11), which contests the book's "complex for beginners" limit (PDF 380). (2) "28-study support" is given without the brief's caveat that the count is author-curated from a non-systematic narrative review. (3) Minor: the early-studies list puts Matveyev 1970 with Krestovnikov 1951 to Korobkov 1960. At PDF 380, Matveyev 1970 is cited separately, for parallel loading improving functions "in the necessary balance." | Rewrite the contested paragraph as follows. "Issurin 2016 agrees that traditional complex training falls short for elite athletes (the brief: the review repeats the book's critique of traditional planning). He contests the remedy: his multi-targeted blocks train a minimal number of targets, not one. He also reports no evidence that amateurs are restricted by concentrated workloads, against the book's 'only to beginners or athletes of average qualification' (PDF 380). The 28-study count is Issurin's own curated, non-systematic synthesis (brief, p. 11)." Move Matveyev 1970 into its own clause. Keep `contested`. |
| claim--concentrated-strength-loading-limited-period-qualified-athletes-and-volume-saving | GO | The contested reason is accurate and correctly scoped. It targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model in team sports and quotes brief p. 6 exactly. It does not overreach to block periodisation in general. | Checked: "up to 2 months" and "4-12 weeks" a paragraph apart, mechanism sentence, block-selection passage (PDF 381 / p.370); citation list, "most appropriate for highly qualified athletes", 13-15% (PDF 382 / p.371); 20% "over a macrocycle" (PDF 305 / p.294); Issurin brief p. 6 quotes; baseline line 183. Optional: add the brief's p. 11 amateur-athlete line as a second contest of "most appropriate for highly qualified athletes." |
| case-study--antonova-and-levchenko-high-strength-volume-lowers-explosive-qualities | FIX | (1) In When NOT to apply, "Both groups were qualified track athletes" contradicts the same sentence's "the long jumpers' level is not stated" (PDF 382 says only "women long jumpers"). (2) Dedup miss: the 6c entry `principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum` (6.10, PDF 374) cites Antonova 1982 and Levchenko 1982 for the same dip-then-rebound finding and is not in Related. (3) Source note not recorded: the book dates Levchenko as 1980 (PDF 382), 1981 (PDF 381) and 1982 (PDF 374). | Change to "Levchenko's subjects were 'highly qualified sprinters'; the long jumpers' level is not stated." Add the 6c principle to Related, with one line on the new angle (this page adds force-time take-off data, stiffness and the injury statement). Add: "The book dates Levchenko 1980 here, 1981 at PDF 381 and 1982 at PDF 374." Checked otherwise: all quotes at PDF 382 / p.371; *cybernetic periodisation* italic; 6.2.2 quote at PDF 340 / p.329; baseline line 74. |
| heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block | GO | Duplicate check against 6c `heuristic--time-technique-and-competition-strength-work-to-the-ldte-window`. The entry names that overlap and adds a genuinely new angle: the learning-then-perfecting split, the daily "freshness" rule, and the specific low-intensity means (PDF 383). | Checked: italic "Although there is a primary emphasis..." (PDF 382); "too late were it to commence in the competitive period" (PDF 382); two stages and the means list (PDF 383 / p.372); Fig 6.32(a) image (block, dotted line, Learning/Perfecting, the STATE curve below zero then highest at right); 6.14.1 technique sentence (PDF 394); baseline line 101 (cosmetic: the quote ends with a doubled quotation mark). |
| heuristic--loading-reduction-for-the-delayed-effect-must-outlast-1-2-weeks | FIX | (1) The book's other figure is missing. Chapter 5 says gains after 4-8 week blocks "may occur most commonly after a latency period of 1-3 weeks" (PDF 305 / p.294). This page says the processes need "far longer than the 1-2 weeks usually allocated" (PDF 383). They measure different things (latency to the first gains versus time for the adaptive processes to finish), but the brief requires both figures to be recorded side by side. The 6c entry `heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next` already draws this latency-versus-duration distinction. (2) Partial duplicate: "do not fill it with more volume" is 6c `heuristic--time-technique...` rule 2 ("The volume of training work, therefore, should not be increased during the period of emergence of the LDTE," PDF 375), which is not linked. The new angle (critique of the usual 1-2 week unload, extra volume as a "barrier" to restoration) is real, so the entry stays. | Add to Why it works: "Chapter 5 gives a 1-3 week latency before gains appear (PDF 305 / p.294). That is the time to the first gains; this page is about how long the reduced-volume stage must last. They are recorded side by side, not as a contradiction." Add `[[heuristic--time-technique-and-competition-strength-work-to-the-ldte-window]]` to Related and name rule 2 as the same instruction. Checked otherwise: all quotes at PDF 383 / p.372; 4-12 weeks and the T2 duration at PDF 375; Bompa 3:1 link resolves. |
| framework--speed-sport-block-organisation-and-two-glycolytic-peaks | FIX | Fig 6.32(b) is misread. The entry says "most curves (Vmax, S-E, Speed, STATE, An-Gly) dip or stay low during it." At 450 dpi, two curves rise during the shaded block. One climbs steadily and ends at the S-E label. The other peaks mid-block and falls, then rises to a second hump, and ends at An-Gly; that shape matches the text's first glycolytic peak "timed to end near the conclusion" of the block (PDF 384). Two curves dip below the time axis during the block and then climb (ending at Vmax and STATE). One curve starts only at the block's end, rises steeply to a mid-panel peak and falls back (ending at Speed), which matches "Speed work begins only at the beginning of the LDTE." | Replace the figure paragraph with: "Fig 6.32(b), read from the image (no numeric scale): during the shaded block two curves fall below the time axis and then climb (ending at Vmax, highest, and STATE). Two rise: one steadily (ending at S-E) and one to a mid-block peak and back down, then to a second hump (ending at An-Gly), matching the text's two glycolytic peaks. One curve starts only at the block's end, peaks and then falls back (ending at Speed). The right-edge labels are the only certain curve identities; the middle crossings are hard to follow." Checked otherwise: all quotes at PDF 384 / p.373; caption at PDF 383; baseline lines 116 and 117 with tags. |
| framework--mesocycle-variants-smooth-rise-versus-concentrated-dip-and-rebound | GO | Optional: "Both variants sit in a chapter whose models all use concentrated loading, which Issurin 2016 questions." Variant A is the "traditional form" (PDF 385), so the Issurin challenge fits only Variant B. | Checked: italic mesocycle definition, "3 and 4 week stages", "4-6 weeks" (PDF 385 / p.374); Variant B points and the qualification rule (PDF 385-386); "usually 3-5 months" (PDF 387); Fig 6.33(a)-(c) image (A volume peaks mid-cycle and GPP peaks early and declines; B volume peaks early, fitness state sigmoid, shaded GPP grows across the cycle); baseline line 106. |
| claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation | FIX | The "Contested inside the book" paragraph treats aim 1 and the monocyclic recommendation as answers to the same question. They are not clearly the same. Aim 1 asks for "at least two large mesocycles... even in sports which traditionally have one main competitive period and use monocyclic periodisation" (PDF 389). So aim 1 itself separates the number of mesocycles from the number of competition peaks. The long-duration model at PDF 396 is "monocyclic... with one competitive stage" but also "within a monocycle... a two-stage organisation of strength and speed training." ## Missing (important ideas in PDF 379-403 that no entry captures)

1. **Table 6.11, javelin model characteristics (Konstantinov 1978, PDF 393 / p.382).** Strength and power norms for international-class throwers: snatch body mass + 15 kg (men) and + 10 kg (women), back squat 2 x and 1.5 x body mass, standing triple jump 10.20 and 7.80 m, vertical jump 95 and 70 cm, standing broad jump 3.20 and 2.80 m, plus throwing-volume norms (170 and 140 average-intensity throws, 35 and 30 above-average). This is the closest thing in the chapter to a power-athlete strength norm table.
2. **Tables 6.7 and 6.10, middle-distance models (Maximenko 1979, PDF 392-393).** They include flexibility (stride and straddle splits, in degrees) as model characteristics, and a defined special-endurance test: 2 x (4 x 400 m), 2 min between reps, 8-10 min between series.
3. **Table 6.12, juvenile sprinter norms by age 11-16 (Alabin & Yushkevitch 1978, PDF 393).** It has a source error worth recording: "Standing quintuple jump (cm)" with values of 9.25-13.70, which must be metres.
4. **The authors' own evidence caveat on microcycles (PDF 387).** "the currently scant experimental findings," and "large unidirectional loading sharply reduces the capability of displaying those qualities and abilities which facilitate the effective and safe execution of training programmes." This bears on the confidence of the microcycle case study.
5. **Long-duration timing (PDF 396).** Because low-intensity work predominates, "the optimal date for increasing the current adaptation reserves is deferred." This is the rationale for the long 6-month preparatory period, and the endurance entry omits it.

## Notes on the special-attention items

- **Fig 6.39 (6.14.1).** Phase boundaries and block positions in the entry hold up. Three curve-timing claims do not (see the FIX row): the strength curves start recovering inside block 1; the first peak is in phase II at about month 5; and Technique rises through most of block 2. For football planning, the image also shows that the model's strength indicators peak at the very end of phase IV (month 11). That fits Eric's November priority window (baseline line 185) better than an early-season peak would. This is my reading of the image, not a statement by the authors.
- **Contested entries and Issurin 2016.** The brief confirms the critique targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, not block periodisation in general, and none of the four entries overreaches to all block periodisation. The problems are elsewhere: the complex-training entry has the direction of disagreement wrong (Issurin shares the critique of complex training); the explosive-strength entry does not say that Issurin's p. 11 favours the model in its own domain; and the tri-cyclic entry, whose domain Issurin names, is not contested.
- **Bi-cyclic "same question".** Aim 1 (PDF 389) is about the number of large mesocycles and explicitly allows one main competitive period. The monocyclic recommendation (PDF 387, 396) is about the number of competition peaks. Only PDF 387's wording merges the two. Recommend recording it as a terminology tension, with `contested` resting on Issurin.
- **Tables 6.8 and 6.9, Fig 6.36(b).** Every value is correct. One flagged inconsistency was spurious (12 h rise then "diminished") and one was missed (5 m vs 15 m).
- **Fig 6.45/6.46 caption vs label.** Described correctly in both entries that mention it. The text supports the labels over the caption for Fig 6.45.

## Overall verdict

**GO AFTER FIXES.** Required fixes:
1. bi-cyclic explosive model: correct the Fig 6.39 curve timing (recovery inside block 1, first peak about month 5 in phase II, Technique rising through most of block 2, block 2 ending early in month 8) and scope the Issurin contest to the football transfer.
2. tricyclic: correct the boxing/swimming citation and make the confidence consistent with Issurin's combat-sport critique.
3. two-mesocycles: rewrite the internal-contest paragraph as a PDF 387 terminology tension; base `contested` on Issurin.
4. complex-training: Issurin agrees with the critique of complex training; the contest is the remedy and the beginners limit; add the brief's caveat on the 28 studies; separate Matveyev 1970.
5. speed-sport: correct the Fig 6.32(b) reading (S-E and An-Gly rise during the block).
6. unidirectional microcycles: drop the spurious 12 h "conflict"; the restoration time is 72 h in the text and about 30-36 h in the figure.
7. Tabachnik: add the 5 m vs 15 m inconsistency.
8. loading-reduction: record PDF 305's 1-3 week latency beside "far longer than 1-2 weeks"; link the 6c time-technique entry (rule 2).
9. Antonova/Levchenko: fix the self-contradictory sentence; link the 6c LDTE principle; note the Levchenko dates.
10. prolonged-competition: change "shorter" to "comparable."
11. follow-a-concentrated-block: note that the text supports the figure labels over the caption.

content.text:
**Verdict: GO AFTER FIXES.** Of the 25 entries, 14 are GO, 11 need fixes and none is NO-GO. Every quote, table value and baseline line I checked is correct; the fixes are about how figures were read and how the contested entries frame Issurin.

The report is at `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/staging/review_supertraining_ch6d_opus.md`.

**Required fixes:**
- **Explosive-strength annual model (Fig 6.39):** the phase boundaries and block positions are right, but three curve readings are wrong. The strength curves start rising again inside block 1. The first peak is about month 5, inside phase II. Technique rises through most of block 2 rather than falling. The Issurin challenge should be limited to transferring the model to football, because Issurin's p. 11 favours this kind of model in jumping-type sports.
- **Tri-cyclic model:** boxing and swimming are cited at PDF 387 as sports that could move away from tri-cyclic, not as examples of it. It is rated `supported` even though Issurin names combat sports, which are its own domain. That is inconsistent with the explosive-strength model being `contested`.
- **Two-mesocycles claim:** it is not the same question. Aim 1 (PDF 389) is about how many large mesocycles, and it explicitly allows one main competition period. The monocyclic advice (PDF 387, 396) is about how many competition peaks. Only the wording at PDF 387 merges the two. `contested` should rest on the Issurin disagreement over stage length and count.
- **Complex training:** Issurin agrees that complex training falls short for elite athletes; what he disputes is the remedy (one target versus a minimal number). The brief also has Issurin finding no evidence that amateurs can't handle concentrated loads, which cuts against the book's "complex for beginners" limit. The entry should add the brief's caveat that the 28 studies are Issurin's own non-systematic selection, and cite Matveyev 1970 separately.
- **Speed sports (Fig 6.32b):** two curves (strength-endurance and anaerobic-glycolytic) rise during the block. The entry says they dip.
- **Swimming microcycles:** drop the flagged conflict about aerobic potential rising for 12 h and then falling, because the figure shows exactly that. Restoration is 72 h in the text but about 30-36 h in the figure, and the entry should give both.
- **Tabachnik sprint tables:** every value matches. The writer's three flagged split sums are correct, but one inconsistency was missed: the men's 5 m from a low start (1.18 s) equals the 15 m time (1.16-1.18 s) for the same 10.0 s goal.
- **Loading reduction after a block:** record the Chapter 5 figure of a 1-3 week wait before gains (PDF 305) next to "far longer than 1-2 weeks", and link the 6c entry with the same no-added-volume rule.
- **Antonova/Levchenko:** one sentence calls both groups qualified and then says the long jumpers' level isn't stated. Link the 6c delayed-effect entry that cites the same studies, and note the book dates Levchenko as 1980, 1981 and 1982.
- **Long competition period:** change "a football season is shorter than 4-5 months" to "comparable".
- **Concentrated block then moderate explosive work:** the book's own text (strength block after the GPP groundwork) supports the figure labels, so the Fig 6.45 caption is the likelier error.

**What held up:**
- **Issurin critique:** the vault brief confirms it is aimed at Verkhoshansky's concentrated single-emphasis model. None of the four `contested` entries stretches it to all block periodisation.
- **Fig 6.45/6.46 caption vs labels:** the mismatch is described correctly.
- **Duplicates:** both 6d heuristics that overlap the 6c delayed-effect entries add a genuinely new angle.
- **Five ideas no entry captures** are listed in the report. They include the Table 6.11 javelin strength norms and a unit error in Table 6.12 (values labelled "cm" are clearly metres).

**Method:** I checked every quote against the text layer. I opened 14 page images myself, including Tables 6.8-6.12, and read Fig 6.39 at 300 dpi plus enlarged crops. The remaining pages carry no figure values the entries depend on, and I checked them by text and an italics scan only; the report says so.
